## Nashville hot wings (style)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/style/nashville-hot/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/style/nashville-hot.json
id: nashville-hot
aliases: hot chicken wings · hot wings, Nashville style
said: The heat levels are the menu: plain, mild, medium, hot, and whatever the house calls the one above that.
facets: state=TN · cut=party wing · base=other · cooked=fried · heat=very hot
region: Nashville, The American South, The United States
what: Hot chicken's method put on a wing: marinate in a water- or buttermilk-based seasoned blend, flour, fry, then paint with a cayenne paste loosened with fat drawn from the fryer. The paste stains the crust deep red and goes on with a spoon and gloved hands, then gets squeezed in. It lands on white bread with pickle chips — the bread catching the grease, the pickles cutting it — and the bread is part of the dish, not a napkin. Heat runs in named steps and the top step is genuinely punishing.
story: Anecdotal evidence puts spicy fried chicken in Nashville's African American communities for generations, perhaps from the 1930s, while the current style of spice paste may date only to the mid-1970s. The origin generally accepted belongs to the family of André Prince Jeffries, who has run Prince's Hot Chicken Shack since 1980; before that it was her great-uncle Thornton Prince's.

The story she tells is an accident. Thornton was, by the family's account, a womanizer; after a late Saturday night his girlfriend cooked him a fried chicken breakfast loaded with pepper as revenge. He liked it, and by the mid-1930s he and his brothers had a recipe and a café, the BBQ Chicken Shack. Wikipedia's article on the restaurant notes the story is impossible to verify.

The café started at 28th and Jefferson, moved downtown into Hell's Half Acre near the Ryman Auditorium, and drew Opry stars after performances — under segregation, with a separate room built at the back for white guests, reached by walking through the main dining room and the kitchen. Thornton's brother Will took over when he died, Will's wife Maude ran it after him, and in 1980 Maude decided the business should go to Thornton's great-niece, who dropped the BBQ from the name. The shop moved to Ewing Drive in East Nashville in 1988. In December 2018 a Ford Explorer crashed into the Ewing Drive strip mall and set it on fire; the restaurant itself was undamaged, but building damage and landlord delays turned a two-week closure into a permanent one seven months later.

*Inference —* the wing is a later cut than the dish. Hot chicken is a breast, thigh or wing quarter in its standard description, and the wing-only plate reads as the method following the market for wings rather than the other way round.

The method left town fast. Bill Purcell, Nashville's former mayor, sponsored the Music City Hot Chicken Festival and called his table at Prince's his "second office". By 2015 about two dozen Nashville restaurants served it. KFC put Nashville Hot Chicken and Nashville Hot Tenders on U.S. menus in January 2016 after a Pittsburgh trial it called the most successful product testing in its recent history, and ran it in the UK from 22 May to 18 June 2017. Buffalo Wild Wings sells a Nashville-hot-style wing. Prince's was named an American Classic by the James Beard Foundation in 2013.
how: Marinate the wings — nearly all hot chicken goes into buttermilk, for flavour and to keep the meat from drying in the oil. Flour them. Fry, in a pan at most houses rather than a deep fryer, though pressure fryers and deep fryers both get used. Make the paste: cayenne first, sometimes sugar, garlic or extra hot sauce, loosened with fat lifted out of the frying oil so it goes on hot and clings. Traditional order is paste after the fryer; some kitchens paste before breading and fry again. Spoon it on, squeeze it in. Serve on white bread with pickles. Recipes and heat steps are house secrets and are not published.
today: Hot chicken restaurants run in Atlanta, New York, Philadelphia, Chicago, Los Angeles, Birmingham, Louisville, Ann Arbor, Columbus, Salt Lake City and Seattle, and abroad in Calgary, Seoul and Melbourne. Chains built on the style include Hattie B's, Dave's Hot Chicken, Howlin' Ray's, Angry Chickz, Joella's and World Famous Hotboys. Hattie B's, founded by a father and son both named Nick Bishop, opened in Midtown Nashville on 9 August 2012, uses ghost peppers in its hottest step, and opened its first Midwestern location in Chicago's Wrigleyville in 2026.
- kin → nashville-hot-oil (sauce): The cayenne paste loosened with frying fat — the single step that makes a fried wing a Nashville one.
- kin → princes-hot-chicken-shack (place): Where the method is generally agreed to have started, run by the Prince family since the 1930s.
- kin → thornton-prince (person): The man the revenge-breakfast story is told about, and whose brothers built the first recipe.
- kin → andre-prince-jeffries (person): Took the shop over in 1980, dropped the BBQ from its name, and kept the recipe unpublished.
- kin → hattie-bs (place): Opened in 2012 and carried the style to nine cities, with ghost peppers at the top of the heat ladder.
- kin → boltons-spicy-chicken-and-fish (place): Another Nashville house on the same method, hot fish included.
- kin → white-bread-and-pickles (dish): Under the wings and on top of them — the plate is not finished without both.
- kin → brine (fry): The buttermilk soak nearly every hot chicken kitchen starts from.
- kin → dredge (fry): The flour coat the paste stains red; without it there is nothing for the paste to grip.
- kin → buffalo (style): The other cayenne wing: that one is tossed in a butter-and-vinegar sauce, this one is painted with a fat-borne paste and served on bread.
- kin → atomic (term): What the top heat step gets called, here and everywhere else that sells one.
- not to be confused with buffalo: Look at the plate. A Nashville wing sits on white bread with pickles and its crust is stained red under a paste; a Buffalo wing sits bare in a basket with celery and a cup of blue cheese, its sauce loose and orange.
- not to be confused with nashville-hot-oil: One is the style, one is the paste. A Buffalo Wild Wings 'Nashville hot' wing uses the flavour without the bread, the pickles or the pan fry.
sources: s:wp-hot-chicken — Hot chicken; s:wp-prince-s-hot-chicken-shack — Prince's Hot Chicken Shack; s:wp-hattie-b-s-hot-chicken — Hattie B's Hot Chicken; s:wp-buffalo-wing — Buffalo wing; s:this-project — Wing Country — this project's own reasoning
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## Old Bay wings (style)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/style/baltimore-old-bay/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/style/baltimore-old-bay.json
id: baltimore-old-bay
aliases: Chesapeake wings · crab-spiced wings · crab seasoning wings
said: Say Old Bay in Maryland and nobody asks which brand. The yellow can is the noun.
facets: state=MD · cut=party wing · base=dry-rub · cooked=fried · heat=mild
region: Baltimore, The United States
what: A wing finished in Old Bay — a blend of eighteen herbs and spices built in Baltimore in 1939, celery salt first, with red and black pepper and paprika, and bay leaves, mustard, cardamom, cloves and ginger among the rest. It goes on dry out of the fryer, or in butter as a wet toss, and it is the same can that goes on steamed blue crab, on fries, on popcorn and around the rim of a beer glass. Salt and celery seed do the work, not heat; a customer who wants heat adds hot sauce on top.
story: The seasoning has a documented history and the wing does not.

Gustav Brunn built a wholesale spice business in Wertheim, Germany, moved it to Frankfurt, and was arrested after Kristallnacht and sent to Buchenwald. His wife paid a lawyer a large sum for his release; the family already held American visas and escaped to New York and then Baltimore, where Brunn had relatives. He arrived with a small spice grinder, founded the Baltimore Spice Company in 1939, and made "Delicious Brand Shrimp and Crab Seasoning", later renamed Old Bay after the Baltimore Steam Packet Company — the Old Bay Line — which ran passenger ships from Baltimore to Norfolk in the early 1900s. McCormick & Company of Hunt Valley bought the brand in 1990.

*Tradition holds —* the wing came later and came sideways, the way everything else in the Chesapeake got seasoned: the can was already on the counter. Wikipedia lists chicken wings among the things Old Bay is put on, alongside fried chicken, french fries, tater tots, corn, boiled peanuts, potato salad and guacamole, and notes that several movie theatres in the region keep it in the condiment section. This project found no source naming a first restaurant, a cook or a year for the wing itself, and none is asserted here.

The can's reach is easier to date than the wing's. Utz of Hanover, Pennsylvania built its Crab Chip on a similar blend; Herr's uses Old Bay itself; Lay's introduced Chesapeake Bay Crab Spice chips in 2018. Flying Dog brewed an Old Bay summer ale, Dead Rise, for the seasoning's 75th anniversary in 2014. McCormick released Old Bay Hot Sauce ahead of Super Bowl LIV in 2020; it sold out within thirty minutes, crashed the website, and $3.49 bottles resold online for between $50 and $200. Old Bay Goldfish crackers followed in 2022 and sold out online in nine hours. The can went from metal to plastic in 2017, and in December 2025 McCormick announced a return to metal.
how: Fry the wing bare so the skin is dry enough to hold powder, then shake it in Old Bay while it is still hot. Wet version: toss in melted butter first, then the seasoning, which gives a paste rather than a dust. Some kitchens mix Old Bay into the dredge as well as onto the finished wing; some steam or bake instead of frying, because the seasoning does not need a crust to read. Serve with whatever the bar pours — this is a seasoning, not a sauce, so blue cheese, ranch and vinegar all sit comfortably beside it.
today: Old Bay wings run on Maryland and Virginia bar menus, through the wider Mid-Atlantic, and into New England and the Gulf Coast where the can already travelled. McCormick sells an Old Bay hot sauce and several blend variants — with garlic, with lemon, with brown sugar — that put the same flavour on a wing by a different route. *Inference —* the style spreads with the can rather than with a recipe, which is why it has no founding restaurant to point at.
- kin → old-bay (sauce): The blend the whole style is — celery salt, red and black pepper, paprika and fifteen more, built in Baltimore in 1939.
- kin → memphis-dry-rub (style): The other American wing finished dry, though that rub comes off a smoker and this one comes off a crab pot.
- kin → atlanta-lemon-pepper (style): Another city's seasoning wing, with citrus where this has celery seed.
- kin → wet-and-dry (term): The pair of words that decide whether the seasoning goes on bare or through butter.
- kin → naked-fry (fry): What the wing has to be for a dry seasoning to stick — no batter to hide under.
- kin → french-fries (dish): Take the same can, at the same bar, in the same basket.
- kin → chickie-and-petes (place): Built a business on a seasoned fry in the next state up, on the same Mid-Atlantic taste for spiced potatoes.
- kin → buffalo (style): The style that made a wing a sauced thing; Old Bay answers with a wing that is seasoned and not sauced at all.
- kin → hot-sauce-labels (art): The yellow can is doing the same work a hot sauce label does — a regional identity you can hold.
- not to be confused with memphis-dry-rub: Look for celery salt and paprika without smoke. Old Bay is salty and celery-forward off a fryer; a Memphis rub carries smoke and comes off a pit.
- not to be confused with atlanta-lemon-pepper: Citrus. Lemon pepper leads with zest; Old Bay leads with celery seed and salt, and there is no lemon in the can.
- image: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/images/baltimore-old-bay/baltimore-old-bay-old-bay-seasoning.jpg · CC0 1.0 · L1veb4y0udi3 · https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3AOld_Bay_Seasoning.jpg
sources: s:wp-old-bay-seasoning — Old Bay Seasoning; s:wp-buffalo-wing — Buffalo wing; s:this-project — Wing Country — this project's own reasoning
provenance default: cited · confidence: medium · needs_verification: True · updated: 2026-09-16

## Rochester breaded wings (style)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/style/rochester-breaded/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/style/rochester-breaded.json
id: rochester-breaded
aliases: Rochester-style wings · breaded wings · Country Sweet wings
said: Order in Rochester and the counter asks which sauce, not how hot. Country Sweet is a sauce, a brand and an answer.
facets: state=NY · cut=party wing · base=sweet-tomato · cooked=fried · heat=medium
region: Rochester, Upstate New York, The United States
what: A chicken wing dredged in seasoned flour before it goes in the oil, fried until the coating sets hard, then glazed rather than tossed loose — most often in Country Sweet, a sweet-and-tangy sauce a Rochester kitchen built in 1977 that is neither barbecue nor cayenne-and-butter. Breading is the whole argument: seventy miles west, Buffalo puts the wing in the fryer bare. Rochester bars also pour plain cayenne sauce, barbecue, teriyaki and garlic parmesan, so a breaded wing is a coating rather than a single flavour.
story: Country Sweet dates itself to 1977, when Tom Lask worked up a sauce in a Rochester home kitchen; the company's own account calls it neither barbecue nor Buffalo. It sells the sauce in mild, hot and BBQ, and sells the wings hand-breaded. That is the firmest dated fact this project could find for the style.

Everything around it is thin. No published history of Rochester's breaded wing turned up in the sources searched here — no founder, no first bar, no year. The city's documented food identity runs elsewhere: the Garbage Plate, trademarked by Nick Tahou Hots and traced to 1918, and the Zweigle's white hot. Wings sit underneath that, carried by menus rather than by writing about menus.

*Tradition holds —* a half-and-half order comes half in the sweet sauce and half in hot, and a 'hot plate' means the wings and the sides under one pour. This project found no published source describing either, so both stay unverified here.

The rivalry gets stated in print even where the history does not. CITY Magazine, naming Jeremiah's Tavern the city's best wings, wrote: "It's easy to find really good wings on damn near every corner in Buffalo. Around here? A little more challenging."
how: Dredge the cut wing in seasoned flour — some shops dip in buttermilk or egg first, some go dry — and drop it in the oil. The coating browns into a shell that holds sauce on its surface instead of soaking it in, which is why a sweet glaze works here and slides off a bare Buffalo wing. Fry, then glaze: Country Sweet goes on as a sticky coat rather than a loose toss in a bowl. Blue cheese and celery come alongside, same as west of here. A tavern that fries bare will say so on the board; breaded and naked both sell in this city.
today: Country Sweet runs shops in Rochester and Greece and bottles the sauce for grocery shelves. Bar menus carry long sauce lists beside the house breading: Jeremiah's Tavern, read on 16 September 2026, offered sixteen sauces including Garlic Parm, Cajun Dry Rub, Jamaican Jerk and Korean BBQ, with ten traditional wings at $17.99 and twelve boneless at $16.00. *Inference —* the breading, not the sauce, is what makes the plate legible as Rochester's; the sauce list is the same list every American wing counter now prints.
- kin → buffalo (style): Seventy miles west, frying the same cut bare — the style this one is defined against, and the argument that gives it a name.
- kin → country-sweet-chicken-and-ribs (place): Dates the sauce to a Rochester home kitchen in 1977 and hand-breads the wings it goes on.
- kin → jeremiahs-tavern (place): Named the city's best wings by CITY Magazine, and prints sixteen sauces beside them.
- kin → breaded-fry (fry): The coating that separates this style from Buffalo's, and the reason a sweet glaze sticks.
- kin → dredge (fry): The flour step Buffalo skips.
- kin → garbage-plate (dish): Rochester's documented dish, trademarked and dated to 1918, where this style has no such paper trail.
- kin → blue-cheese-dressing (sauce): Comes with the wings here too; the city argues about breading, not about the dip.
- kin → extra-crispy (term): What a breaded wing is already, before anyone asks for it.
- kin → the-origin-fight (story): Buffalo's origin is contested in public; Rochester's is simply unwritten.
- not to be confused with buffalo: Bite the skin. A breaded wing has a flour shell that crunches and stays dry under the sauce; a Buffalo wing has bare skin and the sauce is on it, not in a crust.
- not to be confused with garlic-parm: Garlic parm names a sauce and travels anywhere. Rochester-style names a coating, and the sauce on top can be anything the bar pours.
sources: s:web-countrysweet — Country Sweet Chicken & Ribs; s:web-roccitymag-jeremiahs — Best Wings: Jeremiah's Tavern; s:web-jeremiahs-menu — Menu; s:wp-buffalo-wing — Buffalo wing; s:wp-garbage-plate — Garbage Plate; s:wp-rochester-new-york — Rochester, New York; s:this-project — Wing Country — this project's own reasoning
provenance default: cited · confidence: medium · needs_verification: True · updated: 2026-09-16

## Smoked barbecue wings (style)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/style/smoked-bbq-wing/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/style/smoked-bbq-wing.json
id: smoked-bbq-wing
aliases: barbecue wings · smoked wings · pit wings
said: A pit sells wings the way it sells everything else — by the pound, off the same fire, at the same window.
facets: cut=party wing · base=sweet-tomato · cooked=smoked · heat=mild
region: Texas, Kansas City, Memphis, The American South, The United States
what: A wing cooked on a barbecue pit rather than in oil: rubbed, smoked over wood until the fat renders, then finished — brushed with a tomato sauce and set over higher heat to tack up, or dropped briefly in the fryer so the skin crisps. Regional sauce follows regional pit. Kansas City runs thick tomato sauces; Memphis runs the dry-and-wet split; Texas leans on the rub and the wood. The wing is a side item on those menus, cooked with the ribs and the shoulder and sold beside them.
story: American barbecue's regional map is old and well drawn, and the wing arrived on it late. The pits and their dates are documented — Charlie Vergos' Rendezvous in Memphis from 1948, Interstate Bar-B-Que from 1978, Neely's from 1988, Central BBQ from 2002 — and the chicken sits on those menus beside beef and pork. Central BBQ's smoked chicken wings are named in the record of Memphis barbecue, which is one of the few places a smoked wing gets recorded as a menu item at all.

Kansas City is the thick-tomato pole; Gates Bar-B-Q is noted for a spicier version built on cumin and celery salt. Texas splits four ways: East Texas by way of the Southern tradition, Central Texas out of German and Czech butcher shops, West Texas over mesquite with goat and mutton, South Texas barbacoa from a cow's head. Alabama's contribution is the pale sauce: chicken smoked in the pit and then coated or dunked in Bob Gibson's white sauce.

*Inference —* the smoked wing is the pit's answer to the sports-bar wing, not an older tradition with its own history. This project found no source dating a first barbecue-joint wing or naming the pit that started it, and none is asserted.

*Tradition holds —* the finishing step exists because smoke alone leaves wing skin slack, and a pit that wants a wing to eat like a wing puts heat on it at the end.
how: Rub the wings and hold them. Smoke at low heat over wood — hickory through the South, oak and mesquite in Texas — until the fat has rendered and the meat pulls. Then make a decision: brush with sauce and put the wings back over direct heat until the sugar tacks and darkens, or drop them in hot oil for a minute to tighten the skin and sauce them after. Sauce goes on at the end either way, because a tomato sauce with sugar in it burns over a long cook. A dry finish — rub again, no sauce — makes it a Memphis dry wing instead.
today: Barbecue restaurants ship, franchise and appear on television, and the smoked wing travels with them. Home smokers and pellet grills put the method in back yards, where it competes with the fryer and the air fryer for the same bird. *Inference —* what a pit sells as a wing is a cheaper cut of the same labour: hours of wood for a piece that a fryer turns out in ten minutes.
- kin → smoke-then-fry (fry): The finishing move that fixes slack skin, and the one step that makes a smoked wing eat like a fried one.
- kin → honey-bbq-sauce (sauce): The sweet tomato sauce that goes on at the end, once the long cook is over and the sugar can no longer burn.
- kin → memphis-dry-rub (style): The same pit finishing dry instead of sauced; the fork in the road is whether anything gets brushed on.
- kin → alabama-white (style): The same pit finishing pale — smoked and then dunked in a mayonnaise-and-vinegar sauce.
- kin → central-bbq (place): A Memphis pit from 2002 whose smoked wings are named in the record of the style.
- kin → big-bob-gibson-bar-b-q (place): The Alabama pit that smokes chicken and then dunks it, on the same logic.
- kin → memphis-rub (sauce): What goes on before the wood, and again at the end if the wing is going out dry.
- kin → the-toss (fry): The bar's method, which this style replaces with a brush and a second pass over the fire.
- kin → grill (fry): Direct heat, used here at the end rather than throughout.
- kin → par-cook (fry): What a long smoke amounts to when a fryer finishes the job.
- kin → buffalo (style): The fried wing this style answers at the same bar, with hours of wood behind it instead of ten minutes of oil.
- not to be confused with memphis-dry-rub: Whether sauce was brushed on. Both come off the same pit; one goes out red and sticky, the other goes out dusted and dry.
- not to be confused with caribbean-jerk: When the seasoning went on. Jerk marinates before the fire and finishes charred; a barbecue wing is rubbed, smoked plain, then sauced at the end.
- not to be confused with honey-bbq-sauce: One is the cook, one is the bottle. A fried wing tossed in barbecue sauce is not a smoked wing, and most wings sold as 'BBQ' never saw wood.
sources: s:wp-barbecue-in-the-united-states — Barbecue in the United States; s:wp-memphis-style-barbecue — Memphis-style barbecue; s:wp-barbecue-in-alabama — Barbecue in Alabama; s:this-project — Wing Country — this project's own reasoning
provenance default: cited · confidence: medium · needs_verification: True · updated: 2026-09-16

## Alabama white sauce (sauce)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/sauce/alabama-white-sauce/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/sauce/alabama-white-sauce.json
id: alabama-white-sauce
aliases: white barbecue sauce · white sauce
said: A tub of it goes on the table in north Alabama the way a red sauce does everywhere else.
facets: base=dairy · heat=mild
region: The American South, The United States
what: A mayonnaise-based barbecue sauce, thin, pale and sharp. Typical ingredients are vinegar, lemon juice, salt, pepper, cayenne pepper and horseradish stirred into mayonnaise. It goes on barbecue chicken, which is an Alabama speciality, and on wings — dunked whole rather than brushed.
story: White sauce was invented in Decatur, Alabama in 1925. It is believed to have been made by Bob Gibson at Big Bob Gibson Bar-B-Q there.

Alabama barbecue centres on pork cooked in open pits over hickory, with oak and pecan also used. A vinegar-based sauce like North Carolina's is common in the north of the state; a tomato-based one is usual south of Birmingham. White sauce stayed a north Alabama thing until 1994, when it began to be bottled and sold commercially.

Barbecue became popular in Alabama in the early 19th century, with roots in Native American cooking. Local militias held barbecues to get members to turn up for yearly drills, and they served as political and civic gatherings; by the late 1820s some social reformers opposed them, arguing they encouraged "political debasement" or that the alcohol and merrymaking were a moral problem. They failed. The first barbecue restaurants opened in the 1890s; the oldest continuously operating one in the state is Golden Rule Bar-B-Q, founded in 1891. In 2015 the Alabama Department of Tourism ran "The Year of Alabama Barbecue".
how: Dunk, do not brush. A whole smoked or fried chicken goes into the tub and comes out coated; wings go in by the basket. Mayonnaise splits over direct heat, so the sauce meets the bird after the fire, not during. It doubles as a dressing for the slaw beside it.
today: Bottled since 1994 and now sold nationally by several Alabama makers. As of 16 September 2026 the USDA label panel for Saw's Alabama White Sauce reads 300 mg sodium, 1 g sugar and 17 g fat in a 2-tablespoon serving — 150 mg and 0.5 g in one tablespoon, with soybean oil first and two vinegars on the list. Big Bob Gibson's own bottle returns no record in FoodData Central, so its panel is not on this disk. Nobody publishes a Scoville number.
- kin → alabama-white (style): The style is this tub and the chicken that goes into it.
- kin → big-bob-gibson-bar-b-q (place): Decatur, 1925, and the invention claim the sauce carries.
- kin → bob-gibson (person): Credited with making it, at his own pit.
- kin → ranch-dressing (sauce): The other white dip on a wing plate; both start from an oil-and-egg emulsion, this one takes horseradish and vinegar instead of buttermilk and herbs.
- kin → blue-cheese-dressing (sauce): Shares the dairy shelf and the wing plate, and takes its sharpness from vinegar rather than cheese.
- kin → smoke-then-fry (fry): The cooking this sauce meets at the end, never during — mayonnaise splits over fire.
- kin → smoked-bbq-wing (style): The wing most often dunked in it.
- kin → honey-bbq-sauce (sauce): The red barbecue sauce this one is the local answer to.
- not to be confused with ranch-dressing: Sharpness and use. White sauce is vinegar-and-horseradish thin and gets dunked in; ranch is herb-and-buttermilk and sits in a cup.
sources: s:wp-barbecue-in-alabama — Barbecue in Alabama; s:fdc-saws-alabama-white-sauce — Saw's Alabama White Sauce — branded food label (FDC ID 1955770); s:harland-1906 — Marion Harland's Complete Cook Book: A Practical and Exhaustive Manual of Cookery and Housekeeping
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## Blue cheese dressing (sauce)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/sauce/blue-cheese-dressing/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/sauce/blue-cheese-dressing.json
id: blue-cheese-dressing
aliases: bleu cheese · blue cheese · chunky blue
said: In Buffalo it arrives without being ordered. Asking for ranch instead is noticed.
facets: base=dairy · heat=none
region: Western New York, The United States
what: A thick white dip of blue cheese with mayonnaise and buttermilk, sour cream or yogurt, plus milk, vinegar, onion powder and garlic powder. A vinaigrette version exists — salad oil, blue cheese, vinegar and seasonings — and is not what comes with wings. Sold by most major dressing makers in the United States and Canada, and served as the dip beside Buffalo wings and raw vegetables.
story: It reached the wing on the first night, if the Anchor Bar's account holds: Teressa Bellissimo sent the wings out with celery and blue cheese taken off the bar's antipasto tray. Whether that was 1964 is one of the arguments the origin carries.

What is not argued is which dip Buffalo uses. The standard description of a Buffalo wing gives blue cheese or ranch; the same source records that ranch is the most popular wing dip in the United States. Buffalo's own bars serve blue cheese.

The dip has a chemistry problem the argument ignores. Water and oil separate in it — an unstable emulsion — and salad dressings spoil through organisms like Saccharomyces bailii and Lactobacillus fructivorans, the latter an acid-tolerant facultative anaerobe that survives the low pH a blue cheese dressing sits at.

*Inference —* the chunks are the point. A smooth blue cheese dressing and a chunky one taste alike on a spoon and do not behave alike on a wing, because the chunks survive the dip and the smooth part does not.
how: Cold, in a cup, beside the wing — never poured over it. A wing goes in, comes out with a load of cheese, and the celery goes in after to clear the palate. Home versions whisk mayonnaise, buttermilk and sour cream with lemon juice or vinegar and fold blue cheese in at the end, cubed rather than crumbled so some of it stays in pieces.
today: On every wing plate in western New York and in the dip section of every wing chain. As of 16 September 2026 the USDA label panel for Ken's Steak House Chunky Blue Cheese Dressing reads 290 mg sodium, 13 g fat and 1 g sugar in a 2-tablespoon serving — 145 mg and 0.5 g in one tablespoon. Soybean oil is first; blue cheese is fourth, behind water and vinegar.
- kin → buffalo (style): The dip the style serves, and the one a medium order arrives with unasked.
- kin → ranch-dressing (sauce): The rival in the cup, and the best-selling dressing in America since 1992.
- kin → celery-and-carrots (dish): Shares the plate and does the same job from the other direction.
- kin → teressa-bellissimo (person): Took it off the antipasto tray on the night the Anchor Bar dates the wing to.
- kin → anchor-bar (place): Where the antipasto tray was, in the account the bar tells.
- kin → ranch-vs-blue-cheese (story): The long-running argument this dip is one side of.
- kin → buffalo-sauce (sauce): What it is there to cut; the fat in it takes the cayenne off the tongue.
- kin → sauce-on-the-side (fry): The cup is the same idea applied to the dip rather than the sauce.
- kin → alabama-white-sauce (sauce): The other white sauce on a wing, built to be dunked in rather than dipped from a cup.
- not to be confused with ranch-dressing: Cheese against herbs. Blue cheese dressing has visible blue cheese in it; ranch has buttermilk, garlic, onion, chives, parsley and dill.
- image: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/images/blue-cheese-dressing/blue-cheese-dressing-blue-cheese-dressing.jpg · CC BY 2.0 · jules · https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3ABlue_cheese_dressing.jpg
- image: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/images/blue-cheese-dressing/blue-cheese-dressing-hopmonk-march-2026-sarah-stierch-03.jpg · CC0 1.0 · Missvain · https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3AHopmonk_-_March_2026_-_Sarah_Stierch_03.jpg

## Buffalo sauce (sauce)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/sauce/buffalo-sauce/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/sauce/buffalo-sauce.json
id: buffalo-sauce
aliases: wing sauce · hot sauce and butter · medium
said: Nobody in a Buffalo kitchen calls it Buffalo sauce. It is the sauce, and you order it by heat: mild, medium, hot.
facets: base=cayenne-butter · heat=medium · styles=buffalo
region: Western New York, The United States
what: Cayenne pepper hot sauce cut with melted butter. Two things, warmed together and held warm, poured over fried wings in a metal bowl and shaken. More butter reads mild, less reads hot, and a kitchen moves between the three by changing that ratio rather than the pepper. Worcestershire sauce and garlic powder turn up in plenty of versions. Bottled ready-to-use wing sauce does the same job with oil and butter flavouring in place of butter, because butter separates on a shelf.
story: Cayenne pepper sauce arrived in Buffalo in a bottle. Frank's RedHot came out of Cincinnati and a Louisiana pepper farm in 1920; Crystal came out of New Orleans in 1923. Neither was made for wings.

The sauce got its name in 1964, or later, depending on whose account you take. At the Anchor Bar, Teressa Bellissimo fried wings and tossed them in cayenne sauce; the Bellissimo family told three different versions of that night, and Dominic Bellissimo gave Calvin Trillin one of them in 1980. John Young was selling breaded whole wings in a tomato-based mumbo sauce in Buffalo from 1961, and said the Anchor Bar did not carry wings as a regular menu item until 1974.

*Inference —* the butter is the part that travelled least well. A wing tossed at the counter gets butter; a wing that has to survive a shelf, a delivery bag or a factory gets oil and a butter flavouring. Frank's RedHot Buffalo Wings Sauce lists canola oil fifth and natural butter type flavour eighth, with no butter on the label.

Wikipedia's article on the wing notes that Frank's RedHot "was probably not the hot sauce that was used in the original 1964 Anchor Bar recipe." Nobody has produced the bottle.
how: Melt butter. Stir in cayenne pepper sauce off the heat and keep the mix warm, not hot, so it does not split. Fry the wings, drain them a moment, drop them in a bowl, pour the sauce over and shake — sauce after the fryer, never before, or the coating steams instead of sticking. Ratio sets the heat: roughly equal parts reads mild, more sauce than butter reads hot. Add Worcestershire sauce, garlic powder or a little vinegar if the house does.
today: Sold bottled by every large sauce maker and by most bars as house-made. The bottled kind states its heat on the front; the house kind states it at the counter. Nobody publishes a Scoville figure — the capsaicin measure named for the chemist Wilbur Scoville — for a finished Buffalo sauce, because the butter ratio changes it batch to batch. As of 16 September 2026, the USDA label panel for Frank's RedHot Buffalo Wings Sauce reads 460 mg sodium and no sugar in a tablespoon.
- kin → buffalo (style): The whole of what makes a wing Buffalo, and the only sauce that style names.
- kin → franks-redhot (sauce): The cayenne bottle most recipes start from, and the one Buffalo bars buy by the gallon.
- kin → crystal-hot-sauce (sauce): The other cayenne bottle a kitchen may start from; thinner vinegar, darker pepper.
- kin → the-toss (fry): Where this sauce meets the wing: a metal bowl, a pour, a shake.
- kin → blue-cheese-dressing (sauce): Sits beside it in a cup and is the whole point of the cup.
- kin → anchor-bar (place): Says a bowl of it was mixed here on 4 March 1964.
- kin → teressa-bellissimo (person): Tossed the wings in cayenne sauce the Anchor Bar version turns on.
- kin → mumbo-sauce (sauce): What John Young put on his Buffalo wings instead, three years earlier — tomato, not cayenne and butter.
- kin → naked-fry (fry): Needs bare skin to cling to; breading soaks it up instead.
- kin → buffalo-word (term): How this sauce lent a city's name to every spiced fried thing on a national menu.
- not to be confused with franks-redhot: Butter. Frank's RedHot is one ingredient; Buffalo sauce is that bottle plus melted butter.
- not to be confused with mumbo-sauce: Colour and base. Buffalo sauce is orange and vinegar-forward; mumbo is red-brown and starts with ketchup.
