## Crystal Hot Sauce (sauce)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/sauce/crystal-hot-sauce/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/sauce/crystal-hot-sauce.json
id: crystal-hot-sauce
aliases: Crystal · Crystal Louisiana's Pure Hot Sauce
facets: base=vinegar-pepper · heat=mild · styles=buffalo
region: New Orleans, The United States
what: A reddish-orange Louisiana pepper sauce made by Baumer Foods since 1923: aged red cayenne peppers, distilled vinegar, salt. Three ingredients on the 6 fl oz bottle; the gallon jug adds xanthan gum. Writers put it against Tabasco as having "a more prominent dark chile flavor, and a slightly subdued vinegar profile". Buffalo kitchens that do not buy Frank's usually buy this.
story: Baumer Foods started in New Orleans and stayed a family business. Its factory on Tulane Avenue in Mid-City carried a lighted sign — a chef stirring a pot, steam from the plant venting out through the pot — visible from Interstate 10 and known across the city. The preserves the sign advertised went into US military rations in the Second World War and are no longer made.

Hurricane Katrina wrecked much of the New Orleans plant in 2005, sign included. The company moved production up the Mississippi to Reserve, in St. John the Baptist Parish; the sign was replicated and set on top of a new apartment building on the old factory site. As of April 2021 the head office sits in Metairie.

Three million US gallons a year ship to seventy-five countries. The brand is popular in Saudi Arabia, carried there by Louisiana petroleum workers. David Chang has said Crystal is his favourite hot sauce, and Ed Currie, who bred the Carolina Reaper, called it "probably the best tasting of the table sauces."
how: Same job as any cayenne bottle: melt butter, stir the sauce in warm, toss fried wings in it. *Tradition holds —* cooks who choose Crystal over Frank's say it needs a touch less butter, because the vinegar sits further back. It is also the pepper sauce that goes into a Nashville paste, into gumbo and onto eggs.
today: Made in Reserve, Louisiana; head office in Metairie. As of 16 September 2026 the USDA label panel for the 6 fl oz bottle reads 135 mg sodium in a 1 teaspoon serving — 405 mg in a tablespoon — with no sugar. Baumer publishes no Scoville number, which is the usual case: almost no wing-sauce maker does.
- kin → buffalo-sauce (sauce): One of the two cayenne bottles it gets built from.
- kin → franks-redhot (sauce): The rival bottle, and the one the standard Buffalo account names.
- kin → buffalo (style): Named in the style's sauce recipe as the alternative to Frank's.
- kin → nashville-hot-oil (sauce): A slug of Louisiana pepper sauce is one of the things a hot-chicken paste gets built on.
- kin → hot-sauce-labels (art): Its chef-and-steaming-pot sign became a New Orleans landmark before it was a label.
- kin → jerk-marinade (sauce): Both lean on a fermented or aged chile rather than a fresh one, and both run thin.
- not to be confused with franks-redhot: The label. Frank's lists garlic powder; Crystal's small bottle lists three things and no garlic.
sources: s:wp-crystal-hot-sauce — Crystal Hot Sauce; s:wp-buffalo-wing — Buffalo wing; s:wp-carolina-reaper — Carolina Reaper; s:wp-tabasco-sauce — Tabasco sauce; s:fdc-crystal-hot-sauce — Crystal Louisiana's Pure Hot Sauce — branded food label (FDC ID 2300103); s:wp-scoville-scale — Scoville scale; s:harland-1906 — Marion Harland's Complete Cook Book: A Practical and Exhaustive Manual of Cookery and Housekeeping
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## Frank's RedHot (sauce)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/sauce/franks-redhot/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/sauce/franks-redhot.json
id: franks-redhot
aliases: Frank's · Frank's RedHot Original Cayenne Pepper Sauce
said: A bar orders it by the case and says 'Frank's' the way it says 'a Coke'.
facets: base=vinegar-pepper · heat=mild · styles=buffalo
region: The United States, Western New York
what: A thin orange cayenne pepper sauce: aged cayenne red peppers, distilled vinegar, water, salt, garlic powder, in that order on the label. McCormick & Company makes it. The Original blend measures 450 Scoville heat units — the capsaicin scale named for Wilbur Scoville — which puts it below Tabasco, Cholula and Tapatío, and barely above Sriracha; the XTRA Hot blend measures 2,000. It is the bottle most Buffalo wing recipes start from.
story: Jacob Frank founded the Frank Tea and Spice Company in Cincinnati, Ohio in 1896. In 1917 he contracted with the Estilette Pepper Farm in Louisiana and went into partnership with Adam Estilette. They mixed spices, vinegar, garlic and cayenne peppers, aged them, and put the blend on the market in 1920.

Ownership moved: Durkee Famous Foods in 1977, Reckitt Benckiser from 1995, and in August 2017 McCormick & Company closed a $4.2 billion deal that took in both French's mustard and Frank's RedHot. Production sits in Springfield, Missouri.

The wing connection is older than the ownership and thinner than the marketing. Wikipedia's Buffalo wing article says Frank's "was probably not the hot sauce that was used in the original 1964 Anchor Bar recipe." *Inference —* the bottle's grip on the wing was won after the fact, by being cheap, thin, and everywhere.

The brand's television campaign gave it a second life: an elderly woman named Ethel, planted in front of a dignitary, says of her recipes "I put that s*** on everything", bleeped, with a splat over her mouth.
how: Shake. Pour into melted butter for wings, roughly one part to one for mild, more sauce for hot. Straight on eggs, pizza, fried chicken, and into chili. The vinegar is the working part as much as the pepper: it cuts fat and it keeps the sauce thin enough to coat rather than cling.
today: Sold nationally in supermarkets and in food-service jugs. As of 16 September 2026 the USDA label panel for the 5 fl oz Original bottle reads 190 mg sodium in a 1 teaspoon serving — 570 mg in a tablespoon — with no sugar and no fat. The maker publishes the 450 SHU figure for Original; it publishes no Scoville number for its Buffalo Wings Sauce or its Nashville Hot.
- kin → buffalo-sauce (sauce): Half of it, by volume, before the butter goes in.
- kin → crystal-hot-sauce (sauce): The other cayenne bottle; three ingredients against five, and a thinner vinegar line.
- kin → buffalo (style): Named in the standard account of how this style is sauced.
- kin → nashville-hot-oil (sauce): Some Nashville pastes take a slug of it; McCormick also sells a bottled Nashville Hot wings sauce under this brand.
- kin → hot-sauce-labels (art): Its orange-and-black bottle is one of the labels the shelf is read by.
- kin → anchor-bar (place): Credited with the 1964 sauce it probably was not in.
- kin → the-toss (fry): Goes into the bowl warm, with butter, and never before the fryer.
- not to be confused with buffalo-sauce: This is the bottle. Buffalo sauce is the bottle plus melted butter, mixed in the kitchen or in a factory.
sources: s:wp-frank-s-redhot — Frank's RedHot; s:wp-buffalo-wing — Buffalo wing; s:wp-scoville-scale — Scoville scale; s:fdc-franks-redhot-original — Frank's RedHot Original Cayenne Pepper Sauce — branded food label (FDC ID 2565317); s:web-franks-redhot-original-page — Frank's RedHot Original Cayenne Pepper Sauce; s:harland-1906 — Marion Harland's Complete Cook Book: A Practical and Exhaustive Manual of Cookery and Housekeeping; s:wp-cayenne-pepper — Cayenne pepper
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## Garlic parmesan sauce (sauce)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/sauce/garlic-parmesan-sauce/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/sauce/garlic-parmesan-sauce.json
id: garlic-parmesan-sauce
aliases: garlic parm · garlic parmesan
said: 'Garlic parm' at the counter. Half the shops mean a creamy sauce, half mean butter and a dry cheese shake, and the menu rarely says which.
facets: base=herb-garlic · heat=none
region: The United States
what: A pale, garlicky wing coating with parmesan in it. Two versions share the name: a creamy emulsified sauce built on oil and egg yolk with parmesan powder, sold bottled; and a kitchen mix of melted butter, minced garlic and grated parmesan tossed over the wings and finished with more cheese and parsley. Neither has heat in it. Both leave the wing wet and the fingers cheesy.
story: Garlic parm belongs to the sauce-board era. As the market for chicken wings expanded, restaurants began creating and using sauces beyond Buffalo, and a wing menu turned into a list — Wingstop carries thirteen wing sauces, some running only for a marketing window, and sells ranch, blue cheese, honey mustard and cheese sauce as dips beside them.

*Inference —* garlic parm is the wing answer to garlic bread, which is crusty bread topped with garlic and butter and sometimes cheese, then toasted. A kitchen that already had butter, garlic and a tub of grated parmesan did not need a new ingredient to add a flavour to the board.

The sauce splits the same way lemon pepper does: dry shake or wet sauce. The bottled version settles the argument by emulsifying, so the cheese stays suspended and the sauce keeps on a shelf.
how: Melt butter with minced or roasted garlic, off the heat so the garlic does not brown. Toss the fried wings in it, then shower grated parmesan and chopped parsley over the top while the butter is still wet enough to hold them. The bottled sauce skips the melting: it pours cold and clings, because oil and egg yolk hold it together.
today: On the board at every wing chain and most bars. As of 16 September 2026 the USDA label panel for Kinder's Garlic Parmesan Wing Sauce & Dip reads 120 mg sodium and 1 g sugar in a 1-tablespoon serving — the lowest sodium of any bottled wing sauce measured for this set — with soybean oil first and roasted garlic puree second. No Scoville number is published, and the label names no chile.
- kin → garlic-parm (style): The style is this sauce and the cheese shaken over it.
- kin → lemon-pepper-wet (sauce): Built the same way — something wet, then a dry shake — with cheese instead of citrus.
- kin → wingstop (place): Carries it on a board of thirteen wing sauces, beside ranch and blue cheese as dips.
- kin → buffalo-sauce (sauce): The other butter-based wing coating, and the one with cayenne in it.
- kin → ranch-dressing (sauce): Shares the garlic-and-dairy register, and often turns up in the same order as the dip.
- kin → the-toss (fry): Wants the bowl twice: once for the butter, once for the cheese.
- kin → soy-garlic-sauce (sauce): The other garlic-forward wing with no heat, reached through soy and sugar instead of dairy.
- not to be confused with ranch-dressing: Where it goes. Garlic parm coats the wing; ranch sits in a cup beside it. The bottled versions look alike in the jar.
sources: s:wp-buffalo-wing — Buffalo wing; s:wp-wingstop — Wingstop; s:fdc-kinders-garlic-parmesan — Kinder's Garlic Parmesan Wing Sauce & Dip — branded food label (FDC ID 2652872)
provenance default: cited · confidence: medium · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## Honey barbecue sauce (sauce)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/sauce/honey-bbq-sauce/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/sauce/honey-bbq-sauce.json
id: honey-bbq-sauce
aliases: honey BBQ · honey barbeque
said: The order a table puts in for the person who does not want heat, and the one children get.
facets: base=sweet-tomato · heat=none
region: The United States
what: A thick sweet red sauce: corn syrup or sugar, vinegar, tomato, honey, smoke flavour and spices. Sticky enough to hold on a wing without butter, sweet enough to caramelise under a broiler or on a grill. Every wing chain sells one, and it is usually the mildest thing on the board.
story: Barbecue sauce reached the wing through the pizza chains. Domino's added Buffalo wings to its national menu in 1994 after four Super Bowl appearances by the Buffalo Bills, and Pizza Hut followed the next year. As the market grew, restaurants built out sauces beyond Buffalo — some drawing on Chinese, Japanese, Thai, Caribbean and Indian cooking, some inventing combinations like Blueberry BBQ Wing Sauce or Maple/Bacon Glaze to hold customers' interest.

*Inference —* honey barbecue is the sauce that made a wing board possible. Once a menu had a second sauce it needed a sweet one, and every sauce added after that had somewhere to sit.

The sweet-and-sour tomato condiment behind it is much older than the wing: American home cookbooks were bottling a spiced 'chili sauce' of tomatoes, vinegar, sugar, onions and red peppers well before 1930.
how: Warm it — cold barbecue sauce slides off. Toss the fried wings in it, or brush it on a smoked or grilled wing in the last few minutes so the sugar sets without burning. It will burn: the sugar in it catches long before the skin is done, which is why it goes on at the end and never at the start.
today: On every wing board in America. As of 16 September 2026 the USDA label panel for Sweet Baby Ray's Honey Barbecue Sauce reads 300 mg sodium and 15 g sugar in a 2-tablespoon serving — 150 mg and 7.5 g in one tablespoon. High fructose corn syrup is its first ingredient; honey comes fourth, behind tomato paste. No Scoville number is published, and none would mean anything: the label declares no chile at all.
- kin → smoked-bbq-wing (style): The style that brushes it on at the end of a smoke.
- kin → memphis-rub (sauce): The dry half of the Memphis fork; this is the wet half, bottled.
- kin → mild-sauce (sauce): Chicago's carryout relative, poured rather than tossed and sharper on the vinegar.
- kin → mumbo-sauce (sauce): The D.C. relative, thinner and sourer and built on ketchup.
- kin → hot-honey (sauce): What happens when the honey goes in without the tomato and picks up a chile.
- kin → buffalo-wild-wings (place): Sells it on a board of a dozen-plus sauces where Buffalo is one option among many.
- kin → grill (fry): Goes on in the last minutes, because the sugar in it catches before the skin is done.
- kin → wing-night (term): The sauce that lets a table order one round for people who disagree about heat.
- not to be confused with hot-honey: Tomato. Honey barbecue has it and is thick and red; hot honey is honey, chillies and vinegar, and pours.
sources: s:wp-buffalo-wing — Buffalo wing; s:wp-pizza-hut — Pizza Hut; s:fdc-sweet-baby-rays-honey-bbq — Sweet Baby Ray's Honey Barbecue Sauce — branded food label (FDC ID 2017251); s:harland-1906 — Marion Harland's Complete Cook Book: A Practical and Exhaustive Manual of Cookery and Housekeeping; s:wikibooks-barbecue-sauce — Cookbook:Barbecue Sauce I
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## Hot honey (sauce)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/sauce/hot-honey/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/sauce/hot-honey.json
id: hot-honey
aliases: chili honey · spicy honey
said: Drizzled, not tossed. A counter says 'hot honey' and reaches for a squeeze bottle.
facets: base=other · heat=medium
region: The United States
what: Honey with chillies in it. Sweet first, then a heat that builds slowly — the flavour writers describe as "sweet-first" with a "slow-building heat". Goes on pizza, on fried chicken and wings, on roasted vegetables, with cheese, in sandwiches, on desserts, into glazes and marinades and dipping sauces, and into mixed drinks.
story: Mixing honey with chillies has been done in many cultures for a long time. The American trend has a narrower start: Mike Kurtz encountered hot honey while studying in Brazil in 2004 and later founded Mike's Hot Honey, the brand the trend runs alongside.

It became a trend in early 2022, tracked by a steady rise in Google search interest, and spread through TikTok recipes. Business Insider named it a "new food obsession" in 2024. V8 and Tillamook among others released hot-honey snacks and product variations.

*Inference —* it reached the wing by way of the pizza it was already on. A kitchen with a squeeze bottle of it on the pass does not need a new ingredient to put a hot honey wing on the menu.
how: Drizzle it over the wings after they come out of the fryer, or brush it on at the end of a smoke or a grill so the sugar tightens without burning. It is thin enough to pour and thick enough to stay put. Plenty of kitchens use it as the second half of a Buffalo or Nashville wing rather than the whole coating, which is where the sweet-heat order comes from: pepper first, honey last.
today: Sold by dozens of makers, from national brands to single-state apiaries. As of 16 September 2026 the USDA label panel for Mike's Hot Honey reads three ingredients — honey, chilies, vinegar — with 0 mg sodium and 14 g sugar in a 1-tablespoon serving. Red Clay's version lists raw honey, apple cider vinegar and fermented habanero pepper at 15 g sugar and 10 mg sodium. No maker in this set publishes a Scoville number, and no chile is named by variety on the Mike's label.
- kin → hot-honey-word (term): The word, and how it came to name a category rather than a brand.
- kin → honey-bbq-sauce (sauce): The other sweet answer to a wing; that one runs through tomato and this one does not.
- kin → nashville-hot-oil (sauce): Often the sweet finish over a cayenne paste, and the reason a Nashville wing can read sweet.
- kin → jerk-marinade (sauce): Brushed over jerk wings at the end, where honey meets Scotch bonnet.
- kin → buffalo-sauce (sauce): Cut with it at bars selling a hot-honey Buffalo wing: pepper first, honey last.
- kin → buffalo-chicken-pizza (dish): Its first American home was a pizza, and the wing came after.
- kin → sweet-chili-sauce (sauce): The other sweet-and-chile pour on a wing board, thickened and vinegared rather than pure sugar.
- kin → grill (fry): Wants the last minutes only; the sugar in it catches fast.
- not to be confused with honey-bbq-sauce: Read the label. Hot honey's is three or four lines long and starts with honey; a honey barbecue sauce starts with corn syrup and carries tomato.
sources: s:wp-hot-honey — Hot honey; s:fdc-mikes-hot-honey — Mike's Hot Honey, Honey Infused with Chilies — branded food label (FDC ID 2511479)
provenance default: cited · confidence: medium · needs_verification: True · updated: 2026-09-16

## Jerk marinade (sauce)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/sauce/jerk-marinade/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/sauce/jerk-marinade.json
id: jerk-marinade
aliases: jerk seasoning · jerk spice · Jamaican jerk spice
said: One word covers three things: the rub, the wet marinade made from it, and the way of cooking. A jerk stand sells all three at once.
facets: base=other · heat=hot
region: Caribbean America, The United States
what: A wet marinade, or a dry rub, built on allspice and Scotch bonnet peppers — both native to Jamaica and grown there by the Taíno. Scallion, thyme, garlic, ginger, cloves, cinnamon, nutmeg, brown sugar, soy sauce, vinegar and salt turn up in it. The heat is the Scotch bonnet's. The word 'jerk' names the rub, the marinade and mop sauce made from it, and the cooking technique, all three.
story: Jerking came from Jamaica's indigenous people, the Arawak and Taíno, and was taken up by the descendants of 17th-century Jamaican Maroons who lived among them. In 1516 the Spanish historian Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo y Valdés recorded how the Taíno prepared and preserved meat and fish on a barbacoa, seasoning with native hot peppers — Scotch bonnet and cayenne — and pimento. Meats were sometimes wrapped in papaya leaves to tenderise before jerking. Local game went on it: coney, iguana, wild hog, agouti, wild birds, waterfowl, turtle, and a range of seafood.

Spanish colonists adopted Taíno methods to survive and introduced pig, cattle and chicken in the 1500s, curing them over a barbacoa with pimento wood and berries. When the Spanish were invaded in 1655 they freed the enslaved Africans, who fled into the countryside and became some of the first Jamaican Maroons; they intermingled with the remaining Taíno and learned jerking. By the end of the 18th century most groups had switched to imported pork, while the Maroons kept hunting wild hogs and jerking them.

The word comes from charqui, a Spanish term of Quechua origin for dried meat, which became 'jerky' in English.

Method followed portability. Around the 1960s Caribbean entrepreneurs began cutting oil barrels lengthwise, drilling ventilation holes and hinging lids to hold the smoke; the barrel drum is now standard across the island. Jerk stands sell the meat with hard dough bread, bammy, fried dumplings and festival.

Jerk travelled with the Caribbean diaspora — Britain, Canada, the United States, coastal Panama, Costa Rica, Honduras, Nicaragua, San Andrés. In September 2015 the Jamaican government registered Jamaica Jerk as a geographical indication, making Jamaica the first English-speaking Caribbean country to do so.
how: Marinate, then cook over smoke. Blend the wet version and work it under the skin; leave the wings in it for hours. Cook over pimento wood, in a halved oil drum with the lid down, or in a wood-burning oven; a home kitchen uses a grill and finishes in the fryer. Reserve some marinade unheated as a mop sauce and brush it on at the end. The Scotch bonnet's heat sits behind the allspice, which is the flavour people name first.
today: Sold bottled in every Caribbean grocery in the United States and in most supermarkets. As of 16 September 2026 the USDA label panel for Spur Tree Jamaican Jerk Seasoning reads 700 mg sodium and 1 g sugar in a 1-tablespoon serving, with scallion first and Scotch bonnet pepper second. No maker in this set publishes a Scoville number for it.
- kin → caribbean-jerk (style): The style is this marinade and the drum it is cooked in.
- kin → peppas-jerk-chicken (place): A New York jerk counter where the wings come off the drum.
- kin → smoke-then-fry (fry): The method it belongs to: smoke for the flavour, fryer or grill for the skin.
- kin → grill (fry): The barrel with the lid down is a grill doing a smoker's job.
- kin → nashville-hot-oil (sauce): The other wing heat built on a single named chile, and the other one applied by hand.
- kin → crystal-hot-sauce (sauce): Both lean on an aged or fermented chile rather than a fresh one.
- kin → hot-honey (sauce): Turns up brushed over jerk wings at the end, where the sugar meets the Scotch bonnet.
- kin → sweet-chili-sauce (sauce): The other sweet-and-chile dip a jerk counter may put beside the wings.
- image: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/images/jerk-marinade/jerk-marinade-jerk-chicken.jpg · CC BY-SA 2.0 · stu_spivack · https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3AJerk_chicken.jpg
sources: s:wp-jerk-cooking — Jerk (cooking); s:fdc-spur-tree-jerk-seasoning — Spur Tree Jamaican Jerk Seasoning — branded food label (FDC ID 2617055)
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## Lemon pepper (sauce)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/sauce/lemon-pepper-seasoning/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/sauce/lemon-pepper-seasoning.json
id: lemon-pepper-seasoning
aliases: lemon pepper seasoning · LP
said: An Atlanta counter says 'lemon pepper' and means the dry shake; say 'wet' and you have ordered something else.
facets: base=citrus-pepper · heat=none
region: Atlanta, The United States
what: A dry blend of granulated lemon zest and cracked black peppercorns. The zest is mashed into the pepper so citrus oil soaks in, then the mix is baked and dried. Commercial blends add salt, sugar, onion powder, garlic powder, citric acid, lemon flavouring, sometimes cayenne. It started as a seafood seasoning and became the wing seasoning Atlanta is known for.
story: William Shoffeitt, a product engineer in Healdsburg, California, launched lemon pepper seasoning commercially in July 1967 through his company, Shoffeitt's Enhance Seasoners. It sold along the West Coast, went out at food trade shows, and reached the shelves of Sears and JCPenney.

Atlanta made it a wing. Cooks there began adding lemon pepper to Buffalo wings to cut the heat, and the dry wing became emblematic of the city's food. Its mid-2000s run has been attributed to its not marking clothes the way an orange sauce does — a point made about rappers then wearing white t-shirts. Keisha Lance Bottoms, later mayor of Atlanta, said in 2017 that "Lemon pepper wings are Atlanta". Eric Kim wrote in The New York Times in 2022 that "in Atlanta, lemon pepper is queen".

*Inference —* the blend's move from fish counter to wing counter is the whole story of its second life, and the label never changed to follow it.
how: Shaken onto the wings straight out of the fryer, while the skin is hot enough to hold it. No sauce, no bowl — a dry wing stays crisp because nothing wet touches it. Some kitchens shake it over a wing that has already been through butter or Buffalo sauce, which is where wet begins.
today: On every supermarket spice shelf and behind every Atlanta wing counter. As of 16 September 2026 the USDA label panel for McCormick Lemon & Pepper Seasoning reads 180 mg sodium in a ¼-tablespoon serving — 720 mg in a whole tablespoon, which nobody eats. Salt is the first ingredient, ahead of the pepper; the lemon arrives as citric acid at 3 and lemon oil at 10.
- kin → atlanta-lemon-pepper (style): The style this blend defines, and the reason a dry wing is an Atlanta wing.
- kin → lemon-pepper-wet (sauce): What happens when the same shake lands on a wing that has already been through butter or sauce.
- kin → wet-and-dry (term): This is the dry half of the counter's two-word vocabulary.
- kin → american-deli (place): An Atlanta counter that shakes it, and where the wet version was invented.
- kin → jr-cricketts (place): Put 'lemon pepper wet' on the menu in 2017 after a television episode sent people asking for it.
- kin → old-bay (sauce): The other dry shake that owns a city; celery salt and paprika instead of zest and black pepper.
- kin → memphis-rub (sauce): The other dry answer to a wing, built on sugar and paprika rather than citrus.
- kin → all-flats (term): Travels with it in the order that Atlanta made famous.
- kin → naked-fry (fry): Needs a bare crisp skin, because the shake has nothing to stick to on a battered wing.
- not to be confused with lemon-pepper-wet: Whether anything wet touched the wing. This record is the dry shake in the jar.
sources: s:wp-lemon-pepper — Lemon pepper; s:wp-lemon-pepper-wings — Lemon pepper wings; s:fdc-mccormick-lemon-pepper — McCormick Lemon & Pepper Seasoning — branded food label (FDC ID 2034704)
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## Lemon pepper wet (sauce)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/sauce/lemon-pepper-wet/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/sauce/lemon-pepper-wet.json
id: lemon-pepper-wet
aliases: LP wet · lemon pepper wet wings
said: Two words at the counter. 'Wet' means sauce underneath the shake, and for years at one Atlanta restaurant it was not on the menu at all.
facets: base=citrus-pepper · heat=mild
region: Atlanta, The United States
what: A wing that has been through something wet and then through lemon pepper. The wet part varies: a lemon sauce instead of a dry rub at some shops, melted butter at others, Buffalo sauce at others again, with the dry seasoning shaken on after. American Deli in Atlanta invented the version the name usually points at.
story: The dish reached most of America through television. The second episode of Atlanta shows a character handed "lemon pepper wet" wings from J.R. Crickets, a real Atlanta restaurant; the scene went round social media and the dish went with it. At the time J.R. Crickets did not have it on the menu — it had a similar item called "Fester" wings that customers kept calling lemon pepper wet. Writer Stephen Glover said he wanted the character "hooked up" with something that was not on the menu. The wings the show depicted were actually modelled on a dish from American Deli, a different Atlanta restaurant. J.R. Crickets added lemon pepper wet to its menu in 2017 in honour of the show. Mike Jordan of Eater Atlanta credited the episode with popularising it.

It kept collecting names. In 2020 Lou Williams of the Los Angeles Clippers picked up the nickname "Lemon Pepper Lou" after it was reported that he ordered lemon pepper wings with Jack Harlow at the Magic City strip club during a trip outside the NBA Bubble. Magic City already had a dish named for him, "Louwill Lemon Pepper BBQ Wings". He objected to the nickname and later trademarked it.

*Inference —* wet is the only wing order in America whose canonical version was invented by a customer, confirmed by a screenwriter, and then put on the menu by a restaurant that had not been serving it.
how: Fry the wings bare. Toss them in the wet part — lemon butter, plain melted butter, or Buffalo sauce — then shake dry lemon pepper over the top while the coating is still tacky. The order matters: shake first and it slides off; shake last and it sits on the surface where you taste it.
today: On Atlanta menus and, by 2026, on chain menus far from Atlanta. No maker bottles it, because it is not a bottle — it is a sequence. There is no label to read, no sodium figure, no Scoville number, and every shop's wet is a different wet.
- kin → lemon-pepper-seasoning (sauce): The dry shake that goes on last, and the half of the name that comes in a jar.
- kin → atlanta-lemon-pepper (style): The style it belongs to, and the argument inside it: dry or wet.
- kin → wet-and-dry (term): The two words this order is built out of.
- kin → american-deli (place): Invented the version the name points at, and the one the television episode was modelled on.
- kin → jr-cricketts (place): Got the fame and then added the dish, in 2017.
- kin → buffalo-sauce (sauce): One of the things the wet can be, at shops that build it on butter and cayenne.
- kin → the-toss (fry): Happens twice here: once for the sauce, once for the shake.
- kin → all-flats (term): The other half of the order that Atlanta says in one breath.
- not to be confused with lemon-pepper-seasoning: A jar against a sequence. The seasoning is an ingredient; wet is a way of applying it.
- not to be confused with garlic-parmesan-sauce: Both end in a dry shake over a wet wing, but garlic parm's wet part is a creamy garlic sauce, not butter or cayenne.
sources: s:wp-lemon-pepper-wings — Lemon pepper wings; s:wp-lemon-pepper — Lemon pepper; s:douglas-1903 — The Soup and Sauce Book
provenance default: cited · confidence: medium · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## Mango habanero (sauce)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/sauce/mango-habanero/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/sauce/mango-habanero.json
id: mango-habanero
aliases: mango hab · sweet heat
said: Sits near the top of a chain's heat ladder without being the top rung, which is usually something with a name like atomic.
facets: base=other · heat=hot
region: The United States
what: A sweet-then-hot wing sauce: mango purée and corn syrup in front, habanero and cayenne behind. Orange, thick, and built to be tossed. It is the standard second-from-the-top rung on a chain wing board — hot enough to be a choice, sweet enough to finish.
story: It belongs to the sauce-board era. As the market for chicken wings expanded, restaurants began creating and using a variety of sauces beyond Buffalo, some drawn from Chinese, Japanese, Thai, Caribbean and Indian cooking, and some invented as combinations — Blueberry BBQ Wing Sauce and Maple/Bacon Glaze among the examples — to hold customers' interest and grow the business.

Many bars and restaurants also build a deliberately extra-hot sauce for wing-eating challenges, and reward the people who finish with a photograph on the wall, a T-shirt, a free meal, or some combination.

*Inference —* mango habanero is the rung below that. It is where a board puts real heat that a table can still eat a whole basket of, which is why almost every chain carries a version and almost none of them publishes a number for it.
how: Toss, warm or cold — it is thick enough to cling without butter. Chains serve it on bone-in and boneless alike. A kitchen building its own reduces mango purée with vinegar and sugar and blends habanero in at the end, off the heat, because habanero's aroma cooks off before its heat does.
today: On chain boards nationally. As of 16 September 2026 the USDA label panel for Sweet Baby Ray's Mango Habanero Wing Sauce reads 100 mg sodium and 7 g sugar in a 1-tablespoon serving. Five chiles are named on that label — cayenne, habanero, chipotle, chili powder and chili de arbol — and no Scoville number is published for any of it, which is the pattern across this whole shelf.
- kin → atomic (term): The word for the rung above this one, where a board stops being a menu and starts being a dare.
- kin → sweet-chili-sauce (sauce): The same sweet-then-chile idea, reached through sugar and vinegar instead of fruit purée.
- kin → hot-honey (sauce): The other sweet-heat pour on the board, with honey doing the sweetening.
- kin → buffalo-wild-wings (place): Carries a version on a board where Buffalo is one sauce among more than a dozen.
- kin → wingstop (place): One of thirteen wing sauces on the board, some of them running only for a marketing window.
- kin → buffalo-sauce (sauce): The sauce the board was built around, and the one this sits several rungs above on heat.
- kin → boneless-wings (dish): Ordered with it as often as bone-in, because the sauce is thick and the pieces are small.
- kin → the-toss (fry): Goes in the bowl thick and cold, and still coats.
- not to be confused with sweet-chili-sauce: Fruit and corn syrup. Mango habanero leads with high fructose corn syrup and mango purée; sweet chili is water, sugar and pickled chilli.
sources: s:wp-buffalo-wing — Buffalo wing; s:wp-wingstop — Wingstop; s:fdc-sweet-baby-rays-mango-habanero — Sweet Baby Ray's Mango Habanero Wing Sauce — branded food label (FDC ID 2629740); s:wp-scoville-scale — Scoville scale
provenance default: cited · confidence: medium · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## Memphis dry rub (sauce)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/sauce/memphis-rub/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/sauce/memphis-rub.json
id: memphis-rub
aliases: dry rub · Memphis rub · dry
said: 'Dry' in Memphis is not a texture complaint. It is an order, and the other one is 'wet'.
facets: base=dry-rub · heat=mild
region: Memphis, The United States
what: A dry mix of salt, paprika, sugar and spices, patted onto meat before it cooks and shaken over it again after. Memphis barbecue is mostly pork — ribs and shoulders — and its ribs come dry or wet: dry means rub and no sauce, wet means sauce brushed on before, during and after. The same rub goes on wings, which get the rib counter's treatment without the pit.
story: Memphis is one of the four regional styles of American barbecue usually named, with Carolina, Kansas City and Texas. Its cooking is slow, in a pit, and the dry-or-wet fork sits at the centre of it.

The World Championship Barbecue Cooking Contest, held each May, has made the style known beyond the city; Guinness World Records lists it as the largest pork barbecue contest in the world. The Food Network and the BBC cover it and more than 100,000 people attend. Many Memphis barbecue restaurants ship nationally overnight, helped by the FedEx Superhub sitting in the city.

*Inference —* the rub reached the wing sideways. A rib counter already had the mix in a shaker and a fryer or a smoker in the back, and a wing takes the same shake in a tenth of the time.
how: Two applications. Rub the wings before cooking so salt and sugar have time to draw and set a crust; smoke, fry or both; then shake more rub over them the moment they come off. The sugar is why a rubbed wing browns darker and why it will scorch on a hot grill. No bowl, no sauce, nothing to dip in unless you ask.
today: Sold bottled by dozens of makers and mixed by every barbecue kitchen. As of 16 September 2026 the USDA label panel for Adams Reserve Memphis Barbecue Rub reads 40 mg sodium and 1 g sugar in a ¼-teaspoon serving — 480 mg and 12 g in a tablespoon by arithmetic. Brown sugar is its first ingredient and chipotle its last. No Memphis rib house's own shaker carries a published panel, and no maker publishes a Scoville number.
- kin → memphis-dry-rub (style): The style is this shaker, taken off the rib counter and put on a wing.
- kin → central-bbq (place): A Memphis pit whose rub goes on wings as well as ribs.
- kin → wet-and-dry (term): Memphis says these two words about ribs; Atlanta and Baltimore borrowed them for wings.
- kin → old-bay (sauce): The other regional shaker, without the sugar and with celery salt doing the work.
- kin → lemon-pepper-seasoning (sauce): Atlanta's dry answer to the same question, built on citrus.
- kin → smoke-then-fry (fry): The method a rubbed wing most often goes through: smoke for colour, fryer for skin.
- kin → honey-bbq-sauce (sauce): The wet half of the Memphis fork, in a bottle.
- kin → smoked-bbq-wing (style): The style that takes this rub to a smoker rather than a fryer.
- not to be confused with old-bay: Taste the sugar. A Memphis rub is brown-sugar sweet and browns as it cooks; Old Bay is celery salt and stays dusty.
sources: s:wp-memphis-style-barbecue — Memphis-style barbecue; s:fdc-adams-reserve-memphis-rub — Adams Reserve Memphis Barbecue Rub — branded food label (FDC ID 1912757)
provenance default: cited · confidence: medium · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## Mild sauce (sauce)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/sauce/mild-sauce/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/sauce/mild-sauce.json
id: mild-sauce
aliases: Chicago mild sauce
said: 'Mild sauce on it' is a heat instruction nowhere else in America would read as a sauce order.
facets: base=sweet-tomato · heat=mild
region: Chicago, The United States
what: A red-brown condiment poured over fried chicken and wings on Chicago's South and West Sides. Recipes vary a great deal; many versions combine ketchup, barbecue sauce and hot sauce. Close kin to barbecue sauce and to mumbo sauce, and particularly associated with Black communities in Chicago. The name is not a heat rating — it is what the sauce is called.
story: Fried chicken and barbecue restaurants made it: Harold's Chicken Shack, Uncle Remus Saucy Fried Chicken, Lem's Bar-B-Q. The chicken shack pours it over the bird and the white bread underneath, and the bread does the soaking.

*Tradition holds —* every shop guards its own mix, and the argument over whose is best runs shop by shop rather than recipe by recipe.

The trademark history runs through the sauce next door. Argia B. Collins Sr. was using the Mumbo name for a Chicago barbecue sauce from at least 1950; the Trademark Trial and Appeal Board later held that a D.C. company could not take that name from its Chicago founder. *Inference —* mild sauce and mumbo sauce are the same family of Black Chicago carryout condiment, one of which travelled east and picked up a second spelling.
how: Poured over the chicken in the box, not served beside it. A shop with a squeeze bottle asks whether you want mild sauce, hot sauce, both, or neither; both means the mild goes on first. The bread at the bottom of the box is part of the delivery system.
today: Sold bottled by several small makers and mixed in-house at the shacks. As of 16 September 2026 the USDA label panel for Aisha's Mild Sauce reads 280 mg sodium and 11 g sugar in a 2-tablespoon serving — 140 mg and 5.5 g in one tablespoon. No maker publishes a Scoville figure, and the shacks' own sauces carry no label.
- kin → chicago-mild-sauce (style): The style built around it: a shack, a fryer, white bread and this poured over.
- kin → mumbo-sauce (sauce): Its D.C. cousin, and the one that carries the registered Chicago trademark.
- kin → harolds-chicken-shack (place): One of the shops that made it popular, and where the pour goes over bread.
- kin → uncle-remus-saucy-fried-chicken (place): Another of the shops named as making it popular on the West Side.
- kin → argia-b-collins (person): Sold Chicago's other name for this sauce from at least 1950 and registered it.
- kin → white-bread-and-pickles (dish): The bread at the bottom of the box is what catches it.
- kin → mild-sauce-word (term): Why 'mild' here names a sauce rather than a heat level.
- kin → honey-bbq-sauce (sauce): The supermarket relative: same sweet tomato family, different city and a corn-syrup lead.
- not to be confused with mumbo-sauce: The word. Both are sweet tomato carryout sauces; Chicago says mild sauce, D.C. says mumbo or mambo.
sources: s:wp-mild-sauce — Mild sauce; s:wp-mumbo-sauce — Mumbo sauce; s:wp-harold-s-chicken-shack — Harold's Chicken Shack; s:fdc-aishas-mild-sauce — Aisha's Mild Sauce — branded food label (FDC ID 2422784); s:harland-1906 — Marion Harland's Complete Cook Book: A Practical and Exhaustive Manual of Cookery and Housekeeping
provenance default: cited · confidence: medium · needs_verification: True · updated: 2026-09-16

## Mumbo sauce (sauce)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/sauce/mumbo-sauce/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/sauce/mumbo-sauce.json
id: mumbo-sauce
aliases: mambo sauce · Mumbo® Sauce
said: Ordered by the squeeze: 'wings and fries, mumbo on everything.' Spelled mumbo in Chicago and on the trademark, mambo on plenty of D.C. counters.
facets: base=sweet-tomato · heat=mild
region: Washington, D.C., Chicago, The United States
what: A carryout condiment of Washington, D.C.: red-orange, thick, poured over fried chicken wings, french fries, fried jumbo shrimp and fried rice. Close to barbecue sauce but sweeter, and either spicier or more sour depending on whose it is. The consistency and the flavour vary shop to shop. Its origin and its ingredients are both disputed, and so is its spelling.
story: The trademark belongs to Chicago. Argia B. Collins Sr. used the Mumbo name for a barbecue sauce he developed for his Chicago restaurant from at least 1950; his successor-in-interest, Select Brands, LLC, registered it with the US Patent and Trademark Office on 25 May 1999, Registration No. 2,247,855. Select Brands has challenged D.C. sellers who use the term.

The D.C. account runs through a restaurant called Wings-n-Things in the late 1960s, according to Capital City Mumbo Sauce. A John Young's Wings-n-Things had been serving mumbo sauce on chicken wings in Buffalo, New York since the early 1960s, and Young credited a Washington, D.C. restaurant for the sauce — a boxer had told him a D.C. place was doing good business in wings, so he specialised. Since Collins's sauce runs back to the 1950s, before it showed up at Wings-n-Things, the D.C. version is speculated to be a transplant of the Chicago original. After two years of argument the Trademark Trial and Appeal Board found that a D.C.-based company could not take the name from its Chicago founder.

It stays a live argument in the city. In 2018 Mayor Muriel Bowser called mumbo sauce "annoying" in a Facebook post and questioned whether it was "quintessential" D.C.; her spokesperson said the remarks were meant to liven Thanksgiving discussions. McDonald's released a limited-time version on 9 October 2023 with a media campaign and a short YouTube documentary on the sauce's history.

The name carries beyond the counter: the go-go group Mambo Sauce took its name from it, Christylez Bacon performs a song about it, Black Flag Brewing in Columbia, Maryland named a beer Mambo Sauce, and Camille Acker's collection Training School for Negro Girls contains a story called "Mambo Sauce".
how: Poured, not tossed. A carryout squeezes it over the wings and the fries in the box so both arrive wet, or hands it over in a lidded cup. Every shop mixes its own; the bottled Capital City version starts with ketchup, then sugar, then water, then soy sauce, and takes its heat from a cayenne pepper hot sauce well down the list.
today: Bottled by Capital City and by others, and made in-house at carryouts across the District. As of 16 September 2026 the USDA label panel for Capital City Mild Mambo Sauce reads 160 mg sodium and 10 g sugar in a 2-tablespoon serving — 80 mg and 5 g in one tablespoon. Nobody publishes a Scoville number for it. The house sauces have no label at all.
- kin → dc-mumbo (style): The style built on it: a carryout box of wings and fries with this poured over both.
- kin → mild-sauce (sauce): Chicago's near-twin, and the sauce the trademark case says came first.
- kin → john-young (person): Put it on breaded whole wings in Buffalo from 1961, and credited a Washington restaurant for it.
- kin → argia-b-collins (person): Registered the Mumbo name in Chicago and won it back from a D.C. company.
- kin → mumbo-fries (dish): The other half of the box, and where most of the sauce ends up.
- kin → capital-city-mambo-sauce (place): Bottles the D.C. version and tells the Wings-n-Things origin.
- kin → yums-carry-out (place): A D.C. counter where the wings arrive already wet with it.
- kin → mumbo (term): The word itself, and the mumbo-or-mambo argument over it.
- kin → buffalo-sauce (sauce): What Buffalo used instead, and what John Young's wings were not tossed in.
- kin → fried-rice-plate (dish): Goes over this too, at the Chinese carryouts that sell both.
- not to be confused with mild-sauce: City and label. Mild sauce is Chicago's word; mumbo is the registered Chicago trademark that D.C. adopted. The bottles taste close.
- not to be confused with honey-bbq-sauce: Mumbo runs thinner and sourer, and a national honey barbecue sauce leads with corn syrup rather than ketchup.
- image: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/images/mumbo-sauce/mumbo-sauce-mumbo-sauce.jpg · CC BY-SA 2.0 · justgrimes · https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3AMumbo_sauce.jpg
sources: s:wp-mumbo-sauce — Mumbo sauce; s:wp-mild-sauce — Mild sauce; s:wp-buffalo-wing — Buffalo wing; s:fdc-capital-city-mild-mambo — Capital City Mild Mambo Sauce — branded food label (FDC ID 2147935); s:harland-1906 — Marion Harland's Complete Cook Book: A Practical and Exhaustive Manual of Cookery and Housekeeping
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## Nashville hot paste (sauce)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/sauce/nashville-hot-oil/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/sauce/nashville-hot-oil.json
id: nashville-hot-oil
aliases: hot oil · the paste · cayenne paste
said: Ordered by rung: mild, medium, hot, extra hot, and a top rung each shop names for itself.
facets: base=other · heat=very hot
region: Nashville, The United States
what: A cayenne paste, spooned onto fried chicken the moment it leaves the fryer. Fat carries it — lard or a ladle of the frying oil itself — which is why it soaks in rather than sitting on top, and why the bird turns deep red. Some shops add sugar, garlic or extra hot sauce. Some apply it before breading instead of after. Recipes are kept close.
story: Spicy fried chicken has been served in Nashville's African-American communities for generations; anecdotal evidence puts the dish as early as the 1930s, though the current style of spice paste may only run back to the mid-1970s.

The origin generally accepted belongs to the family of André Prince Jeffries, who has run Prince's Hot Chicken Shack since 1980. Before that it belonged to her great-uncle, Thornton Prince III. Jeffries says the development was an accident: Thornton was a womaniser, and after a late Saturday night his girlfriend cooked him a fried chicken breakfast with extra pepper as revenge. He liked it. By the mid-1930s he and his brothers had their own recipe and had opened the BBQ Chicken Shack café.

By 2015 an estimated two dozen restaurants in the Nashville area served hot chicken. Bill Purcell, mayor of Nashville, sponsored the Music City Hot Chicken Festival and called his table at Prince's his "second office". KFC began selling Nashville Hot Chicken across its US restaurants in January 2016 after a Pittsburgh-area trial it called the most successful product testing in its recent history, and ran it in the UK from 22 May to 18 June 2017. Buffalo Wild Wings offers Nashville hot-style wings.

*Inference —* the paste is the only sauce in this set that is applied with a spoon and a gloved hand rather than poured or shaken, and that is what keeps it off supermarket shelves in its own form.
how: Fry the wings. While they drain, whisk cayenne and the shop's other powders into hot fat — lard, or oil dipped straight out of the fryer. Spoon it over with a gloved hand and squeeze it lightly into the crust. White bread underneath catches what runs off; pickle chips go on top. Sauce and bird are never separated, so there is no dip and no bowl.
today: Sold across Nashville and, since 2016, by chains that bottle or powder an approximation. Frank's RedHot sells a Nashville Hot Wings Sauce whose label reads 340 mg sodium and 2 g sugar in a tablespoon as of 16 September 2026 — vinegar-led, with canola oil fourth, which is a bottle's answer to a paste. The shacks' own pastes have no label, no sodium figure and no Scoville number, and are held as secrets.
- kin → nashville-hot (style): The style is this paste and the bread under it.
- kin → princes-hot-chicken-shack (place): Where the accepted origin sits, and where the paste goes on with a spoon.
- kin → thornton-prince (person): The pepper-for-revenge breakfast that the shop's own account starts from.
- kin → andre-prince-jeffries (person): Has run the shop since 1980 and tells the origin.
- kin → white-bread-and-pickles (dish): The plate it lands on; the bread takes the run-off and gets eaten last.
- kin → frying-oil (fry): The fat in the paste often comes straight out of the fryer.
- kin → buffalo-sauce (sauce): The other cayenne answer to a wing; butter and a bowl instead of fat and a spoon.
- kin → franks-redhot (sauce): Sells a bottled Nashville Hot wings sauce under the same brand that anchors Buffalo.
- kin → hattie-bs (place): Runs the heat ladder as a menu, mild through the top rung.
- not to be confused with buffalo-sauce: What carries the cayenne. Buffalo sauce carries it in butter and vinegar; this carries it in frying fat and goes on with a spoon.
sources: s:wp-hot-chicken — Hot chicken; s:wp-prince-s-hot-chicken-shack — Prince's Hot Chicken Shack; s:wp-hattie-b-s-hot-chicken — Hattie B's Hot Chicken; s:fdc-franks-redhot-nashville-hot — Frank's RedHot Nashville Hot Wings Sauce — branded food label (FDC ID 2621729); s:wp-cayenne-pepper — Cayenne pepper
provenance default: cited · confidence: medium · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## Old Bay Seasoning (sauce)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/sauce/old-bay/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/sauce/old-bay.json
id: old-bay
aliases: Old Bay · the yellow can
said: In Baltimore it goes on the wings without being ordered, the way blue cheese arrives in Buffalo.
facets: base=dry-rub · heat=mild
region: Baltimore, The United States
what: A blend of eighteen herbs and spices built on celery salt — salt and celery seed — with red pepper, black pepper and paprika. Bay leaves, mustard, cardamom, cloves and ginger are among the others listed for the original product held at the Baltimore Museum of Industry. Made for crab and shrimp; used on wings, fries, popcorn, eggs, corn and a great deal else across Maryland, Virginia and the rest of the Mid-Atlantic.
story: Gustav Brunn built a wholesale spice business in Wertheim, Germany, selling to food industries when spices ran short in the hyperinflation after the First World War. The company moved to Frankfurt after the Nazi Party took power. Kristallnacht led to Brunn's arrest and his being sent to Buchenwald. According to his son, Brunn's wife paid a lawyer a large sum to get him released; the family already held American visas, and they escaped to New York City and then to Baltimore, where Brunn had relatives.

He arrived with a small spice grinder. In 1939 he founded the Baltimore Spice Company and produced "Delicious Brand Shrimp and Crab Seasoning", later renamed Old Bay after the Baltimore Steam Packet Company — the "Old Bay Line" — which ran passenger ships from Baltimore to Norfolk in the early 1900s.

McCormick & Company of Hunt Valley, Maryland bought the brand in 1990 and kept the yellow can. In 2017 McCormick switched Old Bay to plastic containers to cut packaging costs; in December 2025 it announced a return to metal cans.

The seasoning kept colonising things. Utz made a Crab Chip on a similar blend; Herr's uses Old Bay itself; Lay's brought out Chesapeake Bay Crab Spice chips in 2018. Baltimore bars sell a 'Crabby Bo' — a National Bohemian beer whose glass rim is wetted and dipped in the seasoning. Flying Dog brewed Dead Rise for the 75th anniversary in 2014, and George's Beverage Company made Old Bay vodka in 2022. McCormick launched Old Bay Hot Sauce ahead of Super Bowl LIV in 2020; the 10 fl oz bottles retailed at $3.49, sold out in thirty minutes, crashed the website, and resold online for between $50 and $200.
how: Shaken over the wings hot out of the fryer, dry, with nothing wet underneath — the celery salt does the work a sauce would. Some Baltimore kitchens go wet: melted butter first, then the shake, which turns it into a paste that clings. Also goes on the fries in the same basket.
today: Made by McCormick, sold in the yellow can again from December 2025. As of 16 September 2026 the USDA label panel recorded for the seasoning reads 140 mg sodium in a ¼-teaspoon serving; that works out to 1,680 mg in a tablespoon, a figure the arithmetic gives and nobody eats. The label declares no sugar line. There is no Scoville number for it and there never has been.
- kin → baltimore-old-bay (style): The style is this can, applied to a wing.
- kin → lemon-pepper-seasoning (sauce): The other dry shake that owns a city; salt-and-celery against zest-and-black-pepper.
- kin → memphis-rub (sauce): The third dry answer, and the only one of the three built on sugar.
- kin → wet-and-dry (term): Baltimore uses the same two words Atlanta does, and means the same thing by them.
- kin → french-fries (dish): Gets the same shake in the same basket, usually without being asked for.
- kin → naked-fry (fry): Needs bare crisp skin; a breaded wing swallows the shake.
- kin → hot-sauce-labels (art): The yellow can is a label people recognise from across a shop.
- not to be confused with memphis-rub: Sugar. A Memphis rub leads with brown sugar and browns on the wing; Old Bay leads with celery salt and stays powdery.
- image: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/images/old-bay/old-bay-old-bay-seasoning.jpg · CC0 1.0 · L1veb4y0udi3 · https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3AOld_Bay_Seasoning.jpg
sources: s:wp-old-bay-seasoning — Old Bay Seasoning; s:fdc-old-bay-seasoning — Old Bay Seasoning — branded food label (FDC ID 404289); s:wp-super-bowl — Super Bowl
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## Ranch dressing (sauce)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/sauce/ranch-dressing/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/sauce/ranch-dressing.json
id: ranch-dressing
aliases: ranch · Hidden Valley Ranch
said: Say 'ranch' anywhere in America and a cup arrives. Say it in Buffalo and somebody looks up.
facets: base=dairy · heat=none
region: The United States
what: A savoury creamy dressing of buttermilk, salt, garlic, onion, black pepper and herbs — commonly chives, parsley and dill — mixed into mayonnaise or another oil emulsion. Sour cream and yogurt sometimes stand in for the buttermilk or the mayonnaise. It has been the best-selling salad dressing in the United States since 1992, when it passed Italian, and it is the most popular wing dip in the country.
story: Steve Henson made the first version in the early 1950s in the Anchorage area, where he worked as a plumbing contractor and cooked for his crews. He retired from plumbing at thirty-five, moved with his wife Gayle to Santa Barbara County, California, and in 1956 bought a guest ranch in San Marcos Pass which he renamed Hidden Valley Ranch. He served the dressing at the ranch steakhouse; guests bought jars to take home. His friend Audrey Ovington, owner of Cold Spring Tavern, was the first commercial customer. By 1957 he was selling packets of mix in stores, and mail-ordering the dry ingredients at 75 cents apiece until every room in the house was given over to it.

The Hensons incorporated, built a factory, and sold nationally. Manufacturing moved to San Jose, then Colorado, then Sparks, Nevada in 1972. In October 1972 Clorox bought Hidden Valley Ranch for $8 million and Henson retired. Clorox reformulated it several times — adding buttermilk flavouring to the seasoning so the dressing could be made with cheaper regular milk — and in 1983 developed a shelf-stable bottled version.

The name started a fight. Ranch Style Beans had been on sale since the early 1930s, and in 1975 its Texas maker Waples-Platter sued Kraft Foods and General Foods for using "ranch style" on salad dressings. Judge Eldon Brooks Mahon tried the case in Fort Worth in 1976 and ruled for Waples-Platter; his opinion catalogues the ranch and ranch-style products then on the market, most of them built to compete with Hidden Valley. Henson himself was deposed about the history.

It reached the wing through pizza. Domino's began offering ranch as a condiment with its chicken wings and pizzas in 1994, and the pairing took. Cool Ranch Doritos had arrived in 1987; Hidden Valley Ranch Wavy Lay's in 1994.
how: Cold, in a cup, beside the wing. Home versions mix buttermilk, mayonnaise and sour cream with lemon juice, minced garlic, onion powder, black pepper and dried herbs, and want an hour in the refrigerator before the herbs give anything up. It doubles as the dip for the celery and carrots and as the dressing on the salad nobody ordered.
today: Best-selling dressing in the country and, by the count in the standard wing description, the most popular wing dip. In 2017 a study by the Association for Dressings and Sauces found 40% of Americans named ranch their favourite dressing. As of 16 September 2026 the USDA label panel for Hidden Valley Original Ranch Topping & Dip reads 240 mg sodium and 1 g sugar in a 2-tablespoon serving — 120 mg and 0.5 g in one tablespoon. Soybean oil first, egg yolk third, buttermilk sixth. No Scoville number, and nothing on the label to warrant one.
- kin → blue-cheese-dressing (sauce): The rival in the cup, and the one Buffalo serves.
- kin → ranch-vs-blue-cheese (story): The argument this dip is the winning side of nationally and the losing side of in one city.
- kin → buffalo (style): Named in the style's service alongside blue cheese, and the one Buffalo does not reach for.
- kin → celery-and-carrots (dish): The other thing in the basket it gets dipped in.
- kin → wingstop (place): Sells it as a dip beside thirteen wing sauces.
- kin → buffalo-sauce (sauce): What it is there to cool, and what it is accused of cancelling out.
- kin → garlic-parmesan-sauce (sauce): Shares the garlic-and-dairy register; this one stays in the cup.
- kin → alabama-white-sauce (sauce): The Southern white sauce built for dunking rather than dipping.
- kin → boneless-wings (dish): The order it turns up with most often, and the pairing the argument gets loudest about.
- not to be confused with blue-cheese-dressing: Herbs against cheese. Ranch is buttermilk, garlic, onion and dill; blue cheese has visible cheese in it.
- not to be confused with garlic-parmesan-sauce: Where it goes. Ranch sits in a cup; garlic parm goes on the wing.
- image: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/images/ranch-dressing/ranch-dressing-ranch-dressing.jpg · CC BY 2.0 · Whitney from Chicago, IL · https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3ARanch_dressing.jpg
- image: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/images/ranch-dressing/ranch-dressing-hopmonk-march-2026-sarah-stierch-02.jpg · CC0 1.0 · Missvain · https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3AHopmonk_-_March_2026_-_Sarah_Stierch_02.jpg
