## Soy garlic sauce (sauce)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/sauce/soy-garlic-sauce/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/sauce/soy-garlic-sauce.json
id: soy-garlic-sauce
aliases: ganjang chicken sauce · ganjang-chikin sauce · soy garlic
said: Ganjang (간장) is soy sauce. A Korean counter offers soy garlic or spicy, and banban gets you both.
facets: base=soy-sweet · heat=none
region: Korean America, The United States
what: A brown glaze of soy sauce, sugar and garlic, brushed onto fried chicken after the fryer. Sweet and savoury rather than hot; often heavily garlicky. Ganjang-chikin — soy sauce chicken — is the Korean name for the dish it makes. A honey version, sweeter and stickier, is sold alongside it.
story: Bonchon standardised two flagship sauces, soy garlic and spicy, made with regional Korean ingredients and manufactured centrally in South Korean facilities so every franchise tastes the same. Jinduk Seo founded the chain in Busan in 2002; its name means "my hometown". Its first US location was in Fort Lee, New Jersey, and it is credited as the first Korean fried chicken brand to expand internationally.

The sauce sits in an old lineage. Pogye (포계), a fried chicken dish of the early Joseon dynasty, was sautéed in oil while soy sauce, sesame oil, flour-and-water and vinegar were poured on in turn.

Bonchon stopped retailing in South Korea by the end of 2016 to concentrate on export. VIG Partners took a majority stake in December 2018; the headquarters moved to Dallas, Texas in 2021. Around 500 restaurants operate in over ten countries.

*Inference —* soy garlic is the sauce that carried Korean fried chicken to people who do not want heat, which is most of a mall food court.
how: Double-fry, then paint. The sugar in the glaze catches on a still-hot crust and sets glossy; too much of it and the crust goes soft, which is why it is brushed thin rather than tossed. Serve with pickled radish. Scallion-topped padak is the same bird under shredded scallion instead.
today: Sold at Korean fried chicken chains across the United States and bottled by small importers. As of 16 September 2026 the USDA label panel for We Love You Soy Garlic Korean Chicken Wing Sauce & Glaze reads 430 mg sodium and 6 g sugar in a 1-tablespoon serving, with soy sauce first, sugar second and granulated garlic fourth. Black pepper is the only pepper on it, and no Scoville number is published — for a sauce that claims no heat, none is expected.
- kin → korean-american (style): One of the two sauces the style is ordered by.
- kin → yangnyeom-sauce (sauce): The other half of banban, and the spicy one.
- kin → bonchon (place): Standardised it as a flagship sauce and ships it from Korean plants to every franchise.
- kin → teriyaki-sauce (sauce): The nearest American shelf relative: soy, sugar and a glaze, out of Japan rather than Korea.
- kin → double-fry (fry): The thin crackly crust this glaze is painted onto.
- kin → pickled-radish (dish): Comes in the same box, and cuts the sugar.
- kin → honey-bbq-sauce (sauce): The American sweet-brown wing, reached through corn syrup and tomato instead of soy.
- kin → garlic-parmesan-sauce (sauce): The other garlic-forward wing with no heat in it at all.
- not to be confused with teriyaki-sauce: Garlic. Soy garlic leads on it; a Japanese teriyaki tare is soy, mirin and sugar, and garlic is uncommon in the traditional version.
sources: s:wp-bonchon-chicken — Bonchon Chicken; s:wp-korean-fried-chicken — Korean fried chicken; s:fdc-we-love-you-soy-garlic — We Love You Soy Garlic Korean Chicken Wing Sauce & Glaze — branded food label (FDC ID 2511275)
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## Sweet chili sauce (sauce)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/sauce/sweet-chili-sauce/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/sauce/sweet-chili-sauce.json
id: sweet-chili-sauce
aliases: sweet Thai chili sauce · nam chim kai · น้ำจิ้มไก่
said: Nam chim kai (น้ำจิ้มไก่) is Thai for dipping sauce for chicken. The name says what it is for.
facets: base=other · heat=mild
region: The United States
what: A clear, thickened red sauce of chillies, rice wine vinegar and sugar, often with garlic and sometimes fish sauce. Red chilli peppers — Fresno, Thai or red jalapeños — give it its flecks. Known in Thailand as nam chim kai, a dipping sauce for chicken, and used across Thai, Afghan, Malaysian and Western cooking. In European Chinese restaurants it is the dip for prawn toast, egg rolls, lettuce wraps, spring rolls and chicken wings.
story: It arrived on American wing boards through the takeaway counter rather than the wing bar. In Australia, New Zealand, Europe, Canada and the United States it is stocked as a condiment in takeaway shops and supermarkets, and it is sold bottled everywhere.

The wing board made room for it. As the wing market grew, restaurants created and used sauces beyond Buffalo, some of them drawn from Chinese, Japanese, Thai, Caribbean and Indian cooking.

*Inference —* sweet chili is the sauce that taught American wing menus that sweet and chile could sit in the same bottle without tomato between them. Hot honey and mango habanero both work the same seam.
how: Straight from the bottle. It is already thickened, so it coats a fried wing without warming and does not need butter or oil to carry it. Toss, or serve in a cup as a dip. A kitchen after more heat adds sriracha or fresh chilli, and a kitchen after more bite adds lime.
today: On supermarket shelves and takeaway counters across the country, and on wing boards as a standing flavour. As of 16 September 2026 the USDA label panel for Ka-Me Sweet Chili Sauce reads 220 mg sodium and 6 g sugar in a 1-tablespoon serving, with water first, cane sugar second and pickled chili third. No Scoville number is published — usual for this shelf.
- kin → hot-honey (sauce): The other sweet-and-chile pour on the board; this one is thickened and vinegared, that one is honey.
- kin → mango-habanero (sauce): The American version of the same idea, with fruit doing the sweetening.
- kin → yangnyeom-sauce (sauce): The Korean sweet-chile glaze, fermented rather than vinegared.
- kin → teriyaki-sauce (sauce): Shares the Asian-condiment shelf that wing boards borrow from.
- kin → jerk-marinade (sauce): Turns up beside jerk wings as the sweet dip.
- kin → the-toss (fry): Needs no warming to go in the bowl — it is already thick enough to coat.
- kin → sauce-on-the-side (fry): As often a dip in a cup as a coating on the wing.
- not to be confused with mango-habanero: Fruit. Mango habanero leads with corn syrup and mango puree; sweet chili is sugar, chilli and vinegar with nothing else sweet in it.
sources: s:wp-sweet-chili-sauce — Sweet chili sauce; s:wp-buffalo-wing — Buffalo wing; s:wp-sriracha — Sriracha; s:fdc-ka-me-sweet-chili — Ka-Me Sweet Chili Sauce — branded food label (FDC ID 2523929)
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## Teriyaki sauce (sauce)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/sauce/teriyaki-sauce/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/sauce/teriyaki-sauce.json
id: teriyaki-sauce
aliases: teriyaki · tare
said: Teri (照り) is the shine the sugar gives; yaki (焼き) is grilling or broiling. The sauce is named for what it looks like after the heat.
facets: base=soy-sweet · heat=none
region: The United States, Hawaii, The Pacific Northwest
what: Soy sauce, mirin or sake, and sugar, boiled down to a glaze. The Japanese name for it is tare (タレ). Traditionally the meat is dipped in it or brushed with it while cooking; ginger goes in sometimes, spring onion over the top. In North America the word covers any dish made with a teriyaki-like sauce, including versions using substitutes for sake or mirin, or adding sesame or garlic — both uncommon in Japanese cooking. It goes on chicken wings and is used as a dipping sauce.
story: Teriyaki emerged as a cooking technique in Japan during the Edo period; it is believed to have developed during the 1600s. Fish carry it there — yellowtail, marlin, skipjack tuna, salmon, trout, mackerel — while the West puts it on chicken, pork, lamb and beef.

Japanese immigrants brought it to Hawaii, where it changed with local ingredients and became a fixture of the plate lunch. Seattle grew a teriyaki culture of its own in the 1990s; by 2010 more than eighty-three restaurants in the city had teriyaki in the name, and some outlets call it the city's signature cuisine. The first standalone teriyaki restaurant, Toshi's Teriyaki, opened in Lower Queen Anne in 1976, selling low-cost chicken and beef skewers; by 1996 it had grown to seventeen locations.

The American sauce is generally sweet, though it can be made spicy. Pineapple juice is sometimes used — it sweetens and its bromelain enzymes tenderise the meat. Grilling first and pouring the sauce on afterwards, or using sweet sauce as a marinade, are both non-traditional methods.

*Inference —* the teriyaki wing came off the plate lunch and the skewer counter, not off a Buffalo menu, and arrived on wing boards already familiar to everyone.
how: Blend soy sauce, sake or mirin and sugar over heat, boil and reduce to the thickness you want. Brush it on the wings while they grill or broil, in coats, letting each set before the next. For fried wings, toss them in the reduced sauce off the heat. Cornstarch, potato starch or kuzu root starch thickens a thin one. Sugar is why it goes on late: it darkens fast over direct heat.
today: Bottled by every large soy-sauce maker and on wing boards nationally. As of 16 September 2026 the USDA label panel for Kikkoman Teriyaki Marinade & Sauce reads 610 mg sodium and 2 g sugar in a 1-tablespoon serving — the highest sodium per tablespoon of any sauce measured for this set, ahead of Frank's RedHot at 570. Soy sauce is first; no chile appears on the label and no Scoville number is published.
- kin → soy-garlic-sauce (sauce): The Korean fried chicken relative; soy and sugar again, with garlic pushed forward.
- kin → sweet-chili-sauce (sauce): Shares the Asian-condiment shelf that American wing boards borrow from.
- kin → grill (fry): The cooking the word is named for: teri is the shine, yaki is the grilling.
- kin → honey-bbq-sauce (sauce): The American sweet glaze doing the same job through tomato and corn syrup.
- kin → yangnyeom-sauce (sauce): The other East Asian glaze on a wing board, built on fermented chile paste rather than soy and sugar.
- kin → the-toss (fry): Fried wings meet it in the bowl; grilled wings meet it on the brush.
- kin → buffalo-wild-wings (place): Carries it as one flavour among more than a dozen.
- not to be confused with soy-garlic-sauce: Garlic and mirin. Teriyaki's sweetness comes from mirin or sugar; soy garlic leads with garlic and apple juice concentrate.
- image: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/images/teriyaki-sauce/teriyaki-sauce-teriyaki-sauce.jpg · CC BY 2.0 · David J · https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3ATeriyaki_sauce.jpg
sources: s:wp-teriyaki — Teriyaki; s:wp-buffalo-wing — Buffalo wing; s:fdc-kikkoman-teriyaki — Kikkoman Teriyaki Marinade & Sauce — branded food label (FDC ID 2085929); s:wikibooks-teriyaki-sauce — Cookbook:Teriyaki Sauce
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## Yangnyeom sauce (sauce)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/sauce/yangnyeom-sauce/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/sauce/yangnyeom-sauce.json
id: yangnyeom-sauce
aliases: yangnyeom · seasoned sauce · sweet and spicy
said: 양념 means seasoning. Order banban — 반반, half-half — and the box arrives half in this sauce, half plain.
facets: base=other · heat=medium
region: Korean America, The United States
what: A sweet and spicy glaze built on gochujang — a fermented Korean paste of red chili powder, glutinous rice, fermented soybean powder, barley malt powder and salt — with garlic, sugar and other seasonings. Painted onto fried chicken with a brush after the fryer, in a thin even coat rather than a toss. Yangnyeom chicken is the dish; this is what makes it.
story: Yun Jonggye started it in 1982, at a fried chicken restaurant in Daegu that later became Mexican Chicken. He noticed customers struggling with the hard, crisp layers of fried chicken — scraped palates among the complaints — and decided to soften the shell by marinating the bird sweet and spicy.

The ground was already laid. Frying chicken in Korea goes back centuries; pogye (포계) in the early Joseon dynasty was sautéed in oil with soy sauce, sesame oil, flour-and-water and vinegar poured on in turn. Chicken-eating took off in the late 1960s when Myeongdong Yeongyang Center began selling whole chicken roasted over an electric oven, and US military presence after the Korean War brought deep-frying. The first modern franchise, Lims Chicken, opened in 1977 in the basement of the Shinsegae Department Store on Chungmu-ro in Seoul. Beer made it a habit: chimaek, from chicken and maekju.

Gochujang itself is older than the chile in it. Pepper paste appears in Korean texts from 1433 and 1445, before chili peppers reached Korea — Portuguese traders brought those to East Asia in the early 16th century. Sunchang gochujang has been a regional speciality since the 14th century.

Julia Moskin of The New York Times called yangnyeom chicken "the apotheosis of the Korean style" of fried chicken. By 2026 there were 40,000 fried chicken restaurants in South Korea and 1,800 more run internationally by Korean brands in sixty countries.
how: Double-fry first, so the crust can take a wet coat without going soft. Warm the sauce, then hand-paint it on with a brush — the point is a thin layer over the whole bird rather than a soaked one. Serve with pickled radish and beer. Half-and-half orders get one sauce and one plain in the same box.
today: Made in-house at Korean fried chicken shops and sold bottled by several importers. As of 16 September 2026 the USDA label panel for Roland Spicy Gochujang Korean BBQ Sauce reads 469 mg sodium and 7 g sugar in a 2-tablespoon serving — 234 mg and 3.5 g in one tablespoon, with red pepper paste second. Nobody publishes a Scoville number. Gochujang has its own scale, the Gochujang hot-taste unit, measured by chromatography of capsaicin and dihydrocapsaicin and sorted into five levels from Mild to Extreme Hot — but that rates the paste, not a finished sauce.
- kin → korean-american (style): The style is this glaze, the double fry and the box it arrives in.
- kin → soy-garlic-sauce (sauce): The other half of the order, and the sauce most shops pair it against.
- kin → double-fry (fry): The crust that lets a wet glaze go on without collapsing.
- kin → pickled-radish (dish): The cube of daikon that comes in the same box to cut the sugar.
- kin → bonchon (place): Built a chain on two sauces, of which this is the spicy one.
- kin → sweet-chili-sauce (sauce): The other sweet-chile glaze on an American wing menu; rice vinegar and sugar rather than fermented soybean and rice.
- kin → hot-honey (sauce): Reaches the same sweet-then-heat place with honey instead of fermentation.
- kin → buffalo-sauce (sauce): The American answer to the same question, and the one that shakes rather than paints.
- not to be confused with soy-garlic-sauce: Colour and lead ingredient. Yangnyeom is red and leads with gochujang; soy garlic is brown and leads with soy sauce.
- image: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/images/yangnyeom-sauce/yangnyeom-sauce-korean-fried-chicken-yangnyeom.jpg · CC BY 2.0 · Yosomono · https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3AKorean_fried_chicken_yangnyeom.jpg
- image: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/images/yangnyeom-sauce/yangnyeom-sauce-yangnyeom-chicken.jpg · CC0 1.0 · Brandon Oh · https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3AYangnyeom-chicken.jpg
sources: s:wp-yangnyeom-chicken — Yangnyeom chicken; s:wp-korean-fried-chicken — Korean fried chicken; s:wp-gochujang — Gochujang; s:fdc-roland-gochujang-korean-bbq — Roland Spicy Gochujang Korean BBQ Sauce — branded food label (FDC ID 1958977)
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## beef on weck (dish)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/dish/beef-on-weck/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/dish/beef-on-weck.json
id: beef-on-weck
aliases: beef on kummelweck
said: Weck rhymes with deck. Order it rare, dipped, with horseradish, and expect to be asked how much.
facets: course=main
region: Western New York
what: Rare roast beef, hand-carved thin, on a kummelweck roll topped with kosher salt and caraway seeds. The cut face of the top half gets dipped in jus from the roast; prepared horseradish comes on the side for the eater to spread. Along with wings and sponge candy it is one of the three best-known Buffalo specialties.
story: The sandwich predates the wing by roughly a century, though its history is not well established. A German baker named William Wahr, thought to have come from the Black Forest, is believed to have made the kummelweck roll in Buffalo, possibly modelled on the Swabian Schwäbische Seele, a thin salt-and-caraway roll left as a ceremonial offering for the dead. A Western New York butcher puts the sandwich's creation somewhere in the mid-19th century. A local pub owner is said to have built it on the salted roll so the salt would sell more drink.

Kümmel is German for caraway and Weck means roll in the south-western dialects of the Palatinate, the Saarland, Baden and Swabia. The American roll ended up softer and fluffier than a German Kümmelbrötchen. Buffalo-area bakeries are the only commercial source for it.

The wing dragged the sandwich out of town. Buffalo Wild Wings was started by former Western New York residents and opened as "Buffalo Wild Wings and Weck", abbreviated BW3 — the third W was the weck. The chain dropped it in 1998 and some people still say BW3.
how: Roast the beef slowly, keep it rare, and carve it thin by hand, often at a carving station in view. Dip the cut face of the top half of the roll in the jus. Leave the horseradish to the eater. The salt on the crust is coarse and it is meant to be tasted, which is the part a bar counted on.
today: Expatriates carried it: PJ's BAR-B-QSA in Saratoga Springs is noted for its version, and Bobby Flay and Anthony Bourdain have both put it on television. *Inference —* the roll is the limit on how far it travels, because nobody outside Buffalo bakes it commercially.
- kin → weck (term): The word for the roll, and the German dialect behind it.
- kin → buffalo (style): Shares a city and a bar counter with it; the sandwich is the older of the two by about a century.
- kin → buffalo-wild-wings (place): Opened as Buffalo Wild Wings and Weck and carried this sandwich in its name until 1998.
- kin → the-pitcher (dish): The salted crust was reportedly built to sell more of it.
- kin → wing-basket (dish): The other thing a Buffalo bar hands across the same counter.
- kin → gabriels-gate (place): A Buffalo tavern on this project's wing list; the sandwich and the wing share those rooms.
sources: s:wp-beef-on-weck — Beef on weck; s:wp-buffalo-new-york — Buffalo, New York; s:wp-buffalo-wild-wings — Buffalo Wild Wings
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## boneless wings (dish)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/dish/boneless-wings/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/dish/boneless-wings.json
id: boneless-wings
aliases: boneless · wyngz · boneless chicken wings
said: Ordered by count like a wing and priced like a wing. A kitchen that sells both will ask bone-in or boneless before it asks the sauce.
facets: course=main · cut=boneless
region: The United States
what: Small pieces of skinless, boneless chicken breast coated in flour and spices, then fried or baked, like a chicken nugget, and tossed in or served with the same sauces as a Buffalo wing. Restaurants began offering them after the price of raw wings rose and as some diners wanted a neater way to eat; they are sometimes marketed under the name wyngz.
story: The argument over the word reached a state supreme court. On 25 July 2024 the Supreme Court of Ohio decided Berkheimer v. REKM, L.L.C., slip op. No. 2024-Ohio-2787, 4 to 3. Michael Berkheimer had ordered boneless wings with parmesan garlic sauce at Wings on Brookwood in Hamilton, Ohio, in 2016. A bone lodged in his esophagus and tore it, and the tear caused an infection; CBS News reports the bone at 5 centimetres, while a law-firm note on the case describes it as roughly 1 3/8 inches. He sued, saying the restaurant failed to warn him that boneless wings could contain bones. The trial court gave the restaurant summary judgment and the appeals court affirmed.

Justice Joseph T. Deters wrote for the majority. The Associated Press reports the opinion holding that a diner reading boneless wings on a menu would no more believe the restaurant was warranting the absence of bones than a person eating chicken fingers would think he had been served fingers. CBS News quotes the opinion directly: "The food item's label on the menu described a cooking style; it was not a guarantee."

Justice Michael P. Donnelly dissented, joined by Justices Melody J. Stewart and Jennifer Brunner. He called the majority's reasoning "utter jabberwocky". Of the word itself he wrote: "When they read the word 'boneless,' they think that it means 'without bones,' as do all sensible people." And of the jury the case never reached: "Does anyone really believe that the parents in this country who feed their young children boneless wings or chicken tenders or chicken nuggets or chicken fingers expect bones to be in the chicken? Of course they don't".

*Inference —* the two opinions are arguing about different things. One asks what a menu word does — names a preparation — and the other asks what a customer hears. This project records both and adjudicates neither; the court's own count was four to three.
how: Cut breast into roughly one-inch pieces. Dredge in seasoned flour, or batter, then fry or bake. Sauce goes on the same way it goes on a wing: into a bowl, sauce poured over, shaken. Because there is no skin and no bone, the coating is doing all the work the skin does on a bone-in wing, and it goes soft faster once the sauce hits it.
today: On the menu at nearly every chain and most bars, usually priced per piece against the bone-in count on the same board. *Inference —* the price gap moves with the wholesale wing market rather than with the cost of breast meat, which is why the boneless order is sometimes the cheaper one and sometimes not.
- kin → boneless (term): The word, and the reasoning a 4-3 Ohio Supreme Court majority gave for what it describes.
- kin → boneless-is-not-a-wing (story): The argument itself, with the people who make it named and quoted.
- kin → wing-cut (fry): The step this skips entirely: no joints, no tip, no bone.
- kin → buffalo (style): Lends its sauce and its counting to something cut from the breast.
- kin → buffalo-sauce (sauce): The same sauce goes on, which is most of why the name travelled.
- kin → dredge (fry): The flour-and-spice coat that stands in for skin.
- kin → wingstop (place): Sells bone-in and boneless wings side by side on one menu.
- kin → buffalo-wild-wings (place): Carries both counts on the same board, which is where most Americans meet the choice.
- kin → the-price-of-a-wing (story): The wholesale wing price is the reason this item exists at all.
- not to be confused with wing-cut: Bones. A bone-in wing is two pieces cut from one limb; a boneless wing is breast meat cut into chunks.
- image: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/images/boneless-wings/boneless-wings-seitan-buffalo-wings-8442539976.jpg · CC BY 2.0 · Scott Veg · https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3ASeitan_Buffalo_Wings_%288442539976%29.jpg

## buffalo chicken dip (dish)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/dish/buffalo-chicken-dip/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/dish/buffalo-chicken-dip.json
id: buffalo-chicken-dip
aliases: buffalo chicken wing dip · wing dip
said: Brought in the dish it was baked in, set on a towel, eaten with whatever is nearest.
facets: course=side · styles=buffalo
region: The United States
what: Shredded chicken, cream cheese, cayenne-and-butter wing sauce and a dairy dressing, baked until it bubbles and eaten hot with chips, celery or bread. It takes the flavour of a wing and removes the bone, the skin, the fryer and the plate.
story: The dish belongs to a wider pattern the wing set off. Buffalo as a name is now applied to other spiced fried foods served with dipping sauces — boneless wings, chicken fries, chicken nuggets, popcorn chicken, shrimp, cauliflower — and to dishes seasoned with the sauce rather than fried at all, pizza among them. The sauce travelled and the method stayed behind.

The occasion carried it. The Super Bowl is the second-largest event for American food consumption, behind Thanksgiving dinner, and a baked dip suits a room where nobody is running a fryer.

*Tradition holds —* the dip is a 1990s-and-after home invention, spread by recipe cards, community cookbooks and hot-sauce marketing rather than by any restaurant. This project has not found a source that names a first cook or a first year, and the origin is recorded here as unsettled rather than as anyone's.
how: Shred cooked chicken. Beat it into softened cream cheese with cayenne pepper sauce and butter, or with bottled wing sauce, then fold in blue cheese or ranch dressing and shredded cheese. Bake until it bubbles at the edge. Serve hot in the baking dish with celery, carrots, tortilla chips or torn bread. Cold, it sets solid and is reheated rather than eaten.
today: A fixture of American party tables in winter, and a standing item in supermarket deli cases around the Super Bowl. *Inference —* the dip is how the Buffalo flavour reaches households that will not deep-fry indoors, which is most of them.
- kin → buffalo-sauce (sauce): The cayenne-and-butter sauce this is built from, off the bottle rather than out of a bowl.
- kin → buffalo (style): The style whose taste this keeps and whose method it drops.
- kin → blue-cheese-dressing (sauce): Folded in rather than served beside, which is the whole design of the dish.
- kin → ranch-dressing (sauce): The other dressing folded in, and the more common one nationally.
- kin → celery-and-carrots (dish): Comes along as the dipper, doing at a party what it does on a plate.
- kin → super-bowl-sunday (event): The day this is made for, on the second-biggest American eating day of the year.
- kin → boneless-wings (dish): The other thing Buffalo sauce does to breast meat when the wing gets expensive.
- kin → buffalo-chicken-pizza (dish): The same move onto a different carrier.
sources: s:wp-buffalo-wing — Buffalo wing; s:wp-super-bowl — Super Bowl; s:wp-frank-s-redhot — Frank's RedHot; s:wp-blue-cheese-dressing — Blue cheese dressing; s:wp-ranch-dressing — Ranch dressing
provenance default: cited · confidence: medium · needs_verification: True · updated: 2026-09-16

## buffalo chicken pizza (dish)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/dish/buffalo-chicken-pizza/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/dish/buffalo-chicken-pizza.json
id: buffalo-chicken-pizza
aliases: buffalo chicken pie · wing pizza
said: Ordered with the blue cheese question attached: drizzled on top, or in a cup.
facets: course=main · styles=buffalo
region: Western New York, The United States
what: A pizza sauced with cayenne-and-butter wing sauce instead of tomato, topped with chicken and mozzarella, and finished with blue cheese or ranch. Buffalo is applied here to a dish that is seasoned with the sauce rather than fried in the style at all.
story: The pizza chains and the wing arrived at each other from both directions. In 1994, following four Super Bowl appearances by the Buffalo Bills, Domino's added Buffalo wings to its national menu, and Pizza Hut followed the next year. The wing went onto the pizza menu first; the sauce went onto the pizza after.

*Inference —* the order runs the other way in Buffalo itself, where pizzerias were already selling wings out of the same kitchen. A shop with a fryer for wings and an oven for pizza has both halves of this dish on the line before anyone names it.
how: Brush the base with wing sauce in place of tomato. Cooked chicken — often the same breast meat a boneless order uses — mozzarella, sometimes red onion. Bake. Finish with a drizzle of blue cheese or ranch after the oven, not before, so the dressing does not split. Celery on the side is optional and in Buffalo it is not.
today: Carried by national chains and by independent pizzerias in Western New York, where the wing and the pie have shared a counter for decades. *Inference —* the dish is the clearest case of Buffalo as a flavour word: nothing about it is fried, and the name still reads.
- kin → buffalo-sauce (sauce): Replaces the tomato entirely; that substitution is the whole dish.
- kin → buffalo (style): The style that lent its name to something with no fryer in it.
- kin → buffalo-word (term): The clearest case of the word meaning a sauce rather than a city or a method.
- kin → la-nova-pizzeria (place): A Buffalo house selling pizza and wings across one counter, which is where this combination lives.
- kin → blue-cheese-dressing (sauce): Goes over the top after the oven, or into a cup, and the table argues about which.
- kin → boneless-wings (dish): Uses the same breast meat and the same sauce, on a crust instead of in a basket.
- kin → pizza-logs (dish): Buffalo's other pizza-shaped bar food, fried instead of baked.
- kin → super-bowl-sunday (event): The day both halves of it get delivered.
sources: s:wp-buffalo-wing — Buffalo wing; s:wp-pizza-hut — Pizza Hut; s:wp-blue-cheese-dressing — Blue cheese dressing

## celery and carrots (dish)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/dish/celery-and-carrots/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/dish/celery-and-carrots.json
id: celery-and-carrots
aliases: celery · veggie sticks · the vegetables
said: Nobody orders it. It arrives. In Buffalo a medium order comes with celery and blue cheese whether you asked or not.
facets: course=side · styles=buffalo
region: Western New York, The United States
what: Cut celery, usually with carrot sticks, served cold beside hot wings with a cup of blue cheese or ranch that both the vegetables and the wings go into. Celery here is the petiole — the leaf stalk of Apium graveolens — cut raw to finger length. It cools the mouth between wings, it carries dip, and it is the one item on the plate nobody asks for.
story: The Anchor Bar's account puts the vegetables on the plate from the first night: on 4 March 1964 Teressa Bellissimo fried wings for her son Dominic's friends and brought out cut celery and blue cheese for dipping as hors d'oeuvres. The celery was there to be grabbed because celery was everywhere. The New York Public Library's historical menu archive shows it as the third-most-popular item on New York City menus through the 19th and early 20th centuries, behind only coffee and tea, served in celery vases to be salted and eaten raw; whole varieties have since vanished because they were hard to grow and did not ship. North American commercial growing narrowed onto one cultivar, 'Pascal'.

*Inference —* the wing plate kept a garnish the rest of American dining dropped, so a bar basket in 2026 preserves a habit the city around it stopped having.
how: Cut the petiole into sticks a little longer than a wing. The strings that peel off a stalk are bundles of angular collenchyma cells sitting outside the vascular bundles, which is why celery pulls apart lengthways and not across. Carrots go in raw, as sticks or as whole small carrots. Everything serves cold against hot wings, with the dip in its own cup. Freshly cut celery decays fast, so a kitchen cuts near service and keeps it at 0–2 °C.
today: Wingstop sells veggie sticks — carrots and/or celery — as a side you pay for. A Buffalo counter still puts them on the plate unasked. *Tradition holds —* the celery is the first thing left in the basket and the last thing a Buffalo bar would stop putting there.
- kin → buffalo (style): The style whose plate this sits on; the celery came off the same bar's hors d'oeuvres, not off a recipe.
- kin → anchor-bar (place): Brought out the cut celery and blue cheese with the first wings it claims, on 4 March 1964.
- kin → teressa-bellissimo (person): Fried the wings and sent the vegetables out with them.
- kin → blue-cheese-dressing (sauce): The cup both the celery and the wing go into in Buffalo.
- kin → ranch-dressing (sauce): The dip most of America reaches for instead, and the argument that follows.
- kin → wing-basket (dish): What the vegetables ride in, and why a wing order is a plate rather than a piece of meat.
- kin → white-bread-and-pickles (dish): Nashville's answer to the same problem — something cold and cheap under something hot.
- kin → pickled-radish (dish): Seoul's answer to the same problem, cubed and sweet instead of raw and green.
- image: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/images/celery-and-carrots/celery-and-carrots-buffalo-wings.jpg · CC BY 2.0 · John Tornow · https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3ABuffalo_wings.jpg
- image: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/images/celery-and-carrots/celery-and-carrots-chicken-wings-at-west-side-story-in-february-2025.jpg · CC BY-SA 4.0 · JIP · https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3AChicken_wings_at_West_Side_Story_in_February_2025.jpg

## chicken and waffles (dish)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/dish/chicken-and-waffles/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/dish/chicken-and-waffles.json
id: chicken-and-waffles
aliases: chicken 'n' waffles
said: Butter and syrup on the waffle, hot sauce on the chicken, and the two meet in the middle of the plate.
facets: course=main
region: The American South, New York City, Southern California, The United States
what: Fried chicken on a waffle, eaten with butter and syrup as a waffle would be, and often with hot sauce. It belongs to several culinary traditions at once — Pennsylvania Dutch cuisine and soul food among them — and the two versions are not the same dish.
story: The Pennsylvania Dutch version came first and is not fried: pulled, stewed chicken over a plain waffle, covered in gravy, appearing in the 1600s in Pennsylvania Dutch country. Waffles entered American cuisine with European colonists in the 1600s, and the food's popularity rose after 1789 when Thomas Jefferson bought four waffle irons in Amsterdam. In the early 1800s hotels and resorts outside Philadelphia served waffles with fried catfish; fried chicken gradually replaced the catfish because catfish was seasonal. By the 1860s waffles with chicken and gravy were a common Sunday dish among the Pennsylvania Dutch. By the 1840s broiled chicken and waffles were the celebrated specialty at Warriner's Tavern in Springfield, Massachusetts, run by Jeremy and Phoebe Warriner, two well-known abolitionists.

The fried version is associated with the American South and with soul food, and it grew after the Wells Supper Club opened in Harlem in 1938; the dish was served in Harlem as early as the 1930s at Tillie's Chicken Shack and Richard Wells's jazz nightclub, and in 1935 the trumpeter Bunny Berigan composed an instrumental called "Chicken and Waffles". A traditional account within soul food holds that the combination was a delicacy, and it remained "a special-occasion meal in African American families" for decades. The combination is absent from early Southern cookbooks — not in Mrs. Porter's Southern Cookery Book of 1871, nor in Abby Fisher's What Mrs. Fisher Knows About Old Southern Cooking of 1881, generally considered the first cookbook written by an African American — which may point to a later origin than the traditional account suggests.

Los Angeles got it by 1931, at a restaurant called The Maryland which marketed it as a Southern specialty, and again from 1975 onward through Herb Hudson's Roscoe's House of Chicken and Waffles, opened by a former Harlem resident and now a small chain.
how: Fry the chicken — bone-in pieces, or wings on a wing menu. Bake the waffle to order and serve it as a breakfast waffle, with butter and syrup. Chicken goes on top or beside. Hot sauce is the eater's call; in Baltimore, where the dish is popular enough to be a local custom, so is the order in which it goes on.
today: Served in specialty restaurants across the United States and on brunch menus that have never heard of Harlem or Lancaster County. *Inference —* the wing version is the newest branch: a wing menu can do the whole dish without a second fryer setting, and it lets a bar sell breakfast at eleven at night.
- kin → harolds-chicken-shack (place): Chicago's fried-chicken counter out of the same soul food tradition this dish's Harlem version belongs to.
- kin → uncle-remus-saucy-fried-chicken (place): Another Chicago house frying the chicken half of this plate.
- kin → nashville-hot (style): The other place fried chicken and a starch arrive as one plate, with bread instead of a waffle.
- kin → white-bread-and-pickles (dish): Nashville's starch under the bird; here it is sweet and on top.
- kin → hot-honey (sauce): The sweet-hot finish that does on a wing what syrup does here.
- kin → brine (fry): The buttermilk soak the chicken half usually gets first.
- kin → dredge (fry): The flour coat that makes the chicken half work against syrup.
sources: s:wp-chicken-and-waffles — Chicken and waffles; s:wp-soul-food — Soul food; s:wp-fried-chicken — Fried chicken
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## chicken riggies (dish)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/dish/chicken-riggies/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/dish/chicken-riggies.json
id: chicken-riggies
aliases: Utica riggies · riggies
said: Riggies is rigatoni. Ask for hot and you get cherry peppers; ask for sweet and you get the other kind.
facets: course=main
region: Upstate New York
what: An Italian-American pasta dish from the Utica–Rome area of New York: chicken, rigatoni, and hot or sweet peppers in a spicy cream-and-tomato sauce. Variations are many; the peppers and the rigatoni are the constants.
story: Its origin is unclear, and many chefs from the Utica area claim the dish.

*Inference —* that sentence is the same sentence upstate New York keeps writing about its own food. A hundred miles west, three Bellissimo accounts and one John Young compete over a wing; here a dozen Utica kitchens compete over a pasta, and in neither case does a document settle it. What both traditions do instead is hold contests.
how: Brown chicken, build a sauce of tomato and cream, and load it with peppers — cherry peppers for heat, sweet peppers for the other way. Toss through rigatoni, whose ridges and bore hold a sauce that thin-walled pasta would shed.
today: Served across the Utica–Rome corridor as a restaurant staple and a home dish. *Tradition holds —* riggies, greens and half-moons are the three things a Utica table names as its own.
- kin → buffalo (style): The other upstate New York dish whose origin a dozen people claim; same state, same kind of argument.
- kin → the-origin-fight (story): Runs the same shape here: many claimants, no document.
- kin → pizza-logs (dish): The other Italian-American thing upstate New York fries and passes around.
- kin → garbage-plate (dish): Rochester's claim on a plate, sixty miles west of Utica's claim on a pasta.
- kin → the-pitcher (dish): What a riggies table drinks, the same as a wing table.
sources: s:wp-chicken-riggies — Chicken riggies; s:wp-buffalo-wing — Buffalo wing

## french fries (dish)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/dish/french-fries/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/dish/french-fries.json
id: french-fries
aliases: fries · chips
said: An order is a side until somebody dumps the wings on top of it, and then it is the plate.
facets: course=side
region: The United States
what: Potatoes cut into even batonnet or julienne strips, dried, and deep-fried. Beside wings they do three jobs: they soak the sauce that drips, they stretch a small order into a meal, and in several cities they become the plate the wings sit on.
story: The fry arrived at the wing counter already carrying its own argument about fat. Beef suet was recommended as the superior frying medium in the older literature, and Belgian practice calls for filtered cattle fat — blanc de boeuf, ossewit. McDonald's fried in a mixture of 93% beef tallow and 7% cottonseed oil until 1990, when it changed to vegetable oil with beef flavouring. Horse fat was standard in northern France and Belgium until recently.

*Inference —* that switch is the same argument a wing shop has with itself, one fryer down: the fat is the flavour, and the fat is also the thing a chain answers to a nutrition panel for.
how: Cut even strips and dry them. Fry twice: a first bath at about 160 °C / 320 °F to cook the potato through, then a second at about 190 °C / 375 °F to crisp the outside. For thin 2–3 mm strips the first bath runs about three minutes and the second only seconds. Salt out of the oil. Beside wings the fries usually come out of the same oil as the wings, which means they taste of whatever else that fryer has been doing.
today: Wingstop lists fries among its sides alongside fried corn and veggie sticks. In Washington, D.C. the fries take mumbo sauce; in Chicago they go under the chicken and take mild sauce; in Atlanta they turn up as loaded fries under lemon pepper. *Inference —* wherever a city has its own wing sauce, it also has a fry that carries it.
- kin → mumbo-fries (dish): What these become in a D.C. carryout when the sauce goes over the top.
- kin → jojo-potatoes (dish): The same potato breaded and pressure-fried instead of cut thin and fried twice.
- kin → double-fry (fry): The two-bath method these are built on, and the one Korean wing shops borrowed.
- kin → frying-oil (fry): The argument these carry into the shop: tallow, cottonseed, soy, canola.
- kin → deep-fryer (fry): Shares the wings' oil in most shops, which is why the fries taste of the wings.
- kin → wingstop (place): Sells them as a side beside fried corn and veggie sticks.
- kin → wing-basket (dish): Lines the basket or holds the wings up out of their own sauce.
- kin → garbage-plate (dish): Rochester puts home fries under the meat instead, and calls the result the city's dish.
- image: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/images/french-fries/french-fries-french-fries.jpg · CC0 1.0 · StockSnap · https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3AFrench_Fries.JPG

## Garbage Plate (dish)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/dish/garbage-plate/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/dish/garbage-plate.json
id: garbage-plate
aliases: trash plate · plate · Rochester plate · junkyard plate
said: Order it by what goes on it: two cheeseburgers, mac salad and home fries, hot sauce, onions, mustard. The name belongs to one restaurant; everyone else says plate.
facets: course=main
region: Rochester, Upstate New York
what: Hot dog or hamburger meat and a meat hot sauce piled on a bed of side dishes — usually macaroni salad and home fries — with onions and mustard, and buttered bread alongside. Rochester's signature dish, and a trademark of one restaurant that every other restaurant has to work around.
story: Alexander Tahou, a Greek immigrant, opened West Main Texas Hots in Rochester in 1918. The first version was hots — standard hot dogs or Rochester-style white hots — with potatoes, cold beans and buttered Italian bread. His son Nick took over in the 1940s, renamed the place Nick Tahou Hots, added hamburger meat and macaroni salad, and introduced the chili-like hot meat sauce that holds the dish together; that sauce came from a family recipe belonging to a Mexican friend of Alexander's.

The name arrived from outside. By the 1980s college students were coming in and asking for "that plate with all the garbage on it". The family resisted — as they put it, "it's food; it doesn't sound good" — then filed a United States trademark for Garbage Plate in 1991, which stopped anyone else selling one under that name. So Rochester eats trash plates, junkyard plates, hot plates, rubbish plates, sloppy plates and messy plates instead, and The Red Fern sells a vegan Compost Plate.

Jim Memmott of the Democrat and Chronicle called it "Rochester's signature thing", arguing it eclipses Kodak. In August 2017 the Rochester Red Wings briefly renamed themselves the Rochester Plates for the dish's centenary, brought the name back in 2018 for Thursday home games, and unveiled a plate-themed mascot named Mac in 2019.
how: Build from the bottom: two sides first — macaroni salad, home fries, french fries or beans — then the meat, then the hot meat sauce over everything, then raw onion and mustard. Buttered white bread on the side to push with. Eat it with a fork, standing or sitting, usually late.
today: Versions have spread past the Rochester metropolitan area to New York City, Pittsburgh, Raleigh and Denver. *Tradition holds —* the plate is widely eaten as a hangover remedy, and news outlets repeat that as often as they describe it.
- kin → rochester-breaded (style): Shares the city and the argument: Rochester breads its wings and buries its sides, seventy miles from a city that does neither.
- kin → buffalo (style): The other Western New York dish that made it onto a national menu, and the one that got there first.
- kin → french-fries (dish): One of the two sides underneath, and the one most copycat plates default to.
- kin → jeremiahs-tavern (place): Sells Rochester its wings in the same city that eats the plate.
- kin → country-sweet-chicken-and-ribs (place): The other Rochester counter a plate-eater knows by name.
- kin → the-pitcher (dish): What sits beside it, and part of why it is eaten at the hour it is eaten.
sources: s:wp-garbage-plate — Garbage Plate; s:wp-rochester-new-york — Rochester, New York
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## jojo potatoes (dish)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/dish/jojo-potatoes/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/dish/jojo-potatoes.json
id: jojo-potatoes
aliases: jojos · jo jos · potato jojos
said: Say jojo and a Portland counter knows what you mean; say potato wedge and you get something else.
facets: course=side
region: The Pacific Northwest, Upstate New York, The United States
what: A potato wedge that has been breaded, pressure-fried and spiced — not a bare wedge, and not a fry. The pressure fryer is a pressure cooker filled with hot oil, so the potato cooks fast and hard while keeping its water. Sold beside fried chicken across the Pacific Northwest, and in pockets of Montana, Minnesota, Nebraska, Northeast Ohio and upstate New York.
story: Willamette Week ran down the origin in 2017 and found two accounts. Paul Nicewonger says his father, a Vancouver, Washington salesman, invented the jojo around 1958, demonstrating pressure fryers at a restaurant trade show next to Idaho potato vendors — he needed something cheap and quick to throw in the oil. Ron Echtenkamp of Ballantyne Strong credits Ed Nelson, a Flavor-Crisp salesman, with making them by accident at a Chicago trade show in 1961. The paper did not settle it.

The machine carried the food. Flavor-Crisp, Henny Penny and the Broaster Company of Beloit, Wisconsin built the pressure fryers, and "broasting" became the trade word for what came out of them. Because the fryers were sold region by region, each region came to believe it had invented the jojo.

*Inference —* the jojo is a salesman's demo that outlived the sales route, which is why its map looks like a distributor's territory rather than a cuisine.
how: Cut a potato into thick wedges with the skin on. Bread and season them, then pressure-fry. The lid holds steam over the oil, which raises the boiling point inside the fryer and cooks the wedge through before its crust burns. Out of the basket they go beside fried chicken, and in the same shops that sell chicken they take the same sauce the chicken takes.
today: Grocery-store delis and chicken counters across Oregon and Washington still sell them by the half-dozen. *Tradition holds —* a shop that calls them wedges is selling something else, and a shop that calls them jojos is usually running a pressure fryer.
- kin → french-fries (dish): The other potato at the same counter, cut thin and fried bare rather than breaded under pressure.
- kin → deep-fryer (fry): Needs the pressure version of it, which is where the trade word broasting comes from.
- kin → breaded-fry (fry): Gets the same flour-and-spice coat a Rochester wing gets, on a potato.
- kin → dredge (fry): The coating step that separates a jojo from a plain wedge.
- kin → frying-oil (fry): Shares the chicken's oil in a shop that runs one fryer.
- kin → wing-basket (dish): The side that fills out a chicken order west of the Rockies, where celery does not.
sources: s:web-wweek-jojo — The History of the American Jojo, Which is Definitely Not a Potato Wedge; s:wp-deep-frying — Deep frying
provenance default: cited · confidence: medium · needs_verification: True · updated: 2026-09-16

## mozzarella sticks (dish)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/dish/mozzarella-sticks/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/dish/mozzarella-sticks.json
id: mozzarella-sticks
aliases: mozz sticks · fried mozzarella
said: Ordered by the table, not the person, and judged on the pull.
facets: course=side
region: The United States, Upstate New York
what: Elongated pieces of mozzarella coated in breadcrumbs or batter and fried, served as an hors d'oeuvre with marinara. On a wing menu they are the thing a table orders when half of it does not want wings.
story: Frying cheese in batter is old: a recipe for fried cheese sticks appears in Le Ménagier de Paris in 1393, though food historians hold that medieval French fried cheeses had little in common with what the modern stick became.

The American article dates to the 1970s. The historian Joel Jensen puts it down to two things arriving together: "the increasing availability of mass-produced mozzarella cheese beginning in the 1960s", and new efficient frying technologies for fast-paced food businesses such as bowling alleys and sports bars. The food writer Arthur Schwartz names mozzarella milanese — mozzarella dredged in flour, egg and breadcrumbs, then pan-fried — as the "prototype", a midweek Italian dish made from older mozzarella and eaten "within seconds" of leaving the pan.

*Inference —* the stick and the wing share a birth certificate. Both are cheap protein that only became a menu item once a bar had a fryer running all evening, and both spread through the same bowling alleys and sports bars in the same decade.
how: Cut mozzarella into fingers, coat in breadcrumbs or batter, and bake or fry in oil. Marinara for dipping is the restaurant default; plum sauce, jalapeño jelly, ketchup, barbecue sauce, honey mustard and ranch all appear. Serve immediately — the pull is the point and it is gone in minutes.
today: Provolone, Edam, cheddar and American are all fried the same way. In New York's Capital District the sticks come with raspberry sauce, which is regional and not a mistake. In American public schools, Bosco pizza sticks — soft breadsticks stuffed with mozzarella, with tomato sauce to dip — have become a staple.
- kin → pizza-logs (dish): Western New York's version of the same idea, wrapped in an egg-roll skin instead of breaded.
- kin → deep-fryer (fry): Shares the wings' oil, and arrived on menus when bars got one.
- kin → breaded-fry (fry): The same crumb coat a Rochester wing wears.
- kin → dredge (fry): Flour, egg, breadcrumbs — the sequence its Italian prototype is named for.
- kin → ranch-dressing (sauce): One of the cups it turns up with, on the same table as the wings.
- kin → wing-basket (dish): The order it shares a table with, for the half of the table not eating wings.
- image: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/images/mozzarella-sticks/mozzarella-sticks-mozzarella-sticks.jpg · CC BY-SA 2.0 · travel oriented · https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3AMozzarella_sticks.jpg
sources: s:wp-mozzarella-sticks — Mozzarella sticks; s:wp-deep-frying — Deep frying
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## mumbo fries (dish)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/dish/mumbo-fries/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/dish/mumbo-fries.json
id: mumbo-fries
aliases: mambo fries · fries with mumbo
said: Fries, mumbo on top — or in the cup, which is a different order and the counter knows it.
facets: course=side · styles=dc-mumbo
region: Washington, D.C.
what: French fries under mumbo sauce, from a Washington, D.C. carryout. Mumbo is a sweet, tangy, ketchup-based condiment — like barbecue sauce but sweeter, and somewhat spicier or more sour, with real variation in flavour and consistency between makers.
story: The sauce arrives at the fries with a trademark fight attached. Argia B. Collins Sr. used the Mumbo name for a barbecue sauce he developed for his Chicago restaurant from at least as early as 1950; his successor-in-interest, Select Brands, LLC, registered the trademark on 25 May 1999, Registration No. 2,247,855, and has challenged D.C. uses of the name as infringements. Capital City Mumbo Sauce says the D.C. sauce started at a restaurant called Wings-n-Things in the late 1960s. John Young's Wings 'n Things had been serving mumbo sauce on chicken wings in Buffalo since the early 1960s, and Young himself credited a Washington, D.C. restaurant for the sauce. After two years of proceedings, the Trademark Trial and Appeal Board found that a D.C.-based company could not take the name from its Chicago founder.

In 2018 D.C. Mayor Muriel Bowser called mumbo sauce "annoying" in a Facebook post and questioned whether it was "quintessential" D.C.; her spokesperson said the remarks were meant to liven Thanksgiving discussions. On 9 October 2023 McDonald's released a version as a limited-time dipping sauce in its US locations, with a media campaign and a short YouTube documentary on the sauce's history.
how: Fry the potatoes, salt them, and ladle mumbo over the top so it soaks in at the edges and pools at the bottom of the container. A cup on the side instead is a live option and a live disagreement. The sauce is served at room temperature or warm, not hot.
today: Still a carryout order across the D.C. region, usually as the cheap half of a wing order. *Inference —* the fries are where a first-time customer meets the sauce, because they cost less than the wings and forgive a wrong guess about heat.
- kin → mumbo-sauce (sauce): The sauce, its Chicago trademark and its D.C. claim.
- kin → french-fries (dish): The potato underneath, doing what it does under every city's sauce.
- kin → dc-mumbo (style): The style this belongs to, and the cheapest way into it.
- kin → fried-rice-plate (dish): The other half of the same carryout order.
- kin → capital-city-mambo-sauce (place): Bottles a D.C. version and dates the sauce to a restaurant called Wings-n-Things in the late 1960s.
- kin → mumbo (term): The word, and whose name it legally is.
- kin → john-young (person): Sold wings in mumbo sauce in Buffalo from 1961 and credited a Washington restaurant for it.
- image: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/images/mumbo-fries/mumbo-fries-mumbo-sauce.jpg · CC BY-SA 2.0 · justgrimes · https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3AMumbo_sauce.jpg
sources: s:wp-mumbo-sauce — Mumbo sauce; s:wp-american-chinese-cuisine — American Chinese cuisine; s:web-wp-french-fries — French fries; s:wp-buffalo-wing — Buffalo wing

## pickled radish (dish)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/dish/pickled-radish/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/dish/pickled-radish.json
id: pickled-radish
aliases: chicken-mu · danmuji · 치킨무
said: Comes in a small plastic tub, cubed, in its own liquid, and it is refilled without being asked.
facets: course=side · styles=korean-american
region: Korean America, The United States
what: Cubed pickled daikon in a sweet-sour brine, served cold in a small tub beside Korean fried chicken. Pickled radishes and beer or carbonated drinks are the standard accompaniment; Bonchon lists pickled radish among its side dishes alongside kimchi, coleslaw and Korean street corn.
story: The pickle has a longer name than the tub suggests. Danmuji is the Korean name for takuan, the yellow daikon pickle credited to the Buddhist monk Takuan Sōhō (1573–1645). It came to Korea during the Japanese occupation and was first called dakkwang, a phonetic rendering of takuan; after the occupation ended it was renamed danmuji, meaning sweet radish pickle. The Korean version is usually sweeter and crunchier than the Japanese original.

*Tradition holds —* the cubed white version served with fried chicken is called chicken-mu, mu being the radish, and it is a distinct product from the long yellow danmuji sliced into kimbap. This project has not found a source that dates that split.

*Inference —* the tub does the job celery does in Buffalo and white bread does in Nashville: something cold, cheap and sharp arriving unasked against something hot and fatty. Three traditions, three answers, one problem.
how: Cut daikon into cubes and hold them in a sweetened vinegar brine until they go glassy and squeak. Serve cold, in liquid, in a lidded tub, with the chicken and the beer. Eat one between pieces.
today: Standard at Korean fried chicken shops in the United States, including chains that reached the US market after Korean brands expanded abroad. *Tradition holds —* the refill is free and the tub is the thing that runs out first.
- kin → korean-american (style): The style this tub arrives with, always, and unasked.
- kin → bonchon (place): Lists pickled radish among its sides, next to kimchi and coleslaw.
- kin → yangnyeom-sauce (sauce): The sweet-hot gochujang coat this is served against.
- kin → soy-garlic-sauce (sauce): The other flagship coat, brushed on rather than tossed, and cut by the same pickle.
- kin → the-pitcher (dish): Beer comes with the chicken here too; chimaek is the Korean word for the pairing.
- kin → celery-and-carrots (dish): Buffalo's cold thing on the same plate, raw instead of pickled.
- kin → double-fry (fry): The frying method this pickle is calibrated against — a thin, hard crust needs something sharp.
sources: s:wp-korean-fried-chicken — Korean fried chicken; s:wp-bonchon-chicken — Bonchon Chicken; s:web-wp-danmuji — Danmuji
provenance default: cited · confidence: medium · needs_verification: True · updated: 2026-09-16

## pizza logs (dish)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/dish/pizza-logs/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/dish/pizza-logs.json
id: pizza-logs
aliases: pizza egg rolls
said: Comes in threes or sixes with a cup of marinara, and it is the thing a Buffalo table orders while the wings are still frying.
facets: course=side
region: Western New York, Upstate New York
what: Mozzarella, and often pepperoni, rolled in an egg-roll wrapper and deep-fried, served with marinara to dip. A Western New York bar snack that sits on the same appetizer list as wings and sells in freezer cases across upstate.
story: The name is older than the Buffalo product. Barry Popik dates the phrase in print to 11 March 1970, in an advertisement in The Daily Herald of Provo, Utah for Jeno's Frozen Pizza Logs. The Buffalo article of the name belongs to Finger Food Products of Niagara Falls, New York, which claims a first use of "Original Pizza Logs" on 31 December 1992 and filed for the trademark on 7 February 2013; it registered on 8 October 2013.

*Inference —* the wrapper is the tell. Buffalo took an egg-roll skin off a Chinese-American supply shelf and put pizza inside it, which is the same move the city's Chinese-American carryouts made in the other direction with the wing.
how: Roll mozzarella, and pepperoni if it is going in, tight inside an egg-roll wrapper and seal the edge. Deep-fry until the wrapper blisters. Rest before serving or the cheese runs. Marinara in a cup; ranch in a cup if the table asks for it.
today: Sold frozen by the bag and hot by the basket across Western New York, and pushed as a stadium and arena snack — Popik records the Pittsburgh Penguins naming Pizza Logs their "Official Finger Food" in a post on 14 December 2018.
- kin → mozzarella-sticks (dish): The other fried cheese on the same appetizer list, breaded instead of wrapped.
- kin → buffalo (style): Shares the city, the fryer and the basket; ordered while the wings cook.
- kin → deep-fryer (fry): Goes into the same oil the wings come out of.
- kin → buffalo-chicken-pizza (dish): The other thing Buffalo does by folding pizza into a wing order.
- kin → the-pitcher (dish): The order it shares a table with.
- kin → wing-basket (dish): Arrives in the same basket, often before the wings do.
sources: s:web-popik-pizza-logs — Buffalo: Pizza Logs; s:wp-mozzarella-sticks — Mozzarella sticks

## the fried rice plate (dish)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/dish/fried-rice-plate/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/dish/fried-rice-plate.json
id: fried-rice-plate
aliases: wings over fried rice · wings and rice
said: Order across a turntable in bulletproof glass: wings over fried rice, mumbo on the side or on top.
facets: course=main · styles=dc-mumbo
region: Washington, D.C., The United States
what: Whole fried chicken wings served over egg fried rice with mumbo sauce, sold from Chinese-American carryouts across the Washington, D.C. metropolitan region. The wings are not cut; they go into the oil whole and come out as a set of three-jointed pieces laid over the rice.
story: The dish belongs to two kitchens at once. Chinese-American restaurants pioneered take-out and delivery in the United States — New York delivery was pioneered in the 1970s by Empire Szechuan Gourmet Franchise, which hired Taiwanese students from Columbia to do it — and they were among the first American restaurants to use picture menus. Fried rice earned its place on those menus because it is fast, uses rice cooled overnight, and suited American tastes; the American version takes more soy sauce than the versions found in China.

Mumbo sauce came in from the other side of the counter. It is a takeout condiment specialty of Washington, D.C., put onto fried chicken wings, french fries, fried jumbo shrimp and fried rice, and it is often compared to Chicago's mild sauce, also a takeout sauce of that city's Black neighbourhoods.

*Inference —* the plate is what happens when a Chinese-American carryout menu meets a Black Washington sauce over the same counter, and neither side's cookbook explains it on its own.
how: Fry the wings whole and hard — no cut at the joints, so the drumette, flat and tip arrive attached. Bed of egg fried rice, made from rice cooled overnight. Sauce goes over the wings, or into a cup, depending on what the customer says. The whole thing comes in a hinged foam or plastic container and it is eaten with a plastic fork over the lid.
today: Still the standard order at Chinese-American carryouts across the DMV. *Tradition holds —* every regular has a position on whether the sauce goes over the rice or stays in the cup, and the counter asks.
- kin → mumbo-sauce (sauce): The sauce that makes this plate a D.C. plate rather than a takeout combination.
- kin → dc-mumbo (style): The style this plate is the standard order of.
- kin → mumbo-fries (dish): The same sauce over the other starch, from the same counter.
- kin → yums-carry-out (place): One of the D.C. carryouts this plate is ordered across.
- kin → horaces-and-dickies (place): Another D.C. counter on this project's list, selling out of the same tradition.
- kin → wing-cut (fry): The step this plate skips: the wing goes in whole, tip and all.
- kin → mild-sauce (sauce): Chicago's equivalent condiment, on chicken and fries instead of rice.
sources: s:wp-american-chinese-cuisine — American Chinese cuisine; s:wp-mumbo-sauce — Mumbo sauce; s:wp-mild-sauce — Mild sauce
provenance default: cited · confidence: medium · needs_verification: True · updated: 2026-09-16

## the pitcher (dish)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/dish/the-pitcher/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/dish/the-pitcher.json
id: the-pitcher
aliases: a pitcher · pitcher of beer · chimaek
said: One pitcher, four glasses, and the wings arrive while it is still full.
facets: course=drink
region: The United States, Korean America
what: Draught beer sold by the jug for a table to share. It is the other half of a wing order almost everywhere wings are sold, and in two traditions it is named into the food: Hooters built its concept on wings and beer, and Korean has a single word for the pairing.
story: Korean has the cleaner record of it. The first modern Korean fried chicken franchise, Lims Chicken, opened in 1977 in the basement of the Shinsegae Department Store on Chungmu-ro in Seoul, founded by Yu Seok-ho, and was "embraced as an excellent food pairing for draft beer". The word for that pairing, chimaek, is a portmanteau of chicken and maekju, the Korean word for beer. Pickled radishes and beer or carbonated drinks are the standard accompaniment to Korean fried chicken.

American bars said the same thing in marketing rather than in vocabulary. Hooters, founded in 1983, has put it plainly: "Customers can go to many places for wings and beer." Almost all Hooters restaurants hold licences to sell beer and wine. When a location closed, the company's own notice thanked its guests for "the many years of great times, cold beer, hot wings, and unforgettable memories shared here."

*Inference —* the pitcher is why the wing became bar food rather than restaurant food. Salt and heat sell drink, the drink carries the margin, and the wing was cheap enough in 1964 to be given away against it. Beef on weck is said to have worked the same trick in Buffalo a century earlier, with salt on a roll.
how: Pour from the pitcher into glasses at the table and keep pouring. Cold and light against salt, fat and cayenne; a dark or a high-alcohol beer fights the sauce rather than clearing it. Where a pitcher is not sold, the same job goes to a bucket of bottles, a soda refill, or in Korea to a shared bottle of lager.
today: Standard at American sports bars, and at Korean fried chicken shops that built the pairing into the language. *Tradition holds —* wing night and pitcher pricing move together, and a bar that drops one usually drops both.
- kin → wing-basket (dish): The other half of the order; neither is sold in quantity without the other.
- kin → hooters (place): Built a chain on wings and beer and says so in its own words.
- kin → buffalo (style): The style that started as something given away to people already buying drinks.
- kin → korean-american (style): Names the pairing in one word, chimaek, from chicken and maekju.
- kin → bonchon (place): Grew out of the South Korean chimaek market, where the beer came first.
- kin → wing-night (term): The night the pitcher price and the wing price are set against each other.
- kin → beef-on-weck (dish): Buffalo's older salt-sells-drink trick, on a roll instead of a wing.
- kin → super-bowl-sunday (event): The day the pitcher moves to a living room and stays a pitcher.
sources: s:wp-hooters — Hooters; s:wp-korean-fried-chicken — Korean fried chicken; s:wp-bonchon-chicken — Bonchon Chicken; s:wp-buffalo-wing — Buffalo wing; s:wp-beef-on-weck — Beef on weck
provenance default: cited · confidence: medium · needs_verification: True · updated: 2026-09-16

## the wing basket (dish)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/dish/wing-basket/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/dish/wing-basket.json
id: wing-basket
aliases: a basket of wings · wing order · the plate
said: Six, ten, twenty, fifty. Say the number, then the heat, then the dip. The paper liner comes out soaked and that is the receipt.
facets: course=main · styles=buffalo
region: The United States
what: The unit a bar sells wings in: a count of pieces in a basket or on a plate, lined with paper, with celery and carrots, a cup of blue cheese or ranch, and usually fries. A fry basket is the tool the wings come out of the oil in — it contains the food in the fryer and strains it on the way out — and the serving basket copies its shape.
story: The count came from the knife. A wing off the bird is cut at both joints into a drumette, a flat and a tip; the tip is usually discarded or boiled for stock, so one wing sells as two pieces. Order twenty and twenty pieces arrive, which is roughly ten birds' worth of one wing each.

The basket came from the bar. Chains built around it — Buffalo Wild Wings from 1982, Hooters from 1983 — and Hooters put the pairing in its own words: "Customers can go to many places for wings and beer." Wingstop's sides sit where the wing shop's economics are clearest: fries, fried corn, and veggie sticks of carrots and/or celery, sold rather than given.

*Inference —* the basket is the reason a wing is counted instead of weighed, and the reason a shop can price heat, count and dip separately while charging for none of them by the pound.
how: Fry the pieces, drain them in the basket, tip them into a metal bowl, pour sauce over and shake. Into the lined basket, vegetables on top or beside, dip in a cup, fries underneath or alongside. Extra napkins, and wet wipes at counters that have learned. A dry-rub order skips the bowl and gets tossed with seasoning instead.
today: Standard at chains and independents alike. A shop that sells all flats or all drums charges for the privilege, because splitting a case by piece costs the kitchen its yield. *Tradition holds —* the number in a basket is the one thing about a wing order nobody argues over.
- kin → wing (term): The word and the counting unit this basket is measured in.
- kin → wing-cut (fry): Why a basket of twenty is ten birds' worth of one wing each.
- kin → celery-and-carrots (dish): Rides in the same basket, unasked in Buffalo and priced elsewhere.
- kin → french-fries (dish): Under the wings or beside them, and the cheapest way to make a count into a meal.
- kin → the-pitcher (dish): The other half of the order, and the reason bars sell wings at all.
- kin → deep-fryer (fry): The fry basket the serving basket is shaped after.
- kin → all-flats (term): The special request that breaks the basket's economics, and what a shop charges for it.
- kin → wing-night (term): The night the basket gets priced by the piece and the room fills.
- kin → the-price-of-a-wing (story): What the count costs, and why that number moves.
