## white bread and pickles (dish)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/dish/white-bread-and-pickles/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/dish/white-bread-and-pickles.json
id: white-bread-and-pickles
aliases: bread and pickles · the bread
said: The bread is under the chicken, not beside it, and by the end it is the best thing in the box.
facets: course=bread · styles=nashville-hot
region: Nashville, The American South
what: Two slices of plain white sandwich bread with pickle chips on top, and the hot chicken laid over both. The bread catches the cayenne paste and the fat coming off the bird; the pickles cut it. It is not a side — it is the plate.
story: Nashville hot chicken is served atop slices of white bread with pickle chips, and it is both the spice paste and that presentation that separate it from dishes like the Buffalo wing. The style comes out of African American communities in the Southern United States; anecdotal evidence puts spicy fried chicken in Nashville's Black neighbourhoods for generations, possibly from the 1930s, with the current style of paste dating only to the mid-1970s.

The originating family is generally accepted to be André Prince Jeffries's. She has run Prince's Hot Chicken Shack since 1980; before that it belonged to her great-uncle Thornton Prince III. Jeffries tells the development as an accident: after a late Saturday night, Thornton's girlfriend cooked him a fried chicken breakfast with extra pepper as revenge, and he liked it. By the mid-1930s he and his brothers had a recipe and the BBQ Chicken Shack.

*Inference —* the bread does the work celery does in Buffalo — something cheap and cold against something hot — but it does it underneath instead of alongside, and it ends up eaten rather than left.
how: Lay two slices flat in the box or on the paper. Pickle chips on the bread. Chicken straight out of the fryer on top, paste applied by the server with a spoon and gloves and pressed lightly into the crust by hand. Serve at once; the point is that the bread soaks.
today: Every Nashville hot chicken counter builds it this way, and the chains that took the style national — KFC's Nashville Hot from January 2016, and others — kept the paste and mostly dropped the bread. *Tradition holds —* eating the bread at the end is the standard finish, and the pickles are the only mercy on offer.
- kin → nashville-hot (style): The style this bread is the floor of; no bread, and the paste has nowhere to go.
- kin → princes-hot-chicken-shack (place): The counter the presentation is traced to, run by André Prince Jeffries since 1980.
- kin → hattie-bs (place): Serves the same bread-and-pickle build to a much longer line.
- kin → boltons-spicy-chicken-and-fish (place): Another Nashville counter working the same paste and the same slice of bread.
- kin → nashville-hot-oil (sauce): The cayenne paste the bread is there to catch.
- kin → celery-and-carrots (dish): Buffalo's version of the same job, beside the wing rather than under it.
- kin → andre-prince-jeffries (person): Runs the shack the style is traced to, and tells its origin as an act of revenge.
sources: s:wp-hot-chicken — Hot chicken; s:wp-prince-s-hot-chicken-shack — Prince's Hot Chicken Shack; s:wp-buffalo-wing — Buffalo wing
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## frying oil (fry)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/fry/frying-oil/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/fry/frying-oil.json
id: frying-oil
aliases: the fat · the oil · shortening · tallow
said: Ask what a shop fries in and you learn more about the wings than the sauce list tells you.
facets: kind=oil
region: The United States
what: What the wing is cooked in. Deep frying submerges food in hot fat — traditionally lard, today most commonly oil — and the choice of fat sets flavour, how long the vat lasts, what the shop pays and what goes on the allergen sheet. Four answers cover most American wing counters: beef tallow, peanut, soybean and canola.
story: Beef fat has the oldest claim and the shortest modern run. Beef suet was recommended as superior in the older frying literature, and Belgian tradition requires fries be fried in filtered cattle fat — blanc de boeuf, ossewit. McDonald's used a mixture of 93% beef tallow and 7% cottonseed oil until 1990, when it switched to vegetable oil with beef flavouring. Horse fat was standard in northern France and Belgium until recently.

Soybean oil took the volume. In the United States especially, soybean oil is a popular medium in fast food, and fast food is one of the most common ways deep-fried food is eaten in North America. Trans fats appear in restaurant frying shortenings because they last longer than most conventional oils before going rancid; in the early 21st century non-hydrogenated vegetable oils with longer lifespans became available. Trans fat formed during frying increases with frying temperature, frying time, oil oxidation and oil reuse, and because chains use different fats in different locations, trans fat levels in fast food vary widely.

Canola is rapeseed. Many countries including the United Kingdom use pure or hydrogenated rapeseed oil for deep-frying; the Mediterranean tradition uses olive oil, and research indicates virgin olive oil is unusual among cooking oils for being very rich in monounsaturated fatty acids. Some studies have found frying in olive and sunflower oils less detrimental to health, and in some cases with positive effects on insulin levels.

*Tradition holds —* peanut oil is the fat American cooks name first for frying chicken and turkey, and the allergen is why plenty of shops will not keep it. This project has not found a cited source for either claim, and both are recorded here as unverified.

*Inference —* the argument over frying fat is the same argument the wing has everywhere else: the thing that makes it taste like itself is the thing a national menu has to answer for.
how: Hold the vat at 350–375 °F / 177–191 °C and let it recover between loads. Strain the solids at the end of service; oil can be reused a few times after straining, and excessive reuse breaks it down and releases compounds into the food. Some European countries set public health standards for frying-oil safety. Deep fat frying above 180 °C in the presence of moisture and air drives free radicals, oxidation, hydrolysis, isomerisation and polymerisation — water attacks the ester linkages of triacylglycerols, producing glycerol and free fatty acids, and those acids speed the reaction up. In practice that is what old oil tastes like.
today: Chains publish their frying fat and independents rarely do. *Inference —* a shop that runs one vat for wings, fries, mozzarella sticks and fish is selling the oil as much as the recipe, and regulars taste the schedule before they could name it.
- kin → deep-fryer (fry): The vat this fills, and the temperature it has to hold.
- kin → naked-fry (fry): With no coating in the way, the fat is tasted directly on the skin.
- kin → french-fries (dish): Carries the same tallow argument, with a published date on the switch.
- kin → double-fry (fry): Two passes through the same oil, which ages it faster.
- kin → air-fryer (fry): Replaces the bath with a film, and gives up whatever the fat was contributing.
- kin → the-price-of-a-wing (story): The vat is the other cost line, after the bird.
- kin → jojo-potatoes (dish): Shares a shop's oil with the chicken, which is why they taste related.
sources: s:wp-deep-frying — Deep frying; s:web-wp-french-fries — French fries
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: True · updated: 2026-09-16

## sauce on the side (fry)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/fry/sauce-on-the-side/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/fry/sauce-on-the-side.json
id: sauce-on-the-side
aliases: on the side · naked with sauce · dry with a cup
said: Ask for it on the side in Buffalo and the counter will repeat the order back to you.
facets: kind=method
region: The United States, Western New York
what: Ordering the wings unsauced with the sauce in a cup. The argument is whether the sauce is a step in the cooking or a condiment at the table — and the traditions answer it differently, on the record, in their own methods.
story: Buffalo's account treats the toss as part of the dish: the cooked wings are placed in a bowl or pot and shaken to coat them completely in sauce before serving, and the Anchor Bar states that the sauce is added after the wing has been cooked. Both sentences put the sauce in the kitchen, not on the table.

Other traditions put it elsewhere on purpose. Bonchon brushes sauce onto the chicken by hand after frying rather than tossing it in containers, a process intended to distribute the seasoning evenly without compromising the texture of its double-fried crust. Atlanta runs the same split as a menu choice: lemon pepper wings are tossed in a dry seasoning after cooking, while lemon pepper wet, invented at the American Deli, coats them in sauce instead. Memphis does it as a whole style — wet or dry, and the customer picks. Nashville's paste is applied by the server with a spoon and gloves, immediately after the fryer in the more traditional method, which is neither tossed nor on the side.

What the dip is, nobody disputes: traditionally Buffalo wings are served with blue cheese dipping sauce on the side, and ranch dressing is the most popular wing dipping sauce in the United States. So the side cup has always existed. The argument is only about which cup.

*Inference —* the case for the side is texture and the case for the bowl is distribution, and both are right about their own wing. A bare-fried wing has no crust to protect and a soaked one tastes of the sauce all the way round; a double-fried shell has a crust worth protecting and goes dull the moment it soaks. This project reports the positions and takes none of them.
how: Fry as usual and skip the bowl. Sauce warm in a cup, wings dry in the basket, and the eater dips piece by piece — which puts sauce on the outside only and leaves the skin tight. A middle course exists and shops use it: toss half the order and cup the rest, or brush rather than shake. A dry-rub order is already this arrangement under a different name.
today: Available almost everywhere and asked for often, particularly for children and for takeout, where a tossed wing goes soft on the drive. *Tradition holds —* Buffalo counters will do it and will not pretend to like it, and takeaway containers have made the request common enough that most menus no longer note it.
- kin → the-toss (fry): The step this order refuses, and the one Buffalo treats as part of cooking.
- kin → buffalo (style): The style whose own account puts the sauce in the kitchen rather than the table.
- kin → blue-cheese-dressing (sauce): The cup that was always on the side, which is why the request sounds reasonable.
- kin → ranch-dressing (sauce): The most popular dipping sauce in the country, and always served this way.
- kin → double-fry (fry): The method with the most to lose from a bowl, and the one that brushes instead.
- kin → wet-and-dry (term): Memphis runs the same choice as a style rather than as a special request.
- kin → lemon-pepper-wet (sauce): Atlanta's name for choosing the sauced side of this argument.
- kin → boneless-is-not-a-wing (story): The other argument this tradition holds at full volume, with the same rule: quote it, do not settle it.
sources: s:wp-buffalo-wing — Buffalo wing; s:wp-anchor-bar — Anchor Bar; s:wp-bonchon-chicken — Bonchon Chicken; s:wp-lemon-pepper-wings — Lemon pepper wings; s:wp-hot-chicken — Hot chicken
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## smoke then fry (fry)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/fry/smoke-then-fry/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/fry/smoke-then-fry.json
id: smoke-then-fry
aliases: smoked and flashed · smoke-fried wings
said: Smoked wings, flashed. The second step takes seconds and it is the one the kitchen worries about.
facets: kind=smoke
region: Memphis, The American South, The United States
what: Cooking the wing through in smoke, then dropping it briefly into hot oil or onto high heat to tighten the skin. Smoke gives flavour and colour that a fryer cannot; the fryer gives a crust that smoke alone leaves flabby. The rub or the sauce goes on after.
story: The temperatures explain the problem. Hot smoking runs at 52–80 °C / 126–176 °F, which cooks food while flavouring it but is far below the 177–191 °C a crust needs; smoke roasting, above 121 °C / 250 °F, combines roasting and smoking and still leaves poultry skin soft. Above 85 °C / 185 °F foods can shrink, buckle or split, so a smoker cannot simply be turned up. Hickory, oak, pecan, apple and mesquite are the common North American woods; different tree species have different ratios of components and so give different flavours.

Buffalo's own reference text records the alternatives without endorsing them: traditionally the wings are deep-fried, but alternatively they may be baked, grilled, or broiled.

*Tradition holds —* barbecue houses that sell wings usually smoke first and finish in the fryer, and describe the finish in seconds rather than minutes. This project has not found a published house method that states a time.

*Inference —* the technique is a barbecue kitchen borrowing a bar's last step, which is why it shows up on menus where the pit is the main business and the wing is the appetiser.
how: Dry the wings, rub if the house rubs. Smoke at a hot-smoking temperature until cooked through, taking colour from the wood. Rest and dry the surface. Drop into hot oil for a short finish, or onto direct high heat, only long enough to set the skin. Sauce or dust after; a sauce applied before the fryer burns, and a rub applied before the smoke can turn bitter over a long cook.
today: Standard at barbecue counters that sell wings, and increasingly at bars with a smoker out back. *Inference —* it is also a scheduling method: the smoke happens in the morning and the fryer happens to order, so a slow cook reaches a bar's service speed.
- kin → smoked-bbq-wing (style): The style this method makes, and the one that argues with the fryer for possession of the wing.
- kin → central-bbq (place): A Memphis pit on this project's list, where a wing arrives out of the smoke rather than the vat.
- kin → big-bob-gibson-bar-b-q (place): The Alabama house whose white sauce is built for smoked chicken.
- kin → memphis-dry-rub (style): The dust that goes on after, in place of a sauce.
- kin → alabama-white-sauce (sauce): The mayonnaise-and-vinegar dip this method is usually finished into.
- kin → deep-fryer (fry): Borrowed for the last thirty seconds, and only for the skin.
- kin → grill (fry): The other finish, over direct heat instead of in oil.
- kin → wet-and-dry (term): The choice this method forces at the end: dust it or sauce it.
sources: s:web-wp-smoking-cooking — Smoking (cooking); s:wp-buffalo-wing — Buffalo wing
provenance default: cited · confidence: medium · needs_verification: True · updated: 2026-09-16

## the air fryer (fry)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/fry/air-fryer/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/fry/air-fryer.json
id: air-fryer
aliases: air frying · countertop convection oven
said: It is a small convection oven with a basket, and the word fryer in the name is doing a lot of work.
facets: kind=tool
region: The United States
what: A small countertop convection oven that reaches deep-frying temperatures without submerging the food in oil. It circulates air at up to 200 °C / 392 °F to brown food coated in a thin layer of oil, where conventional frying drives the same browning reactions at 140–165 °C / 284–329 °F by putting the food in hot oil instead. Food sits in a basket over a drip tray, and for small pieces the basket must be shaken.
story: The machine is younger than most people assume. Groupe SEB introduced the first air fryer in 2006 under the Actifry brand in the French market. The Dutch engineer Fred van der Weij invented it that same year and took it to Philips four years later; Philips launched the Airfryer at IFA Berlin in 2010 and patented the technique as Rapid Air. By 2018 air fryer was being used generically.

Adoption ran fast. A reported 36% of US households had a convection oven in 2020 and an estimated 60% in 2023; food manufacturers responded by adding air-frying instructions to products and selling pre-air-fried ones. In the UK a 2024 study claimed one in five Britons surveyed named the air fryer their most-used cooking device.

The verdict is not settled and this project does not settle it. Some reviewers find regular convection ovens or convection toaster ovens produce better results; others say air frying is essentially the same as convection baking; others praise the machines for cooking faster, being easier to clean and making crisp results easier than a full-size convection oven.

*Inference —* the wing is the machine's best case. It is small, it is mostly skin, and it carries its own fat, so the one thing the machine cannot supply is the one thing a wing brings with it.
how: Dry the wings, oil them thinly, and lay them in a single layer with space between; a crowded basket steams. Shake or turn partway, by hand or by the fryer's own paddle. Many cooks bring the baking powder trick over from the oven method. Sauce after, in a bowl, off the machine — sauce in the basket bakes onto the drip tray.
today: Sold as paddle types, cylindrical basket types up to about 2.8 litres, countertop convection ovens of about 24 litres with racks, halogen types under a radiant element, and barrel-shaped oil-less turkey fryers. *Tradition holds —* the tradition treats it as a home appliance rather than a shop one, and the shops that describe their method never describe this.
- kin → baking-powder-bake (fry): The chemistry most air fryer wing recipes borrow wholesale.
- kin → deep-fryer (fry): The machine it is named after and does not contain.
- kin → naked-fry (fry): The bare-skin result it is trying to reach with a tablespoon of oil instead of a vat.
- kin → the-toss (fry): Still the last step, done in a bowl off the machine.
- kin → frying-oil (fry): Uses a film of it rather than a bath, which changes what the fat can contribute.
- kin → super-bowl-sunday (event): The day the household machines outnumber the commercial ones by a wide margin.
sources: s:wp-convection-oven — Convection oven; s:wp-deep-frying — Deep frying
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## the baking powder bake (fry)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/fry/baking-powder-bake/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/fry/baking-powder-bake.json
id: baking-powder-bake
aliases: oven wings · baked wings · no-fry wings
said: Baking powder, not baking soda. Recipe writers put that in capitals because readers keep getting it wrong.
facets: kind=method
region: The United States
what: The home method that gets wing skin to crisp in an oven: toss dried wings with baking powder and salt, bake low to render and dry, then hot to brown. No fryer, no pot of oil, and a crust that holds sauce for about as long as it takes to eat.
story: The trick is a pH trick. Baking powder is alkaline — the opposite of acidic — so, as Christine Pittman of TheCookful puts it, "The addition of the baking powder therefore raises the pH level in the chicken, allowing the peptide bonds in the skin to break down, which in turn lets the skin get more crisp and brown." Nagi Maehashi of RecipeTin Eats describes the same result by a different mechanism: "the baking powder draws moisture to the surface of the skin so it can evaporate, thereby making the skin crispier."

The method arrived with the appliance. Convection — a fan moving air around the food to heat it evenly — was already in home ovens, and small countertop convection ovens are now marketed as air fryers; US household ownership was reported at 36% in 2020 and estimated at 60% in 2023.

*Inference —* this is the version of the wing most Americans actually cook. The fryer belongs to the bar; the oven belongs to the house, and the baking powder is what closes the gap between them.
how: Dry the wings thoroughly. Toss with baking powder and salt — RecipeTin Eats uses 5 teaspoons of baking powder and 3/4 teaspoon of salt for 4 lb / 2 kg of wings. Rack over a tray so air reaches underneath. Bake low first, 120 °C / 250 °F for 30 minutes, to render fat and dry the skin, then raise to 220 °C / 425 °F for 40–50 minutes to cook through and brown. Sauce after the oven. Use baking powder, not baking soda; RecipeTin Eats warns in capitals that readers who have swapped them found the result "INEDIBLE".
today: The standard home recipe across American food sites, and the method most often reached for on Super Bowl Sunday, the second-largest American eating day after Thanksgiving. *Inference —* the recipes agree on the ratio and the two temperatures and disagree on the chemistry, which suggests the method was found by cooking rather than by explanation.
- kin → air-fryer (fry): The countertop convection oven this method runs in when the big oven is busy.
- kin → naked-fry (fry): The bar method this is trying to reproduce without a pot of oil.
- kin → deep-fryer (fry): What this exists to avoid, and the thing it is always measured against.
- kin → buffalo-sauce (sauce): Goes on after the oven, the same way it goes on after the fryer.
- kin → the-toss (fry): Still the last step; the bowl does not care how the wing got cooked.
- kin → super-bowl-sunday (event): The day this method cooks more wings than any fryer.
- kin → brine (fry): The other way salt is used on skin here — drawing water out rather than holding it in.
sources: s:web-cookful-crispy-wings — How To Bake Chicken Wings That Are SOOO Crispy; s:web-recipetin-crispy-wings — Truly Crispy Oven Baked Chicken Wings; s:wp-convection-oven — Convection oven; s:wp-super-bowl — Super Bowl
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## the breaded fry (fry)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/fry/breaded-fry/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/fry/breaded-fry.json
id: breaded-fry
aliases: breaded · dredged and fried · Rochester-style
said: Rochester says breaded and means flour. Elsewhere breaded means crumbs, and the two do not eat alike.
facets: kind=coating
region: Rochester, The United States
what: Coating a wing before it goes in the oil — flour, seasoned flour, batter or crumbs — so the crust rather than the skin carries the crunch and holds the sauce. One common method for preparing food for deep frying involves adding multiple layers of batter around the food, such as cornmeal, flour or tempura; breadcrumbs may also be used.
story: Breading was the Buffalo practice before bare frying was. From 1961 John Young served uncut chicken wings that were breaded, deep fried, and dressed in his own tomato-based mumbo sauce at John Young's Wings 'n Things; he had heard from a travelling boxer about a Washington, D.C. restaurant doing good business in wings and decided to specialise. He registered the name at the county courthouse and left the Buffalo area in 1970, and in 2013 the National Buffalo Wing Festival inducted him into its Hall of Flame.

The method did not leave the region when he did. It held seventy miles east, and it holds across fried chicken generally: Nashville's hot chicken is marinated in buttermilk, floured and fried before the paste goes on.

*Inference —* the coat changes what sauce does. On bare skin sauce sits and slides; on a crust it soaks, which is why breaded traditions tolerate a thinner, sweeter sauce than a bare fry does.
how: Dry the wing, then dredge — straight seasoned flour, or flour then egg then crumb for a thicker jacket. Rest the coated pieces a few minutes so the flour hydrates and stops shedding. Fry at 177–191 °C / 350–375 °F. A coated wing browns faster than a bare one, so it comes out earlier by eye, not by clock.
today: Standard across Rochester and through most of American fried chicken; the argument with Buffalo is seventy miles long and unresolved. *Tradition holds —* a shop that breads will describe its flour as a recipe, and a shop that fries bare will describe having no recipe at all.
- kin → rochester-breaded (style): The style this method defines, and the case it makes against its neighbour.
- kin → naked-fry (fry): The other answer to the same question, seventy miles west.
- kin → dredge (fry): The coating step itself, and what each layer is for.
- kin → john-young (person): Breaded his wings in Buffalo from 1961, three years before the Anchor Bar's date.
- kin → nashville-hot (style): Flours its chicken too, then puts the cayenne on after the fryer as a paste.
- kin → jojo-potatoes (dish): The same coat on a potato, under pressure.
- kin → mozzarella-sticks (dish): The crumb version of the same idea, on cheese.
- kin → extra-crispy (term): What a menu calls a coat taken further, and what that word does and does not settle.
- image: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/images/breaded-fry/breaded-fry-buffalowingsplate.jpg · Public domain · Alvis at English Wikipedia · https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3ABuffalowingsplate.jpg
sources: s:wp-buffalo-wing — Buffalo wing; s:wp-deep-frying — Deep frying; s:wp-hot-chicken — Hot chicken; s:wp-fried-chicken — Fried chicken; s:wp-national-buffalo-wing-festival — National Buffalo Wing Festival
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## the brine (fry)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/fry/brine/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/fry/brine.json
id: brine
aliases: brining · buttermilk soak · dry brine
said: Wet brine or dry. In a chicken kitchen the wet one is usually buttermilk and nobody calls it a brine.
facets: kind=prep
region: The United States
what: Salting the bird before it cooks. Brining treats food with brine or coarse salt, which preserves and seasons it while enhancing tenderness. A wet brine immerses the meat in salt water; a dry brine covers it in coarse salt, which draws moisture out of the interior to the surface where it mixes with the salt and is then reabsorbed.
story: Two accounts of the mechanism compete and both are current. In the first, salt ions enter the cells while other solutes stay trapped inside, raising cellular salinity so the cells take up water by osmosis and hold it through cooking. In the second, the salt denatures the cell's proteins, which coagulate into a matrix that traps water molecules and holds them during cooking. Meat and fish are typically brined for under 24 hours; heavy salting for preserving fish uses at least 20% salt, light salting for immediate eating 2–3%; a dry brine works over several hours.

Fried chicken traditions do it with dairy. Nearly all Nashville hot chicken is marinated in buttermilk, to impart flavour and to retain the meat's juices on frying.

*Inference —* on a wing the payoff is small and the risk is real. A wing is mostly skin and bone with little muscle to protect, so a long soak seasons the skin, softens it, and works against the crust the whole rest of the method is chasing. The dry version — salt, rack, fridge, overnight — is the one that suits the cut, and it is also what the baking powder method is quietly doing.
how: Wet: salt water, cold, under 24 hours, then dry the pieces thoroughly before any flour or any oil goes near them. Buttermilk instead of plain water for a chicken kitchen, which seasons and also gives flour something to grip. Dry: coarse salt over the skin, on a rack, uncovered in the fridge for several hours or overnight; the surface comes out matt and tight. Either way the wing goes into the oil dry, because water in hot oil is a hazard before it is a texture problem.
today: Standard in Southern fried chicken kitchens and in most home wing recipes; largely absent from the Buffalo account, which describes a wing fried straight. *Tradition holds —* a Buffalo house asked about brining tends to answer that it does nothing to the wing at all before the fryer.
- kin → dredge (fry): The step after: a brined surface is what flour grips.
- kin → baking-powder-bake (fry): Runs a dry brine inside it — salt on skin, overnight, for the same drying reason.
- kin → nashville-hot (style): Buttermilk is the brine there, and nearly every version uses it.
- kin → chicken-and-waffles (dish): The fried half usually starts in a buttermilk soak.
- kin → naked-fry (fry): The method with no prep at all, which is the argument against this one.
- kin → par-cook (fry): The other way a kitchen buys time before service.
sources: s:web-wp-brining — Brining; s:wp-hot-chicken — Hot chicken; s:wp-buffalo-wing — Buffalo wing
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## the deep fryer (fry)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/fry/deep-fryer/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/fry/deep-fryer.json
id: deep-fryer
aliases: the fryer · fry vat · chip pan · pressure fryer
said: A bar counts its age in fryers. Forty years on one vat is a thing people say about a place before they say anything about the sauce.
facets: kind=fryer
region: The United States
what: The machine or pot the wing goes into: food submerged in hot fat rather than shallow-fried in a pan. A commercial vat, a chip pan, a wok, a Dutch oven or a cast-iron pot all do it. Industrially, a pressure fryer or a vacuum fryer may be used. Fry baskets contain the food in the fryer and strain it on the way out, and a thermometer is the other tool that matters.
story: The physics is the reason the method works and the reason it burns people. Deep frying puts food in oil typically between 350 °F / 177 °C and 375 °F / 191 °C, though fryers can pass 400 °F / 205 °C. Hot oil heats the water inside the food and steams it; the vapour pushes outward and oil cannot travel against that flow, so as long as the oil is hot enough and the food is not in too long, penetration stays at the surface — foods deep-fried at proper temperatures absorb less than about 2 tbsp per 2.5 cups of oil used. Cook too long and the water is gone and the oil comes in.

The informal tests are older than the thermometers. A pinch of flour should sizzle without burning. A piece dropped in should sink a little and come back up: sinking without resurfacing means the oil is too cold, not sinking at all means it is too hot.

The pressure version runs a different physics. A pressure fryer is a pressure cooker filled with hot oil, so food cooks fast at high heat while keeping its water — the machine behind broasting, and behind the jojo.

*Inference —* the fryer is what made the wing a bar food rather than a kitchen food. It needs no cook watching a pan, it turns out a countable portion in minutes, and it will do fries, mozzarella sticks and pizza logs out of the same oil while it waits.
how: Bring the oil to temperature and hold it there; a basket of cold wings drops it, so fry in loads the vat can recover from. Dry the food before it goes in. Drain over the vat, not onto paper, or the crust steams itself soft. Strain solids out at the end of service — oil can be reused a few times after straining, and excessive reuse of the same oil breaks it down. Never water on an oil fire: water flashes to steam and throws burning oil in all directions, which is a slopover. Class F extinguisher, a lid, or a fire blanket; most commercial deep fryers carry automatic foam suppression.
today: Fast food is one of the most common ways deep-fried food is eaten in North America, and soybean oil is a popular medium there. *Tradition holds —* a shop's oil schedule is the thing regulars notice and never name; they say the wings taste different on a Tuesday.
- kin → frying-oil (fry): What fills it, and the choice that changes how everything out of it tastes.
- kin → naked-fry (fry): The bare wing that meets this oil with nothing between them.
- kin → double-fry (fry): Two passes through it, with a rest that is part of the method.
- kin → par-cook (fry): The first pass held back for service, which is how a busy vat keeps up.
- kin → air-fryer (fry): The countertop machine that reaches for the same result without the oil.
- kin → jojo-potatoes (dish): Comes out of the pressure version of this machine, which is where broasting got its name.
- kin → wing-basket (dish): The fry basket the serving basket is shaped after.
- kin → mozzarella-sticks (dish): Shares the oil with the wings, which is why both taste of the shop.
- image: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/images/deep-fryer/deep-fryer-only-ate-19-wings-2521632544.jpg · CC BY 2.0 · istolethetv · https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3AOnly_ate_19_wings_%282521632544%29.jpg
sources: s:wp-deep-frying — Deep frying; s:web-wweek-jojo — The History of the American Jojo, Which is Definitely Not a Potato Wedge; s:wp-buffalo-wing — Buffalo wing
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## the double fry (fry)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/fry/double-fry/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/fry/double-fry.json
id: double-fry
aliases: frying twice · two-stage fry
said: Fry, rest, fry. The rest is not a pause in the method; it is the method.
facets: kind=method
region: Korean America, The United States
what: Frying in two passes with a rest between them. The first pass cooks the piece through and drives water out of the skin; the rest lets the surface dry and the interior even out; the second pass, hotter, builds the crust. The result is the thin, hard, glassy shell that will not go soft under sauce.
story: Korean fried chicken is the tradition that made the method famous. Julia Moskin of The New York Times described it as having a "thin, crackly and almost transparent crust". Bonchon Chicken, founded in Busan in 2002 by Jinduk Seo, built a brand on it: its recipe cooks the chicken in two steps, the first until the fat from the skin is cooked off and the moisture is held in the meat, then a rest, then a second cook. That dehydration produces a thin crispy shell that acts as a protective layer against moisture getting back in. Because the shell is the product, Bonchon brushes sauce on by hand rather than tossing in containers, to spread it without wrecking the texture.

The potato got there first. French fries use the same architecture: a first bath at around 160 °C / 320 °F to cook the fries through, a second at 190 °C / 375 °F to crisp the exterior.

*Inference —* double frying and saucing are in tension. The method exists to make a crust that survives liquid; the Buffalo bowl exists to soak a crust in liquid. Shops that do both usually brush rather than toss, which is the argument sauce-on-the-side is having in a different accent.
how: Fry the first pass at a moderate heat until cooked through and the skin has given up its fat. Lift, drain and rest — minutes, not seconds, and uncovered, so steam leaves rather than condensing back. Second pass hotter and short, until the surface goes hard and the colour sets. Sauce after, brushed or tossed. Wings hold the rest well because they are small and the skin is most of the surface.
today: Standard at Korean fried chicken shops in the United States and in the chains that expanded out of a saturated home market — by 2026 South Korea had about 40,000 fried chicken restaurants, with 1,800 more run internationally by Korean brands in 60 countries. American bars borrow the method under the words extra crispy without always borrowing the rest.
- kin → korean-american (style): The style built on this method, and the one that named the crust.
- kin → bonchon (place): Built a franchise on a two-step fry and a brushed sauce.
- kin → par-cook (fry): The first pass, taken on its own and held for later service.
- kin → french-fries (dish): The same two-bath architecture, on a potato and with published temperatures.
- kin → soy-garlic-sauce (sauce): Brushed onto this crust rather than tossed, so the shell survives.
- kin → yangnyeom-sauce (sauce): The sweet-hot coat this crust is built to carry without softening.
- kin → sauce-on-the-side (fry): The argument this method keeps starting: a crust worth protecting, and a sauce that wants to soak it.
- kin → extra-crispy (term): The American menu word that often means this, and sometimes means only longer.
sources: s:wp-korean-fried-chicken — Korean fried chicken; s:wp-bonchon-chicken — Bonchon Chicken; s:web-wp-french-fries — French fries; s:wp-deep-frying — Deep frying
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## the dredge (fry)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/fry/dredge/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/fry/dredge.json
id: dredge
aliases: dredging · the flour · the breading station
said: Three trays: flour, egg, crumb. One hand wet, one hand dry, or you end up with a glove.
facets: kind=coating
region: The United States
what: Coating food before it fries. One common method for preparing food for deep frying involves adding multiple layers of batter around the food — cornmeal, flour or tempura — and breadcrumbs may be used. On a wing it is the difference between Buffalo and Rochester; on everything else at the counter it is simply how the thing is made.
story: Every tradition at this counter has its own dredge. Nashville hot chicken is marinated in buttermilk to carry flavour and hold the meat's juices, then floured and fried, with the cayenne paste applied by the server afterward with a spoon and gloves. The mozzarella stick's Italian prototype, mozzarella milanese, is mozzarella dredged in flour, egg and breadcrumbs and pan-fried. John Young's Buffalo wings from 1961 were breaded, deep fried and served in a tomato-based mumbo sauce.

*Inference —* the three-stage dredge is a moisture problem solved in order. Flour dries the surface so egg will grip; egg is glue; crumb is the crust. Skip a stage and the coat slides off in the oil, which is why a station is set up as trays and not as a bowl.
how: Dry the pieces first; wet food sheds flour. Season the flour, not the meat, if the coat is the only seasoning going on. Flour, then egg, then crumb — one hand for dry trays and one for wet, or both hands cake. Rest the coated pieces a few minutes so the flour hydrates and bonds. Shake off surplus: loose flour burns in the oil and dirties the vat for the next load. A single flour dredge gives a thin crust; a double dip gives a craggy one.
today: Standard across American fried chicken, and the practice a Buffalo house defines itself against. *Tradition holds —* a shop's flour is the part of the recipe it will not discuss, and the part customers assume is a secret when it is often just flour, salt and pepper.
- kin → breaded-fry (fry): What this step produces, and the style built on it.
- kin → rochester-breaded (style): The city that made this step its own.
- kin → naked-fry (fry): The method that omits this entirely, and argues that omission is the point.
- kin → brine (fry): The step before it: buttermilk or salt water, which is also what makes flour stick.
- kin → nashville-hot (style): Buttermilk, flour, fryer, then paste — this step in the middle of that order.
- kin → mozzarella-sticks (dish): Flour, egg, breadcrumb on cheese; the sequence its prototype is named for.
- kin → boneless-wings (dish): The coat here is standing in for skin that was never there.
- kin → jojo-potatoes (dish): The same step on a potato wedge, before the pressure fryer.
sources: s:wp-deep-frying — Deep frying; s:wp-hot-chicken — Hot chicken; s:wp-mozzarella-sticks — Mozzarella sticks; s:wp-buffalo-wing — Buffalo wing; s:wp-fried-chicken — Fried chicken
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## the grill (fry)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/fry/grill/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/fry/grill.json
id: grill
aliases: grilled wings · over coals · the drum
said: Grilled wings is a menu category almost everywhere and a fighting word in one city.
facets: kind=heat
region: Caribbean America, The United States
what: Cooking the wing over direct heat instead of in oil. Buffalo's own reference text lists it among the alternatives — traditionally deep-fried, but alternatively baked, grilled, or broiled — and the Anchor Bar's account rules it out for its own wings: they are not grilled, but only deep-fried and slightly crispy.
story: The Caribbean tradition arrives at the wing from the grill rather than the fryer. Jerked meat was first cooked by the indigenous Taínos; in 1516 the Spanish historian Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo y Valdés documented them preparing and preserving meat and fish on a barbacoa, seasoned with native hot peppers and pimento. The Taíno term barabicu, framework of sticks, covers a range of wooden structures including a raised grill for roasting and smoking. Spanish colonists adopted the method for the pigs, cattle and chicken they introduced in the 1500s, curing them over pimento wood and berries.

The hardware changed in living memory. Around the 1960s Caribbean vendors looking for a portable method began cutting oil barrels lengthwise, drilling ventilation holes and hinging the lids to hold the smoke; fired with charcoal, those drums are now used across Jamaica. Wood-burning ovens do the job too.

*Inference —* a wing suits a grill badly and a drum well. Direct flame flares on rendering fat and burns the skin before the joint cooks; a closed drum runs the fire to one side and turns the same fat into smoke.
how: Two zones, always: fire on one side, wings on the other, lid down. Cook through off the heat, then move over the fire for the last minute to colour. Sugar-bearing sauces go on at the very end or they carbonise. A jerk marinade of allspice and Scotch bonnet goes on before, because it is a marinade rather than a glaze.
today: On chain menus as a lighter option and on Caribbean-American counters as the whole point. *Tradition holds —* a Buffalo house will tell you unprompted that it does not grill, which is the clearest sign that plenty of places do.
- kin → caribbean-jerk (style): The style built over fire rather than in oil, and the one with the longest documented history here.
- kin → jerk-marinade (sauce): Allspice and Scotch bonnet, applied before the heat rather than after.
- kin → peppas-jerk-chicken (place): A New York counter working the drum-grill tradition.
- kin → smoke-then-fry (fry): The other way out of the fryer, with the crust bought back at the end.
- kin → naked-fry (fry): The method Buffalo holds to, and the one its houses name this against.
- kin → air-fryer (fry): The indoor attempt at browning without submerging.
- kin → anchor-bar (place): States in its own account that its wings are not grilled.
- image: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/images/grill/grill-chicken-wings-made-in-a-wood-fired-pizza-oven.jpg · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Zacatillo1 · https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3AChicken_Wings_made_in_a_Wood-fired_pizza_oven.jpg
sources: s:wp-jerk-cooking — Jerk (cooking); s:wp-buffalo-wing — Buffalo wing; s:wp-anchor-bar — Anchor Bar
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## the naked fry (fry)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/fry/naked-fry/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/fry/naked-fry.json
id: naked-fry
aliases: naked · unbreaded · bare
said: Naked on a menu means no flour touched it. In Buffalo it is not a menu word, because there is nothing else to order.
facets: kind=coating
region: Western New York, The United States
what: Frying a wing with nothing on it — no batter, no flour, no crumb. The skin browns and crisps on its own, the fat under it renders into the oil, and the sauce goes on afterwards. A Buffalo wing is an unbreaded chicken wing section, deep-fried and then coated or dipped in cayenne sauce and melted butter.
story: The Anchor Bar states the rule flatly in its own account: the wings are not grilled, only deep-fried and slightly crispy, and the sauce is added after the wing has been cooked. Traditionally the wings are deep-fried in oil, without breading or flour, until well browned.

Seventy miles east the same bird goes in dredged, and that is the oldest argument in the tradition. John Young's Buffalo wings from 1961 were breaded too — uncut, breaded, deep fried and served in his own tomato-based mumbo sauce — so the bare fry is not even the older Buffalo practice, only the one the city kept.

*Inference —* the bare fry is a bet on skin. With no coat, everything the eater tastes as crisp is rendered chicken skin, which means the fry temperature and the time have nowhere to hide.
how: Dry the pieces. Into hot oil bare, at a high enough heat that water leaving the skin pushes oil away from the surface — foods deep-fried at proper temperatures absorb very little. Fry until well browned and the skin crackles. Drain, then into the bowl with sauce. Sauce goes on after the fryer, never before; sauce in the oil burns and breaks.
today: The Buffalo houses hold the line on it, and the National Buffalo Wing Festival's field is built around it. *Tradition holds —* a shop that fries bare will say so unprompted, and a shop that breads will not call it breading.
- kin → buffalo (style): The style built on this method; take the coat off and the argument with Rochester starts.
- kin → breaded-fry (fry): The other answer to the same question, seventy miles east.
- kin → naked (term): The menu word for this, and what it does and does not promise.
- kin → anchor-bar (place): States the rule in its own words: deep-fried only, sauce added after.
- kin → the-toss (fry): The step that follows, and the only step that touches the wing after the oil.
- kin → frying-oil (fry): With no coat between skin and oil, the fat is tasted directly.
- kin → john-young (person): Breaded his Buffalo wings from 1961, which makes the bare fry the younger local practice.
- kin → air-fryer (fry): The home attempt at the same result without a pot of oil.
- image: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/images/naked-fry/naked-fry-fried-chicken-wings.jpg · CC BY-SA 4.0 · 白洛嘉 · https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3AFried_chicken_wings.jpg
sources: s:wp-buffalo-wing — Buffalo wing; s:wp-anchor-bar — Anchor Bar; s:wp-deep-frying — Deep frying; s:wp-national-buffalo-wing-festival — National Buffalo Wing Festival
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## the par-cook (fry)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/fry/par-cook/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/fry/par-cook.json
id: par-cook
aliases: par-frying · blanching · the first fry · pre-cooking
said: A shop that gets wings out in four minutes at eight o'clock cooked them at four.
facets: kind=method
region: The United States
what: Cooking the wing most of the way in advance and finishing it to order. The first pass drives out water and cooks the meat through; the finishing pass, hotter and short, browns it. It is the same architecture as a double fry, separated by hours instead of minutes and done for service rather than for texture.
story: The potato wrote the manual. A french fry is fried in two baths: the first at around 160 °C / 320 °F to cook the fries through, the second at 190 °C / 375 °F to crisp the exterior; for thin 2–3 mm strips the first takes about three minutes and the second only seconds. Industrial fries are blanched and frozen between those two baths, which is why a bag of frozen fries finishes in a home fryer at all.

Korean shops run the same split for texture rather than for timing: cook until the fat from the skin is rendered and the moisture stays in the meat, rest, then cook again, and a thin hard shell forms that keeps moisture out.

*Inference —* a bar that sells hundreds of orders on a Sunday cannot start every one cold, so the wings are cooked ahead and finished on the ticket. That is not a lesser method; it is the same method with the rest extended, and it is why chain wings and bar wings can taste closer than either side would like.
how: First pass at a moderate heat until cooked through. Lift, drain, spread in a single layer and cool fast — stacked hot wings steam each other and go slack. Hold cold. On the ticket, straight from cold into hot oil for a short finish, then into the bowl. A wing held longer than a shift loses the skin's tension and no second fry brings it back.
today: General practice across chains and busy bars, and the reason a twenty-piece order arrives at the same time as a six. *Tradition holds —* shops do not advertise it, and customers who suspect it usually put the evidence down to a fryer rather than a schedule.
- kin → double-fry (fry): The same two passes, separated by minutes instead of hours and done for the crust.
- kin → deep-fryer (fry): The vat this exists to keep up with on a Sunday.
- kin → french-fries (dish): The published version of this method, with temperatures and times.
- kin → smoke-then-fry (fry): Another split cook: the slow part in the morning, the fast part on the ticket.
- kin → wing-basket (dish): How a count of fifty reaches a table at once.
- kin → super-bowl-sunday (event): The day no kitchen in America starts a wing order cold.
sources: s:web-wp-french-fries — French fries; s:wp-bonchon-chicken — Bonchon Chicken; s:wp-deep-frying — Deep frying; s:wp-korean-fried-chicken — Korean fried chicken
provenance default: cited · confidence: medium · needs_verification: True · updated: 2026-09-16

## the toss (fry)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/fry/the-toss/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/fry/the-toss.json
id: the-toss
aliases: the bowl · tossing · shaking the wings
said: Wings come out of the fryer and go in the bowl. You can hear it from the bar.
facets: kind=method
region: Western New York, The United States
what: The metal bowl. Cooked wings go into a bowl or pot, sauce goes over them, and the whole thing is shaken to coat the wings completely before serving. It is the last step of a Buffalo wing and the only one that touches the wing after the oil.
story: The step is in the earliest account. The Anchor Bar's own telling has Teressa Bellissimo deep-frying the wings and then flavouring them with a mixture of butter, cayenne pepper and other ingredients; the bar states the rule as plainly as it can be stated — the sauce is added after the wing has been cooked.

How much butter is in the bowl is how heat is set. Cayenne pepper sauce, melted butter and vinegar are the standard base, made mild, medium or hot, sometimes with Worcestershire sauce and garlic powder; more butter reads mild, less reads hot, and a bar's mild and its hot come out of the same two bottles.

Korean shops refuse the bowl. Bonchon brushes sauce on by hand rather than tossing in containers, to spread the seasoning evenly without compromising the texture of a double-fried shell.

*Inference —* the bowl is a texture decision disguised as a saucing decision. Tossing puts sauce everywhere and softens everything; brushing puts sauce on top and keeps the crust. Every regional style is somewhere on that line, and most of them are arguing about where.
how: Hold the sauce warm, not hot — butter splits if it boils. Tip the drained wings into a stainless bowl, pour the sauce over, and shake with the wrist rather than stirring with a spoon; a spoon tears skin and leaves bald patches. Empty the bowl straight onto the plate and let the residue go with it. A dry-rub order gets the same bowl and a dust instead of a liquid.
today: Standard in every Buffalo house and in the chains that copied them. *Tradition holds —* the sound of the bowl is a house's signature and the order in which a bar tosses — hottest last, so the bowl does not carry heat into the next order — is an unwritten rule most kitchens keep.
- kin → buffalo-sauce (sauce): What goes into the bowl, and the ratio that sets the heat.
- kin → buffalo (style): The style whose final step this is; skip it and you have fried chicken.
- kin → naked-fry (fry): The step before: bare skin, so the sauce has something to stick to and nothing to soak.
- kin → sauce-on-the-side (fry): The argument about whether this step is compulsory.
- kin → anchor-bar (place): States the rule in its own words: sauce after the fryer, never before.
- kin → wet-and-dry (term): The two things the bowl can hold — a liquid or a dust.
- kin → soy-garlic-sauce (sauce): Brushed on instead, by shops that will not risk the crust in a bowl.
- kin → wing-basket (dish): Where the bowl empties, residue and all.
sources: s:wp-buffalo-wing — Buffalo wing; s:wp-anchor-bar — Anchor Bar; s:wp-bonchon-chicken — Bonchon Chicken
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## the wing cut (fry)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/fry/wing-cut/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/fry/wing-cut.json
id: wing-cut
aliases: breaking down a wing · segmenting · jointing the wing
said: Two cuts, three pieces, two of them sold. A kitchen says segmenting; a menu says wings.
facets: kind=cut · cut=party wing
region: The United States
what: Where the knife goes on a chicken wing. The wing comes off the bird in three segments and the cook cuts it at both joints: the drumette, shaped like a small drumstick and white meat; the middle flat, also called the wingette, containing two bones; and the tip, often discarded or used for stock. Two pieces go in the basket, so one wing off the bird sells as two wings on a menu.
story: The cut is why the wing could be given away in 1964 and counted by the piece ever since. Chicken wings were inexpensive and undesirable then, normally thrown away or kept for soups and stock — the tip's job, extended to the whole limb. Cutting at the joints turned an offcut into a countable serving: twenty pieces is roughly ten birds' worth of one wing each, and a menu that says twenty wings is selling ten.

Some restaurants leave the tip attached to the flat and serve it that way. In Japan the wing is frequently separated into teba-moto, wing base, and teba-saki, wing tip. In Washington, D.C. carryouts the wing goes into the oil whole and comes out uncut, which is how John Young sold them in Buffalo from 1961.

*Inference —* every argument downstream starts here. Flats against drums is an argument about which of these two pieces you get; all-flats is a request that breaks a kitchen's yield, because one bird produces exactly one of each.
how: Find the two joints by flexing the wing; the cartilage gives and the bone does not. Cut through the joint, not through bone — a knife through the gap needs no force and leaves no splinters. First cut separates the drumette from the flat, second takes the tip off the flat. Keep the tips: boil them for stock, where they have more collagen per gram than either piece that got sold. A grocery sells the two kept pieces already split as party wings.
today: Most American wings arrive at the shop pre-split and frozen, sold as party wings or wing sections, so the cut happens at a processing plant rather than on a bar's board. *Inference —* that is also why a shop can offer all flats at a premium: someone upstream already sorted them.
- kin → wing (term): The word this cut redefines: what a menu calls a wing is one of the two pieces it makes.
- kin → drumette (term): The upper piece this cut frees, white meat on one bone.
- kin → flat (term): The middle piece, two bones and the most skin, which is the argument's other side.
- kin → wing-tip (term): The third piece, usually cut off and boiled for stock rather than sold.
- kin → party-wing (term): What a grocery calls the two kept pieces when it sells them already split.
- kin → all-flats (term): The request this cut cannot grant without somebody upstream sorting a case.
- kin → the-flat-and-the-drum (story): The argument this cut creates, with both sides said in full.
- kin → boneless-wings (dish): Skips this entirely — breast meat chunked, no joints to find.
- kin → fried-rice-plate (dish): Skips it too: D.C. carryouts fry the wing whole, tip and all.
- kin → wing-basket (dish): Why a basket of twenty is ten birds' worth of one wing each.
sources: s:wp-buffalo-wing — Buffalo wing; s:wp-chicken-as-food — Chicken as food; s:wp-poultry — Poultry; s:wp-american-chinese-cuisine — American Chinese cuisine
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## American Deli (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/place/american-deli/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/place/american-deli.json
id: american-deli
aliases: American Deli International, Inc.
facets: state=GA · status=open · founded=1989 · cooked=fried · styles=atlanta-lemon-pepper
region: Atlanta
what: A counter chain out of Atlanta, open since 1989, that sells wings by the ten-piece with a long board of seasonings and sauces. Lemon pepper wet — wings sauced and then hit with dry lemon pepper — was invented here, and the company now runs more than 200 stores across ten states.
story: American Deli opened in 1989 with one store in Atlanta. The company describes itself as a small family-owned business at the start; it does not name its founders on its own pages, and this project could not find a source that does.

The wing that carried the name out of Georgia is lemon pepper wet. Wikipedia's account credits the variation to American Deli: wings coated in sauce rather than left dry, then seasoned. The dish travelled further than the store did. An episode of the FX series Atlanta put lemon pepper wet in a character's hands and attached it to J.R. Crickets instead; the writer Stephen Glover has said the wing on screen was drawn from American Deli's.

*Inference —* the chain sits in this set as a counter, not a bar: no dining room to speak of, a sealed clamshell, a bag. The wing goes home.
today: As of 2026 the company reports more than 200 locations across ten states and gives its corporate address as 275 Scientific Drive NW, Peachtree Corners, Georgia. Its own press page collects the Atlanta rappers, mayors and ballplayers who name it. Atlanta Eats, in April 2025, called it "Arguably the spot that started the lemon pepper wing craze in ATL".
address: Atlanta, GA
geo: 33.749, -84.388 (town)
- kin → atlanta-lemon-pepper (style): Sells the city's wing in both its forms, dry and wet, at a counter price.
- kin → lemon-pepper-wet (sauce): Invented here, per Wikipedia's account of the dish.
- kin → lemon-pepper-seasoning (sauce): Goes on last, after the sauce, which is what makes the wing wet rather than dry.
- kin → jr-cricketts (place): Got the television credit for lemon pepper wet that the show's writer says belonged here.
- kin → wet-and-dry (term): The two words an order here has to choose between.
- kin → wingstop (place): The other chain that took lemon pepper national, from Texas rather than Georgia.
- kin → fried-rice-plate (dish): Shares the counter format: wings and a starch in one clamshell, carried out.

## Anchor Bar (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/place/anchor-bar/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/place/anchor-bar.json
id: anchor-bar
aliases: Anchor Bar Buffalo · Frank & Teressa's Anchor Bar
facets: state=NY · status=open · founded=1935 · cooked=fried · styles=buffalo
region: Western New York
what: A bar and restaurant at Main and North in Buffalo, open since 1935, which claims the Buffalo wing and has trademarked the phrase. Frank and Teressa Bellissimo opened it; their son Dominic ran it and sold the story. The dining room keeps the motorcycles, the jukebox and the original bar, and the wings go out bare-fried with blue cheese and celery.
story: Frank and Teressa Bellissimo opened the Anchor Bar in 1935. The wing story the house tells dates to the evening of 4 March 1964: Dominic behind the bar, friends arriving late, little food left, and Teressa frying the wings that were meant for soup and tossing them with butter and cayenne. She sent out celery and blue cheese alongside, and the first plates went out free.

Frank died in October 1980, aged 84. Teressa died in her apartment above the bar in November 1985, also 84. Dominic died in March 1991, aged 68. Ivano Toscani, who started working for the Bellissimos in the mid-1970s and later owned the place, died in November 2018.

The claim has never gone unchallenged. A 1969 local newspaper piece about the bar does not mention wings. Duff's began selling them across town that year. John Young was selling wings in Buffalo from 1961.
today: Bottled Anchor Bar sauces sell through Tops and Wegmans in the United States and Sobey's and Metro in Canada. The company began opening other locations in 2012 and ran 18 of them as of 2026.
address: 1047 Main Street, Buffalo, NY, 14209
geo: 42.90743, -78.87261 (street)
- kin → buffalo (style): Says the style started here, on 4 March 1964, and owns the trademark on the phrase.
- kin → teressa-bellissimo (person): Cooked here and gets the credit the house gives.
- kin → dominic-bellissimo (person): Tended this bar the night the story turns on, and told the story for thirty years.
- kin → duffs-famous-wings (place): Started selling wings across town in 1969, the year a paper wrote this bar up without mentioning them.
- kin → the-origin-fight (story): Holds one side of it, in three versions.
sources: s:wp-anchor-bar — Anchor Bar; s:wp-buffalo-wing — Buffalo wing; s:trillin-1980 — An Attempt to Compile a Short History of the Buffalo Chicken Wing

## Atomic Wings (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/place/atomic-wings/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/place/atomic-wings.json
id: atomic-wings
facets: state=NY · status=open · founded=1989 · cooked=fried · styles=buffalo
region: New York City, The United States
what: A New York wing chain founded in 1989 by a man trying to reproduce what he had eaten as a student in Buffalo. Wings are cut by hand and breaded on the premises, which is not the Buffalo method, and sauced from more than a dozen house mixes. Shops are small — 800 to 1,500 square feet — and built for takeout rather than for sitting.
story: The founder is Adam Lippin, and the house dates the idea eight years before the first shop: "Back in '81, our fearless founder, Adam, was on a mission: to recreate the hot, crispy wings he chowed down on during his college days in Buffalo." The first Atomic Wings opened in New York City in 1989, on the Upper East Side.

*Inference —* the name reads as a heat claim rather than a place claim, which is how a New York shop sells a Buffalo idea to people who have not been to Buffalo. The word does its own work; see the term record.

What the chain actually sells is a departure from the style it descends from. Restaurant Business, in a September 2020 piece the company reprints, names the difference: "fresh, hand-cut wings that are breaded in-house." A Buffalo wing is fried bare. Breading a wing and calling it Buffalo is the thing Rochester gets argued with about, and Atomic Wings does it in Manhattan without anyone raising it.

Zak Omar bought in and runs the company as owner and chief executive. The same 2020 piece counted eleven shops with sixteen more in the pipeline, and quoted Omar drawing a boundary: "Atomic Wings doesn't aspire to being Buffalo Wild Wings."
how: Wings arrive fresh, get cut by hand, get breaded in the shop, fry, then take one of more than a dozen house sauces, most of them gluten-free. The chicken is "all-natural, antibiotic- and hormone-free" in the house's words. Small rooms, counters, delivery.
today: Shops across New York City, Albany, Buffalo and beyond, with a franchise list running into other states as of September 2026. The record's address is the Harlem shop on Frederick Douglass Boulevard, which OpenStreetMap carries with its hours and phone; the first shop was on the Upper East Side.
address: 2090 Frederick Douglass Boulevard, New York, NY, 10026
geo: 40.8025114, -73.9565294 (street)
- kin → atomic (term): Put the heat word on a sign in 1989 and made it a brand.
- kin → breaded-fry (fry): Breads every wing in the shop, which is the choice that separates it from the Buffalo rooms it copies.
- kin → buffalo (style): Descends from it by a student's memory, and then breads the wing the style fries bare.
- kin → anchor-bar (place): One of the Buffalo rooms its founder studied before opening in Manhattan.
- kin → duffs-famous-wings (place): The other Buffalo room its founder studied.
- kin → buffalo-wild-wings (place): The comparison its owner rejects: small shops built for delivery, not a sports bar.
- kin → rochester-breaded (style): Does in Manhattan what Rochester gets argued with for doing seventy miles from Buffalo.
sources: s:web-atomic-wings-about — About Us; s:web-atomic-wings-rb — 5 Things to Know About: Atomic Wings; s:osm — OpenStreetMap

## Bar-Bill Tavern (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/place/bar-bill-tavern/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/place/bar-bill-tavern.json
id: bar-bill-tavern
aliases: Bar Bill · Bar-Bill
facets: state=NY · status=open · cooked=fried · styles=buffalo
region: Western New York
what: A tavern on Main Street in East Aurora, fifteen miles southeast of Buffalo and not in the city at all, whose wings are brushed with sauce by hand rather than tossed. An order comes as five drums and five flats around a bowl of blue cheese made on the premises. Beef on weck comes off the same kitchen, carved to order.
story: The name is the two owners: Visit Buffalo says it is "named after the tavern's original owners, Barbara and Bill Korzelius," and that the trade sits "inside a 150-year old building that formerly housed an ice cream parlor." Visit Buffalo's spotlight piece says the tavern "just celebrated its 55th anniversary and has been one of Western New York's go-to wing place for decades."

*Inference —* that puts the opening somewhere in the late 1960s, but this project could not read a page that states the year, and the arithmetic depends on when the spotlight was written. Treat the founding year as open.

What East Aurora argues about is the brush. Staff "methodically hand-brush each wing with housemade sauces like honey butter BBQ and spicy Asian" rather than shaking a basket of wings in a bowl, which is the ordinary Buffalo method. The count is fixed too: "Every order features exactly five drums and five flats perfectly centered around a dipping bowl of blue cheese made in-house daily." A drinker who wants all flats is out of luck here and knows it.
how: Wings fry, then each one is painted. House sauces run mild, medium and hot — Visit Buffalo notes "the normal mild, medium and hot run spicy" — alongside honey butter BBQ, spicy Asian and a suicide sauce. Blue cheese is made daily. The beef for the weck is hand carved while the order stands there.
today: Two doors on Main Street in East Aurora as of September 2026: the tavern at 185 and Bar Bill Takeout at 191 Main Street rear, behind Aurora Brew Works. The house does not publish a set of hours this project could read; the East Aurora Chamber directory carries the address and the phone and no hours at all.
address: 185 Main Street, East Aurora, NY, 14052
geo: 42.7675581, -78.6279118 (street)
- kin → the-toss (fry): Refuses it: each wing here is brushed by hand instead of shaken in a bowl.
- kin → all-flats (term): The order that cannot be placed here — five drums and five flats, every time.
- kin → beef-on-weck (dish): Comes off the same kitchen, hand carved, and is half of why East Aurora fills up.
- kin → blue-cheese-dressing (sauce): Made here daily, and the bowl the ten wings are arranged around.
- kin → buffalo (style): Cooks the style fifteen miles outside the city that named it, and brushes it on instead of tossing.
- kin → the-flat-and-the-drum (story): Settles the argument by decree: five of each, centred on the dip.
- kin → mammosers-tavern (place): The other out-of-town tavern on the trail, twelve miles west in Hamburg, arguing pepper against brushwork.

## Big Bob Gibson Bar-B-Q (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/place/big-bob-gibson-bar-b-q/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/place/big-bob-gibson-bar-b-q.json
id: big-bob-gibson-bar-b-q
aliases: Big Bob Gibson's Bar-B-Q · Big Bob Gibson
facets: state=AL · status=open · founded=1925 · cooked=smoked · styles=alabama-white, smoked-bbq-wing
region: The American South
what: The Decatur, Alabama pit where white barbecue sauce was invented: mayonnaise, vinegar and black pepper, made for smoked chicken. Bob Gibson started it in 1925; four generations of his family have run it since, and its competition team won first place for smoked wings at Memphis in May in 2021.
story: Bob Gibson (1888-1972) worked for the L&N Railroad and barbecued at weekends over a dugout pit in his backyard off Danville Road, on an oak plank nailed to a sycamore. The house quotes the line that turned it into a business, from Roslyn Mitchell: "Your future is not in the railroad, but in Bar-B-Q." He opened a restaurant on Moulton Road with his brother-in-law Sam Woodall called Gib-All's, then continued under his own name.

The white sauce was his. He split and seasoned chickens, smoked them about three hours over hickory, and dunked them in mayonnaise, vinegar and black pepper. It began as a chicken sauce and stayed one.

In 1952 Gibson handed the operation to his daughter Catherine McLemore (1919-2004) for half ownership and opened on Sixth Avenue. After his death five grandchildren and their spouses ran it, led by Don McLemore (1941-2026). Chris Lilly, from Florence, joined in 1992 on marrying Amy McLemore, Gibson's great-granddaughter, and runs the competition team. Don McLemore recorded an oral history with the Southern Foodways Alliance on 15 November 2006, for the Alabama BBQ leg of the Southern BBQ Trail: the 1925 backyard start, the meringue pies, a 1988 fire that took the original building, and a rebuild next door that kept the old neon.

The sources disagree on small things. The Encyclopedia of Alabama dates Gibson's death to 1972 and a Sixth Avenue building to 1987; the oral history says McLemore joined in 1972, a year before Gibson died, and puts the fire in 1988. The 1952 Sixth Avenue opening is in both.

At Memphis in May the family has taken five grand championships — 2000, 2003, 2011, 2014 and 2017 — twelve category wins in pork shoulder, and, in 2021, first place in smoked wings.
how: Split the bird, season it, smoke it about three hours over hickory, then dunk it in the white sauce — mayonnaise, apple cider vinegar, lemon juice, black pepper and salt, thin enough to take a whole split chicken. The sauce goes on after the smoke and was made for chicken only.
today: Two Decatur restaurants. The Sixth Avenue room at 1715 6th Avenue SE, phone (256) 350-6969, is open seven days, 9.30 a.m. to 8.15 p.m. for dine-in and to 8.30 p.m. at the drive-through. The Danville Road room at 2520 Danville Road SW, phone (256) 350-0404, keeps the same times Monday to Saturday. The pit turned a hundred in 2025.
address: 1715 6th Avenue SE, Decatur, AL, 35601
geo: 34.5794626, -86.9785639 (street)
- kin → alabama-white (style): Invented it here in 1925, for smoked chicken, and the style has carried the pit's name ever since.
- kin → alabama-white-sauce (sauce): Mayonnaise, vinegar, lemon juice, black pepper and salt, thin enough to dunk a split bird in.
- kin → bob-gibson (person): Built the backyard pit in 1925 and made the sauce that outlived him.
- kin → smoked-bbq-wing (style): Won first place in smoked wings at Memphis in May in 2021, off a pit that was built for whole chickens.
- kin → central-bbq (place): The Memphis pit whose founders came off the same competition circuit.
- kin → southern-foodways-alliance (org): Recorded Don McLemore here in 2006 for the Southern BBQ Trail.
- kin → ranch-vs-blue-cheese (story): Offers a third answer to the dip question, and it is mayonnaise with vinegar in it.

## Blondies Sports (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/place/blondies-sports-bar/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/place/blondies-sports-bar.json
id: blondies-sports-bar
aliases: Blondies Sports Bar · Blondie's
facets: state=NY · status=open · cooked=fried · styles=buffalo
region: New York City
what: A sports bar on West 79th Street between Amsterdam and Broadway, on Manhattan's Upper West Side, with televisions in every sightline and a wing order most of the room is there for. NYC Tourism calls it "a female-owned fixture on the Upper West Side for more than 35 years." It runs late — later than almost any wing room in this set.
story: Manhattan does not have a wing style of its own. What it has is bars that import Buffalo's and keep them open until the West Coast games finish, and Blondies is the Upper West Side's.

The ownership is on the record where it matters: NYC Tourism, the city's own visitor bureau, describes it as female-owned and "one of the city's few women-owned sports bars." Neither that listing nor any other page read here names the owner.

The all-you-can-eat wing night is the room's best-known offer and the least stable fact about it. NYC Tourism puts it on Monday nights. A local listings site writing in June 2026 warns the other way: "The all-you-can-eat wings deal has come and gone over the years — check whether it's running before counting on it." Both are in the record; a reader crossing town on a Monday should ring first.
how: Fried and sauced in the Buffalo manner, served with the game. Time Out's phrase for the kitchen is "greasy pub grub like wings and burgers," which is the compliment a sports bar is fishing for.
today: Open seven days as of September 2026. Closing times run late and disagree between sources: Time Out's listing runs 1am Sunday and Monday to 4am Friday and Saturday, while a 2026 listings page puts weeknights nearer midnight and says game days run longer.
address: 212 West 79th Street, New York, NY, 10024
geo: 40.7832747, -73.9791292 (street)

- kin → buffalo (style): Serves the style four hundred miles from where it started, to a room watching somebody else's game.
- kin → super-bowl-sunday (event): The day this room exists for, and the day the wing trade counts its year by.

## Bolton's Spicy Chicken & Fish (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/place/boltons-spicy-chicken-and-fish/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/place/boltons-spicy-chicken-and-fish.json
id: boltons-spicy-chicken-and-fish
aliases: Bolton's Famous Hot Chicken & Fish · Bolton's
facets: state=TN · status=open · founded=1997 · cooked=fried · styles=nashville-hot
region: Nashville
what: A small East Nashville counter at 624 Main Street selling spicy fried chicken and spicy fried fish, opened in 1997 by Bolton Matthews and Dolly Ingram. The recipe came down from Matthews's uncle Bolton Polk. Its heat is the reference point other Nashville houses get measured by.
story: Bolton Polk built a family recipe for spicy fried chicken and ran The Chicken Shack in East Nashville in the 1980s. He fell ill, the shop closed in the 1990s, and the recipe went to his nephew Bolton Matthews. Matthews and Dolly Ingram had run janitorial services before this; they opened Bolton's Spicy Chicken and Fish on Main Street in 1997, his chicken and her fried fish on one board. By 2007 they had a school bus converted into a mobile kitchen.

Ingram recorded an oral history with the Southern Foodways Alliance on 31 May 2008, interviewed by Amy C. Evans for the Nashville Eats project. From it: "They're banging on the door and they're wanting their chicken…they have a craving for it…Says it gives them a rush."

The Infatuation's review puts the heat plainly: "The highest intensity level at most hot chicken joints is like a medium at Bolton's." The hot fish — catfish or whiting, onions, mustard, pickles — is the order that review calls "the true star of the show." Wings come off the same board as the rest of the bone-in pieces; the menu is parts, not a wing counter.

*Inference —* the fish half is not a sideline. Hot fish is its own Nashville line, a breaded whiting or catfish filet under the same cayenne treatment, and a counter that runs both is running one fryer culture, not two.
today: Still at 624 Main Street in East Nashville in September 2026, in the same small building, now also billed as Bolton's Famous Hot Chicken & Fish.
address: 624 Main Street, Nashville, TN, 37206
geo: 36.1739636, -86.7613291 (street)

- kin → princes-hot-chicken-shack (place): The kitchen Bolton Polk is said to have come up through before his own shack.
- kin → hattie-bs (place): The house whose printed ladder starts, by one reviewer's reckoning, below this counter's baseline.
- kin → nashville-hot-oil (sauce): Made here from a recipe handed down inside one family since the 1980s.
- kin → white-bread-and-pickles (dish): Two slices and a handful under everything that leaves the fryer.
- kin → southern-foodways-alliance (org): Recorded Dolly Ingram here in 2008 for the Nashville Eats project.
- kin → wing-cut (fry): Sold as bone-in pieces off one bird rather than as a wing order with its own menu heading.
