## National Chicken Council (org)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/org/national-chicken-council/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/org/national-chicken-council.json
id: national-chicken-council
aliases: NCC · National Broiler Council
facets: state=DC · status=open · founded=1954
region: Washington, D.C., The United States
what: The trade association of the US chicken industry, and the keeper of the number every Super Bowl story quotes. Founded in Richmond, Virginia in 1954 as the National Broiler Council, moved to Washington in 1965, renamed in 1999. Its producer and processor members account for about 95 percent of the chickens raised in the United States. Each January it publishes the Chicken Wing Report, a projection of how many wings Americans will eat on Super Bowl weekend.
story: The Wing Report is a press release, and it works like one. The 2026 edition went out on 28 January, headlined "Americans to Eat 1.48 Billion Chicken Wings for Super Bowl LX", about 10 million more than the year before; the 2025 figure was 1.47 billion. The release converts the number into pictures — wings laid end to end circling the planet almost three times, 3,400 loaded semi-trucks, a 40-mile convoy — and quotes NCC spokesperson Tom Super: "Especially when it comes to the Super Bowl, where wings rule the roost."

What the release names, it names precisely. Retail wing prices down 2.8 percent year on year at a four-week average of $3.47 a pound, from Circana by way of a Wells Fargo report. Broiler production up 2.2 percent in 2025. Cold storage at 57 million pounds at the end of November, the lowest November total in over ten years outside 2020, from USDA. Wing units up 19.8 percent nationally over the four-week playoff window, from Circana's point-of-sale data.

What it does not name is how the 1.48 billion itself was reached. Three council pages read on 16 September 2026 — the 2026 release, the 2025 release and an older wing feature — carry no method for the headline figure. *Inference —* the figure is a trade association's estimate of its own members' product, not a government statistic, and it should be read as the industry's own projection. That distinction survives every retelling badly: the number arrives in news copy each February with the council's name attached and its status as an estimate dropped.

One older council page does define the unit, which matters more than the size of the number. The count is of wing portions, not whole birds' wings: the third joint, the flapper, is mostly exported to Asia, and the meatier first and second joints are split into drumette and flat for the domestic trade. The same page, built on the 2012 Wing Report, put that year's count at 1.25 billion portions and more than 100 million pounds, and quoted then chief economist Bill Roenigk saying roughly half come from restaurants and half from grocery stores.
how: Beyond the Wing Report, the council lobbies Congress and federal agencies for the chicken industry, runs eight standing committees, and publishes economic and trade statistics for members. It sponsors EatChicken.com, a recipe and food-safety site. Officers and a board are elected each October.
today: Based at 1152 Fifteenth Street NW in Washington. The most recent Wing Report, dated 28 January 2026, projects 1.48 billion wings for Super Bowl LX.
address: 1152 Fifteenth Street NW, Suite 430, Washington, DC, 20005
geo: 38.9050148, -77.0352736 (street)
- kin → super-bowl-sunday (event): Supplies the number the day is measured in: 1.48 billion wings, projected on 28 January 2026.
- kin → wing (term): Counts the word in portions, not birds — the unit behind every billion-wing headline.
- kin → flapper (term): Explains where the third joint goes: exported, mostly to Asia, while the drumette and flat stay home.
- kin → party-wing (term): The split pair its count is made of, drumette and flat sold as two pieces.
- kin → the-price-of-a-wing (story): Publishes the price and supply data the argument runs on: $3.47 a pound retail, four-week average, January 2026.
- kin → us-poultry-and-egg-association (org): The other national poultry association — that one runs research and the processing expo, this one runs Washington.
- kin → wingstop (place): Told the council in 2012 it expected to sauce 5.6 million wings on Super Bowl Sunday alone.
- kin → wing-bowl (event): Covered in the council's own 2012 wing feature, competitive eating and all.

## Southern Foodways Alliance (org)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/org/southern-foodways-alliance/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/org/southern-foodways-alliance.json
id: southern-foodways-alliance
aliases: SFA
facets: state=MS · status=open · founded=1999
region: The American South, The United States
what: An archive that records what cooks say about their own work. The Southern Foodways Alliance is based at the University of Mississippi's Center for the Study of Southern Culture and, in its own words, "documents, studies, and explores the diverse food cultures of the changing American South." It collects oral histories, makes short documentary films, publishes and podcasts as Gravy, and holds an annual symposium. For a wing record, it is the difference between a claim about a kitchen and a transcript from one.
story: Author and activist John Egerton convened a two-day meeting in Birmingham, Alabama on 22 July 1999; fifty people lent their names to the new non-profit. The organising meeting was held at Southern Living, the dinner at Frank and Pardis Stitt's Highlands Bar and Grill. John T. Edge was elected the first director.

What the archive holds matters more here than how it was founded. Amy C. Evans interviewed the Gibson family in Decatur, Alabama about Big Bob Gibson, who was smoking pork and chicken at weekend barbecues in 1925 while working for the L & N Railroad, and whose vinegar-and-mayonnaise white sauce is now on wings across north Alabama. The alliance recorded André Prince Jeffries at Prince's Hot Chicken Shack in Nashville, where the line is longer at ten at night than at lunchtime, and gave her a Guardian of the Tradition award on 11 August 2006.

*Inference —* an oral history is a source a wing record can cite where a press profile cannot reach: the cook's own sentence, dated, transcribed, and held by a named institution.
how: Interviews are recorded, transcribed, and published with the interviewer named and the date given, grouped into projects by place or trade. Films sit beside them. The symposium meets each autumn in Oxford, Mississippi.
today: Still at the Center for the Study of Southern Culture. The 2026 symposium is set for 10–11 October.
address: Oxford, MS
geo: 34.3663773, -89.5187664 (town)
- kin → princes-hot-chicken-shack (place): Recorded the family that made hot chicken, and gave André Prince Jeffries an award in 2006.
- kin → big-bob-gibson-bar-b-q (place): Recorded the Decatur family whose white sauce reached the wing, in an interview by Amy C. Evans.
- kin → andre-prince-jeffries (person): Sat for its interview, and named the shack a late-night place in her own words.
- kin → nashville-hot (style): The style's oral record lives partly in this archive.
- kin → alabama-white (style): The sauce's oral record runs back to a 1925 railway worker's weekend barbecues, as told to this archive.
- kin → adrian-miller (person): Writes the history of Black cooks and fried chicken that this kind of transcript supports.
- kin → the-origin-fight (story): The kind of archive that would have settled it, had anyone recorded Buffalo in 1964.

## U.S. Poultry & Egg Association (org)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/org/us-poultry-and-egg-association/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/org/us-poultry-and-egg-association.json
id: us-poultry-and-egg-association
aliases: USPOULTRY · Southeastern Poultry & Egg Association · SOUTHEASTERN
facets: state=GA · status=open · founded=1947
region: The American South, The United States
what: The trade association that funds the research and runs the equipment show behind the bird. Poultry and egg dealers met in Louisville in March 1947 and founded the Southeastern Poultry & Egg Association; it took the name U.S. Poultry & Egg Association as its membership spread coast to coast, moved to Tucker, Georgia in 1993, and calls itself an "All Feather" association — broilers, turkeys, ducks, eggs, breeding stock and the firms that supply them. It runs the International Production & Processing Expo in Atlanta each January.
story: The founding problem was a railway car. The southeastern industry of the 1940s needed to feed and water live chickens on the way to New York, and needed answers on health, breeding, processing and Washington besides. Thirteen states made up the original association. Albert Mott of Nashville was the first executive secretary, part-time.

The expo started as a convention. About 200 people came to the Ansley Hotel in Atlanta in January 1948; registration for the first full convention a year later cost $2 and more than 600 people came; the first real trade show, in January 1951, had 67 exhibitors and about 2,000 attendees. The American Feed Industry Association joined in 2007, the Meat Institute in 2013, and the combined event was renamed the International Production & Processing Expo.

*Inference —* this is the wing's upstream. A boneless wing exists because breast meat is cheap and a deboning line is available; a party wing exists because a machine cuts a wing into two pieces faster than a cook does; a wholesale wing price moves because broiler production moved. The association does not sell wings. It funds the science and hosts the floor where the machinery that makes them is sold — the expo is, in its own words, "the world's most extensive display of equipment, supplies and services used in the production and processing of poultry, eggs, meat and animal food products."
how: Research grants to university poultry science departments, seminars and workshops by segment, training programmes for member companies, economic data, and the Harold E. Ford Foundation for student recruitment, founded 1994. In fiscal year 2025 the association says more than $4 million went into industry programmes covering promotion, education, communication and research.
today: Based at 1530 Cooledge Road, Tucker, Georgia, with affiliations in 27 states. Nath Morris became president in August 2023. The 2027 expo runs 26–28 January in Atlanta.
address: 1530 Cooledge Road, Tucker, GA, 30084
geo: 33.8275948, -84.2359607 (street)
- kin → national-chicken-council (org): The other national association — that one lobbies Washington and publishes the Wing Report, this one funds research and runs the expo.
- kin → wing-cut (fry): Hosts the floor where the machines that make the cut are sold, every January in Atlanta.
- kin → flapper (term): The piece the processing line sends abroad, decided upstream of any kitchen.
- kin → drumette (term): One of the two pieces a processing line turns a wing into before a bar ever sees it.
- kin → boneless-wings (dish): A deboned breast product, which exists because the line that debones breasts exists.
- kin → the-price-of-a-wing (story): Publishes the production and economic data the price argument rests on.
sources: s:web-uspoultry-about — Association Overview; s:web-uspoultry-history — A History of Service to the Poultry and Egg Industry; s:wp-poultry — Poultry; s:wp-chicken-as-food — Chicken as food

## National Buffalo Wing Festival (event)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/event/national-buffalo-wing-festival/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/event/national-buffalo-wing-festival.json
id: national-buffalo-wing-festival
aliases: Wing Fest · National Buffalo Chicken Wing Festival
facets: state=NY · status=open · founded=2002 · when=Labor Day weekend · styles=buffalo
region: Western New York
what: A two-day wing festival held on Labor Day weekend at Sahlen Field, the minor-league ballpark in downtown Buffalo. Drew Cerza founded it in 2002. Vendors sell wings by the order, contests run all weekend — the US Chicken Wing Eating Championship on the Sunday since 2003, plus amateur sauce contests, a 5K, Miss Buffalo Wing and Bobbing for Wings — and a Hall of Flame inducts the people, families and restaurants that shaped the wing.
story: Cerza, whom the Buffalo News calls the Wing King, took the idea from a fictional festival in the 2001 film Osmosis Jones, and from a Buffalo News column by Donn Esmonde; the festival inducted both Esmonde and Bill Murray for it, in 2009 and 2011. Jill Greenburg accounted for the run this way: roughly $200,000 raised for local charities, almost 3,000,000 wings and 100 sauce varieties served to over 500,000 visitors. The festival's own site put the charity total at about $550,000 when read on 16 September 2026.

The eating contest keeps the records. Joey Chestnut took the trophy from seven-time champion Sonya Thomas on 2 September 2012 with 191 wings, 7.61 pounds, in twelve minutes; he lost it to Miki Sudo in 2013, won it back with 192 in 2014, set 205 in 2015 and 220 in 2017. Geoff Esper ate 281 in 2019. Miki Sudo took the women's title in 2021 with 246. James Webb beat Chestnut in 2023. The 2020 festival was cancelled for the pandemic, the nineteenth deferred to 2021; 2021 and 2022 ran at Highmark Stadium in Orchard Park, and the festival returned to Sahlen Field in 2025.

The Hall of Flame is the festival's own archive of the argument. Frank and Teressa Bellissimo went in first, in 2006, as creators of the original Buffalo wing sauce. Frank's RedHot followed in 2008, as the sauce used in 1964. Wingstop's Antonio Swad went in in 2010, Duff's in 2017, La Nova in 2016, Gabriel's Gate in 2019 for fifty years of wings. In 2013 the hall inducted John Mack Young, posthumously, as an early wing seller who may have predated the Anchor Bar's date — an induction that puts both sides of the origin argument in the same room.
how: Pay at the gate, then pay per order inside. Admission was $20 a day for the 2027 festival as advertised on 16 September 2026, children eight and under free, VIP Party Deck $45 a day; a single order of ten wings was about $13.80 plus tax. Vendors come from Buffalo and from out of state, and the Battle of the Border and Buffalo Buffet Bowl set them against each other.
today: The 2026 festival, the 25th, inducted the Perdue family into the Hall of Flame. The next one runs Saturday 4 September 2027, 11am to 8pm, and Sunday 5 September, 11am to 6pm, at Sahlen Field.
address: 1 James D. Griffin Plaza, Sahlen Field, Buffalo, NY, 14203
geo: 42.8804994, -78.8737899 (street)

- kin → john-young (person): Inducted posthumously in 2013, which is the closest the origin argument has come to an official second answer.
- kin → joey-chestnut (person): Won here in 2012, 2014, 2015 and 2017, taking the record from 191 wings up to 220.

## National Chicken Wing Day (event)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/event/national-chicken-wing-day/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/event/national-chicken-wing-day.json
id: national-chicken-wing-day
aliases: Chicken Wing Day · July 29
facets: state=NY · status=open · founded=1977 · when=29 July · styles=buffalo
region: Western New York, The United States
what: A food day on 29 July, kept by bars, chains and marketing departments across the United States. It comes from one city and one piece of paper: in 1977 Buffalo issued a proclamation honouring Anchor Bar co-owner Frank Bellissimo and declared 29 July Chicken Wing Day. The word national was added later, by everyone else.
story: Mayor Stan Makowski signed it. The fragment of the wording that circulates says "thousands of pounds of chicken wings are consumed by Buffalonians in restaurants and taverns throughout the city each week" — a claim about how much the city was already eating, thirteen years after the night the Anchor Bar dates its invention to.

*Inference —* the date has no argument attached to it, which is probably why it spread. A proclamation that honours one man in one bar became a national date that any restaurant can mark, and the chains that mark it with a free-wing offer have no stake in who invented the wing.

The full proclamation text is not in this project's sources. Two pages carry the same quoted fragment and the same mayor's name: a Buffalo radio station's account from 29 July 2020 and the site that promotes the day.
how: No organiser, no venue, no ticket. Restaurants run offers, radio stations run features, and the date turns up in food calendars. Buffalo's own wing festival keeps to Labor Day weekend instead, five weeks later.
today: Marked on 29 July. *Tradition holds —* Buffalo bars mark it, and this project has found no ordinance behind the observance beyond the 1977 proclamation itself.
address: Buffalo, NY
geo: 42.8867082, -78.879256 (town)

## Super Bowl Sunday (event)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/event/super-bowl-sunday/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/event/super-bowl-sunday.json
id: super-bowl-sunday
aliases: Super Sunday · the Big Game
facets: status=open · founded=1967 · when=the second Sunday in February, since 2022 · styles=buffalo
region: The United States
what: The biggest wing day in the United States, and the second-biggest American eating day of any kind after Thanksgiving dinner. The National Football League's championship game has been played on a Sunday since 1967 and on the second Sunday in February since 2022. The National Chicken Council projected 1.48 billion wings eaten around Super Bowl LX, in a release dated 28 January 2026 — a trade association's estimate of its own industry's product, not a government count.
story: Wings arrived at the Super Bowl through the 1980s and 1990s, on the back of the chains and the pizza companies. Buffalo Wild Wings opened in 1982 and Hooters in 1983. Domino's put Buffalo wings on its national menu in 1994, after the Buffalo Bills had gone to four straight Super Bowls and lost all four; Pizza Hut followed in 1995.

The number is now an annual ritual of its own. The council's Wing Report goes out in late January, and the figure walks into February news copy with the council's name attached and the word estimate usually dropped: 1.42 billion for LVI, 1.45 billion for LVII, 1.47 billion for LIX, 1.48 billion for LX. The 2026 release translated that into wings circling the planet almost three times and a forty-mile convoy of trucks.

The unit is a wing portion, not a bird's wing. An older council page, built on the 2012 report, says so plainly and adds that about half come from restaurants and half from grocery stores, that the flapper is mostly exported, and that then chief economist Bill Roenigk reckoned three times as many Americans eat wings on this Sunday as on an ordinary one.

Prices run on the same calendar. Wholesale wings rise in the fourth quarter as restaurants stock up and usually peak in January. For LX the council reported fresh retail wings at a four-week average of $3.47 a pound, down 2.8 percent year on year, with US broiler production up 2.2 percent in 2025 and cold storage at 57 million pounds — the lowest November total in more than a decade outside 2020.

The league's lawyers shape how the day is sold. The NFL polices the phrases Super Bowl and Super Bowl Sunday, so non-sponsors advertise wing deals against "the Big Game" instead.
how: Wings get ordered for a time, not for a table: bars and shops take orders days ahead, kitchens batch-fry from mid-afternoon, and grocery cases fill with heat-and-eat trays that are the same product restaurants buy. Boneless and bone-in go out together; celery, carrots, blue cheese and ranch go out beside them; buffalo chicken dip covers the people who did not want to hold a bone.
today: Super Bowl LX was played on 8 February 2026 at Levi's Stadium in Santa Clara, California, where Seattle beat New England 29–13. The Wing Report for that game, dated 28 January 2026, projected 1.48 billion wings, about 10 million more than the year before.
- kin → national-chicken-council (org): Publishes the number this day is measured in, and is a trade association rather than a statistical agency.
- kin → wing-bowl (event): Held on the Friday before, by a city whose team kept missing the game.
- kin → wingstop (place): Told the council in 2012 it expected 5.6 million wings on this one Sunday, at 290 percent of an average Sunday's sales.
- kin → buffalo-wild-wings (place): A sports bar built for exactly this afternoon.
- kin → boneless-wings (dish): Shares the platter, and doubles the count without touching a wing.
- kin → buffalo-chicken-dip (dish): The party-table version, for the half of the room that will not hold a bone.
- kin → buffalo-chicken-pizza (dish): Arrived on national menus in the same stretch: Domino's added wings in 1994, Pizza Hut in 1995.
- kin → the-price-of-a-wing (story): Sets the annual peak: wholesale wings climb through the fourth quarter and top out in January.
- kin → party-wing (term): The cut the billion is counted in — drumette and flat, sold as two pieces.

## Wing Bowl (event)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/event/wing-bowl/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/event/wing-bowl.json
id: wing-bowl
aliases: Wing Bowl Las Vegas
facets: state=PA · status=open · founded=1993 · when=the Friday before the Super Bowl · styles=buffalo
region: Philadelphia
what: A competitive wing-eating contest run by a Philadelphia sports radio station on the Friday before the Super Bowl. Al Morganti and Angelo Cataldi of WIP started it in 1993, for a city whose football team kept not reaching the Super Bowl. Two eaters and 150 spectators in a hotel lobby the first year; crowds over 20,000 in an arena by the 2000s, at six in the morning, with a field of qualifiers, costumed entourages, and women called Wingettes escorting the eaters. WIP ended it in 2018. A Las Vegas edition ran on 7 February 2026.
story: Morganti came up with it because the Eagles were going nowhere, and, it is also said, because he had had enough of the Buffalo Bills reaching Super Bowls and losing them. Wing Bowl I was held in the lobby of the Wyndham Franklin Plaza in Center City. Joan Brewington turned up in a bathrobe and boxing gloves, punching the air; Carmen Cordero won and took home a hibachi.

Entry came two ways: perform an eating stunt live on the WIP morning show with Morganti judging — twenty cups of oatmeal, five Big Macs, a gallon of milk — or win a Wingoff at a bar in Philadelphia or South Jersey. Morganti disallowed stunts he considered cheating, like dunking bread to get it down. Mayor Ed Rendell handed out a Liberty Bell trophy at four of them. Umpire Eric Gregg was commissioner from the second year until his death in 2006, then Pat Croce, then Jon Dorenbos for the last five.

The counts climbed and climbed. Jonathan Squibb won three straight from 2009 to 2011, ending at 255. Takeru Kobayashi ate 337 in 2012. Molly Schuyler ate 363 in 2014, Patrick Bertoletti 444 in 2015, Schuyler 429 in 2016 and then 501 in the last Philadelphia edition, Wing Bowl XXVI on 2 February 2018. Prizes by then ran to a truck, a motorcycle, a ring and cash.

The criticism is part of the record and was published while the event still ran. Philadelphia Magazine's Richard Rys, writing on 18 January 2015 under the headline "Wing Bowl: Is It Time to End It?", called it "WIP's annual celebration of the most primal male instincts (gluttony, protracted leering, getting shitfaced on Miller Lite at six in the morning)" and described what he had watched happen to women in the crowd: "I've seen men grab two women by their heads and try to make them kiss, or claw at women's shirts when the camera pans past." Columnist Ronnie Polaneczky, quoted in the same piece, described a strip-club mentality in which all women are for sale. WIP announced the end on 30 October 2018, nine months after the Eagles won Super Bowl LII; program director Spike Eskin said "When Wing Bowl started … a large part of it was the lead-up to the Super Bowl never involved the Eagles. We just wanted to get to the promised land." When a documentary, No One Died: The Wing Bowl Story, arrived in August 2026, the Philadelphia Inquirer quoted Taggart, who made it, on what it had to carry: "You have to show the El Wingador stuff. You have to show the ugly of the fights and some of the misogyny."
how: Thirty minutes of eating in the Philadelphia years, judged by wing count. The Las Vegas revival ran twenty competitors in rounds for a $5,000 winner-takes-all prize, and the winning 189 was scored 85, 71 and 33 across three of them.
today: The Plaza Hotel & Casino in Las Vegas held Wing Bowl on 7 February 2026, the first outside Philadelphia. Molly Schuyler won it with 189 wings, ahead of Bob Shoudt on 162 and Dan Kennedy on 117 — her fourth Wing Bowl win, after 2014, 2016 and the 501 of 2018.
address: 3601 South Broad Street, Philadelphia, PA, 19148
geo: 39.9011004, -75.1720165 (street)
- kin → angelo-cataldi (person): Co-founded it and hosted it on WIP for twenty-six years.
- kin → al-morganti (person): Thought it up, because the Eagles were not going to the Super Bowl, and judged the qualifying stunts.
- kin → bill-simmons-el-wingador (person): Five-time champion, and the name the documentary says you cannot leave out.
- kin → joey-chestnut (person): Won Wing Bowl XIV after talking his way in with a gallon of milk.
- kin → super-bowl-sunday (event): Scheduled against it — the Friday before, for a city whose team was not playing.
- kin → national-buffalo-wing-festival (event): The Buffalo festival crowned champions too, and was born of a city's own dish rather than a radio show.
- kin → buffalo (style): Ate the style by the hundred, 300 miles from where it started.
sources: s:wp-wing-bowl — Wing Bowl; s:web-phillymag-wing-bowl-2015 — Wing Bowl: Is It Time to End It?; s:web-inquirer-wing-bowl-doc — A new Wing Bowl documentary chose to celebrate the event instead of focusing on the 'ugly'; s:web-eatfeats-wing-bowl-lv-2026 — Molly Schuyler wins 2026 Las Vegas Wing Bowl; s:wp-joey-chestnut — Joey Chestnut
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## all flats (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/word/all-flats/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/term/all-flats.json
id: all-flats
aliases: all drums · all flats no drums · flats only
said: Tacked to the end of the order: 'twenty, lemon pepper, all flats.'
root: all + flats (plural of flat); an order-modifier phrase, mirrored by all drums · first seen: 2018, in 2 Chainz's 'Hot Wings': "She just want her 20-piece/ All flats with the lemon pepper" — the earliest dated printing this project can name · *Inference —* the phrase can only exist where a counter holds enough volume to sort, which is why it belongs to high-turnover wing counters and chains rather than to a bar running one case a night.
facets: letter=A · part_of_speech=phrase
region: Atlanta, The United States
what: An order that refuses half the bird. A wing splits one-for-one into a drumette and a flat, so a kitchen filling an all-flats order has to sell the drumettes to somebody else — which is why the answer is often no, and why the places that say yes charge for it.
how: Say it last, after count and flavour, and expect a wait: somebody is picking through a pan. Chains that will do it price it per wing rather than per order. A counter that cannot do it will say 'they come mixed', which is the polite form of no.
- kin → flat (term): The piece the order is asking for, and why.
- kin → drumette (term): The piece the order leaves behind, which is somebody else's problem.
- kin → the-flat-and-the-drum (story): The argument this phrase is the loud end of.
- kin → atlanta-lemon-pepper (style): The style the phrase travels with in the songs that carry it.
- kin → wingstop (place): One of the counters with enough volume to sort a pan, and it prices the sorting.
- kin → wing (term): One bird, two pieces, which is the arithmetic the phrase runs into.
sources: s:wp-lemon-pepper-wings — Lemon pepper wings; s:wp-buffalo-wing — Buffalo wing; s:wp-wingstop — Wingstop

## atomic (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/word/atomic/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/term/atomic.json
id: atomic
aliases: atomic wings · nuclear · triple atomic
said: Always last on the heat list, and usually printed in red.
root: Ancient Greek átomos 'uncuttable' → Latin atomus → English atom → atomic; the wing sense borrows the bomb's connotation from the mid-20th century, not the physics · first seen: 1989 as a business name: Adam Lippin opened Atomic Wings in New York City that year, by the company's own account of its thirtieth anniversary in 2019. That dates the word's use for a wing business, not its first use as a heat level, which this project could not date · *Inference —* the ladder needs a top rung that sounds like consequence rather than measurement. Mild, medium and hot describe; atomic threatens. That is why the next rung up is usually a repetition — triple atomic, atomic scorpion — rather than a new word.
facets: letter=A · part_of_speech=adjective
region: The United States
what: Top of a house heat ladder, and a word that only means something inside one bar's list. Wingstop's own description of its Atomic flavour is "It's the hottest we've got. Find out for yourself" — Spice Level 5, the end of its scale. An atomic at one counter can be milder than a hot at another, because nothing standardises the rungs.
story: The word carries a whole apparatus with it. Bars and restaurants make an extra-hot sauce specifically so there is something to fail at, and reward whoever finishes with a photograph on the wall or the website, a commemorative T-shirt, a free meal, or some combination.

Quaker Steak & Lube runs the form at its most elaborate: its Atomic Scorpion sauce is published at 800,000 Scoville heat units, entrants sign a standard waiver, silicone gloves stay on, no bathroom breaks, and the finishers get a free t-shirt and their names on a chalkboard. Drinks are allowed, and there is no clock.

*Inference —* the waiver is the point of the word. A signature turns an order into an event, and an event is what gets photographed, which is what the wall is for.
how: Ordered by someone else's dare, eaten with a dairy dip within reach — blue cheese or ranch, both of which cut capsaicin better than beer does. Kitchens usually serve it in a small count and usually will not sauce a whole basket.
- kin → atomic-wings (place): The New York chain that took the word for its name, in 1989.
- kin → wingstop (place): Publishes the word at the top of its own five-level scale.
- kin → mango-habanero (sauce): The rung below it on most chain lists — heat with a fruit to hide behind.
- kin → nashville-hot-oil (sauce): Heat built into the cooking fat rather than bolted on as a top rung.
- kin → wing-bowl (event): The other place wings became a spectacle with a crowd and a prize.
- kin → ranch-vs-blue-cheese (story): The dip argument, which an atomic order settles by force.
sources: s:wp-buffalo-wing — Buffalo wing; s:web-wingstop-atomic — Atomic | Wingstop Flavors; s:web-chowhound-spice-challenges — The 9 Most Intense Restaurant Spice Challenges In The US; s:web-atomic-wings-30th — Nationwide Chain Atomic Wings Celebrates 30th Anniversary; s:wp-scoville-scale — Scoville scale
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## boneless (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/word/boneless/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/term/boneless.json
id: boneless
aliases: boneless wings · wyngz · boneless bites
said: An adjective that got promoted: on most menus 'boneless' is now a noun and the wing is silent.
root: bone + -less, the Old English privative suffix; the menu sense attaches the adjective to 'wing' and then lets the noun drop, leaving 'boneless' standing alone · first seen: 25 July 2024 as a term of art in Ohio law, when the Supreme Court of Ohio construed 'boneless wings' in Berkheimer v. REKM, L.L.C., 2024-Ohio-2787 — a dated judicial reading, not the word's first use, which is older and undated here · The related spelling 'wyngz' is a labelling rule, not a joke. Consumer Reports, reporting the FSIS policy in February 2011, records that the agency allows the spelling for a product shaped like a wing or sold as a bite-size appetizer only under conditions including that the poultry is white chicken and "the product does not contain any wing meat", and that "no other misspellings are permitted". Wiktionary glosses it as a respelling of wings.
facets: letter=B · part_of_speech=adjective
region: The United States
what: Breast meat cut into pieces, floured and spiced, fried or baked, then sauced like a wing and sold under the wing's name. Wikipedia describes them as "essentially small pieces of skinless, boneless chicken breast that are coated in flour and spices, then fried or baked, like a chicken nugget", sometimes marketed as wyngz. Restaurants added them as raw wing prices rose and as some diners asked for a neater plate.
story: The word went to court. Michael Berkheimer ordered boneless wings with parmesan garlic sauce at Wings on Brookwood in Butler County, Ohio, and days later an emergency room found a chicken bone lodged in his oesophagus. He sued the restaurant, its supplier and the chicken farm. On 25 July 2024 the Supreme Court of Ohio affirmed summary judgment against him, 4-3.

Justice Joseph T. Deters wrote for the majority that the label was "merely a description of the cooking style", and that "A diner reading 'boneless wings' on a menu would no more believe that the restaurant was warranting the absence of bones" than believe the item came off a wing. Justice Michael P. Donnelly, dissenting, called that reasoning "utter jabberwocky" and wrote: "The reasonable expectation that a person has when someone sells or serves him or her boneless chicken wings is that the chicken does not have bones in it." He also asked: "Does anyone really believe that the parents in this country who feed their young children boneless wings or chicken tenders or chicken nuggets or chicken fingers expect bones to be in the chicken? Of course they don't."

The holding is Ohio's and it is about negligence, not about menus: it decides who bears a risk, not what a word ought to mean. Four justices and three justices read the same two words differently, in writing, and both readings are on the record.
how: Ordered the way a bone-in wing is — count, sauce, dip — and eaten with fingers or a fork, which is the point people who order them make. They come in pieces of roughly even size, so a twenty-piece boneless and a twenty-piece bone-in are not the same amount of food.
- kin → boneless-wings (dish): The dish this word names, and where the eating is described.
- kin → wing (term): The word it borrows, which is the whole dispute.
- kin → boneless-is-not-a-wing (story): The argument, with the people who make it quoted by name.
- kin → buffalo-word (term): The other word the sauce carried onto breast meat.
- kin → breaded-fry (fry): The coating that makes it possible; skinless breast needs one.
- kin → wingstop (place): Sells them beside bone-in, in the same flavours, at its own price.
- kin → buffalo-wild-wings (place): Built a menu on the pair and lets a table order both.
sources: s:wp-buffalo-wing — Buffalo wing; s:web-berkheimer-opinion — Berkheimer v. REKM, L.L.C., 2024-Ohio-2787; s:web-berkheimer-nbc — It's OK for 'boneless' chicken wings to have bones, Ohio Supreme Court rules; s:web-berkheimer-hklaw — Court Decision Concerning "Boneless Chicken Wings" Ignites Political Firestorm in Ohio; s:web-wyngz-consumer-reports — Stephen Colbert's right wyngz rhetoric; s:web-wyngz-wiktionary — wyngz; s:wp-chicken-nugget — Chicken nugget
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: True · updated: 2026-09-16

## Buffalo (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/word/buffalo-word/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/term/buffalo-word.json
id: buffalo-word
aliases: buffalo-style · buffalo sauce (attributive)
said: Lower-cased on most menus now, which is what happens to a place name that becomes a flavour.
root: Buffalo, New York (the city) → attributive adjective meaning 'dressed in cayenne hot sauce and melted butter'; the city takes its name from Buffalo Creek, whose own name is disputed · first seen: 25 August 1980, in the title of Calvin Trillin's New Yorker piece 'An Attempt to Compile a Short History of the Buffalo Chicken Wing' — the earliest dated printing this project can name, not a claim about the phrase's first use · The creek's name is argued over. The Buffalo History Museum records the Seneca reading 'Place of the Basswood' for the area, and separately the *folk* etymology that French speakers called it beau fleuve, beautiful river — that one first appeared in print on 23 March 1895, in an unsigned Buffalo Evening News review of a talk by Rev. Samuel T. Clarke, and the museum notes that no copy of Clarke's speech survives, so nobody knows whether he offered evidence. Second *folk* reading, heard at tables everywhere: that the wing has something to do with bison. It does not.
facets: letter=B · part_of_speech=adjective
region: Western New York, The United States
what: A city's name working as an adjective. Buffalo now modifies a sauce rather than a place: vinegar-based cayenne hot sauce cut with melted butter, and anything wearing it. The word travelled further than the bird it started on — it has been applied to boneless wings made from breast, to chicken fries, nuggets and popcorn chicken, to shrimp, to cauliflower, to dip and to pizza.
story: Buffalo, New York is a port city at the head of the Niagara River, named for the creek. The wing took the city's name the way a garment district takes one: from outside. Nobody in Buffalo orders a Buffalo wing; they order wings, and the qualifier belongs to everyone else. *Inference —* that is the tell of a regional name that went national — the region drops it, the country picks it up.

The adjective then detached from the meat entirely. Once Buffalo meant a sauce, it could be put on a vegetable, and cauliflower dressed in cayenne and butter is Buffalo cauliflower without anybody claiming it is a wing. *Inference —* what carried is the flavour formula, not the animal, which is why the word survives a menu with no chicken on it at all.
how: As an adjective it takes the front of the name: Buffalo wings, Buffalo shrimp, Buffalo chicken dip. Where a menu wants distance from the city it writes 'buffalo-style' instead, and where a chain wants the heat named it writes 'medium' and 'hot' after it.
- kin → buffalo (style): The style this word was cut from, and the only one that does not need it.
- kin → buffalo-sauce (sauce): What the adjective actually names: cayenne hot sauce and melted butter.
- kin → buffalo-chicken-dip (dish): The adjective applied to a bowl, with no wing in it.
- kin → buffalo-chicken-pizza (dish): The adjective applied to a pie, which is how far it has travelled.
- kin → boneless (term): The other word the sauce carried onto breast meat.
- kin → calvin-trillin (person): Printed the phrase in The New Yorker in 1980 and sent it out of the city.
- kin → anchor-bar (place): The bar the word is usually traced to, in a claim other people contest.
- kin → the-origin-fight (story): The argument over who the adjective should be crediting.
sources: s:wp-buffalo-wing — Buffalo wing; s:web-buffalo-history-name — How Did Buffalo Get Its Name?; s:trillin-1980 — An Attempt to Compile a Short History of the Buffalo Chicken Wing; s:wp-buffalo-new-york — Buffalo, New York
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## drumette (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/word/drumette/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/term/drumette.json
id: drumette
aliases: drum · drums · wing drumette · first segment wing portion
said: A counter says 'drums'. A grader says 'first segment wing portion'.
root: drum (the drumstick it resembles) + -ette, the French diminutive that English borrowed for small versions of things · The National Chicken Council writes it as the trade does: "The wing is usually split into two parts or portions, known as the 'drumette' and the mid-section or 'flat'". USDA's Agricultural Marketing Service labels the same piece 'Grade A First Segment Wing Portion (Wing Drumette)' in its grading photographs — the parenthesis is the government conceding the kitchen's word. *Inference —* the -ette says small drumstick, which is what a diner sees, not what an anatomist sees: the drumette is the humerus, the arm bone, not a leg at all.
facets: letter=D · part_of_speech=noun
region: The United States
what: Upper of the three wing segments, and the meatiest. One bone, meat bunched at one end, skin all round: it eats like a small drumstick, which is where the name comes from. White meat, same as the breast. Two per bird.
how: Hold it by the narrow end and eat down, or stand it up and push the meat off the bone in one piece — bar tables argue about which. Sauce pools in the cup at the thick end, so a drumette carries more of whatever it was tossed in than a flat does.
today: Grocery party-wing packs print drumette and flat on the label together; Sanderson Farms sells it as 'Chicken Party Wings Flats & Drummettes', with the second m that the trade spelling keeps dropping.
- kin → wing (term): One of the two pieces a menu means when it says wing.
- kin → flat (term): The other piece off the same joint, and the one people compare it against.
- kin → wing-tip (term): Cut from the far end of the same wing, and usually not sold.
- kin → wing-cut (fry): The knife that makes it: through the joint between humerus and radius.
- kin → the-flat-and-the-drum (story): The argument this word is one half of.
- kin → party-wing (term): What a grocery calls it when it is bagged with the flats.
- kin → national-chicken-council (org): Writes 'drumette' into its own trade wording, which is how the word travels.
sources: s:wp-buffalo-wing — Buffalo wing; s:wp-chicken-as-food — Chicken as food; s:wp-poultry — Poultry; s:web-ncc-wings-hot-topic — Chicken Wings – A Hot Topic!; s:web-usda-ams-wing — Chicken Wings (poultry grading photographs); s:web-openfoodfacts-party-wings — Chicken Party Wings Flats & Drummettes — Sanderson Farms

## extra crispy (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/word/extra-crispy/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/term/extra-crispy.json
id: extra-crispy
aliases: well done · hard fried · crispy
said: 'Extra crispy' at the register; 'well done' on the ticket.
root: extra (Latin extra 'outside, beyond') + crispy (Old English crisp, from Latin crispus 'curled', re-pointed in English to mean brittle) — an intensifier stuck to a texture word · *Inference —* the phrase is an instruction wearing the grammar of a flavour. It goes in the same slot on the ticket as 'hot' or 'lemon pepper', but it asks the fryer for time rather than the sauce station for anything.
facets: letter=E · part_of_speech=phrase
region: The United States
what: An order for more time in the oil. Not a flavour, not an upcharge in most places: a request that the wing stay down until the skin goes hard and the colour goes past golden. Kitchens read it as a range, which is why the same words get you different wings at two counters a block apart.
how: A cook answers it three ways — leave them longer in one fry, pull the basket up and drop it back for a second hit, or run the whole order through a proper double fry. Ordering it costs minutes, so a busy kitchen will sometimes decline. Ask for it and for sauce on the side and the crust survives the drive home; ask for it and a heavy toss and you have undone it.
- kin → double-fry (fry): The technique that delivers what the phrase asks for, when a kitchen has time for it.
- kin → deep-fryer (fry): The machine the instruction is aimed at.
- kin → naked (term): The other instruction a counter takes about texture, this one about coating.
- kin → sauce-on-the-side (fry): Ordered with it by anyone who wants the crust to last past the parking lot.
- kin → the-toss (fry): The step that undoes it, second by second.
- kin → air-fryer (fry): Bought largely by people chasing this phrase at home.
sources: s:wp-buffalo-wing — Buffalo wing; s:wp-deep-frying — Deep frying
provenance default: tradition · confidence: medium · needs_verification: True · updated: 2026-09-16

## flapper (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/word/flapper/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/term/flapper.json
id: flapper
aliases: pointer · flipper
root: flap (verb) + -er, the agent suffix — the part that does the flapping; pointer is built the same way off point · Two agent nouns for one piece, each naming a different property: flapper names what it did on the bird, pointer names its shape on the plate. Wikipedia's Buffalo wing article lists them together, "flapper or pointer". *Inference —* nobody arbitrates between them because the piece is rarely sold, so neither word has to win.
facets: letter=F · part_of_speech=noun
region: The United States
what: Cook's name for the wing tip: the pointed third segment, the one that carried the flight feathers. Skin and cartilage over two thin bones. It is the piece that gets thrown in the stock bucket, which is why most people who eat wings weekly have never heard the word.
how: Said in a kitchen, not at a table. A cook breaking cases says flapper; the same cook writes 'tips' on the stock log.
- kin → wing-tip (term): The same piece under the butcher's name, and the one a label prints.
- kin → wing (term): Its third segment, counted by anatomy and not by the menu.
- kin → flat (term): The piece it hangs off until the first cut.
- kin → wing-cut (fry): The cut that decides whether this word ever gets said.
sources: s:wp-buffalo-wing — Buffalo wing; s:wp-poultry — Poultry

## flat (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/word/flat/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/term/flat.json
id: flat
aliases: wingette · flats · wing flat · second segment wing portion · mid-section
said: 'Flats or drums?' — and most places cannot answer it.
root: the adjective flat, turned into a noun for the piece it describes; the competing name wingette is wing + -ette, the same diminutive that built drumette · Two words, one piece. The National Chicken Council calls it "the mid-section or 'flat'"; Wikipedia's poultry article gives it as "the 'wingette' (also called the 'flat')". USDA's grading captions use neither, labelling it 'Grade A Second Segment Wing Portion (Wing Flat)'. *Inference —* wingette reads as packer's English and flat as counter English, and the counter is winning.
facets: letter=F · part_of_speech=noun
region: The United States
what: Middle segment, two bones with a gap between them, and more skin per bite than any other piece of a chicken. Flat because it is — it lies down in the fryer basket and comes out on one plane. Two per bird.
how: Twist out the smaller bone, then pull the larger one, and the meat comes free in a strip; people who order all flats are usually doing that. More surface means more crust and more sauce clinging, which is the case its partisans make against the drumette.
- kin → drumette (term): The other half of the split, and the side of the argument this one is against.
- kin → wing (term): One of the two pieces a menu means when it says wing.
- kin → all-flats (term): The order that asks for nothing but these.
- kin → wing-tip (term): Attached to this piece until somebody cuts it off; a few kitchens leave it on.
- kin → the-flat-and-the-drum (story): The argument this word is the other half of.
- kin → wing-cut (fry): Where the second cut goes, and why this piece keeps two bones.
- kin → party-wing (term): Bagged with the drumettes and sold as one product.

## hot honey (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/word/hot-honey-word/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/term/hot-honey-word.json
id: hot-honey-word
aliases: chili honey · spicy honey
said: A brand name doing duty as a category name, the way people say a xerox.
root: hot (chile-hot, not temperature-hot) + honey; an English compound that names the two ingredients and nothing else · first seen: 2010, as the brand Mike's Hot Honey, founded by Mike Kurtz in Brooklyn — the dated point from which the phrase became a product category rather than a description · Kurtz met honey steeped with chillies at a pizzeria while studying in Brazil in 2004. Mixing honey with chillies is old and widespread; the *phrase* is what is recent. *Inference —* the word arrived in English with a label on it, which is why its history is a company's history.
facets: letter=H · part_of_speech=noun
region: The United States
what: Honey infused with chillies, and the two-word name that turned it into a menu category. On wings it is a finish rather than a toss: drizzled over crust after the sauce, or whisked into a sauce to sweeten and thicken it. It reaches wings by way of pizza and fried chicken, where it landed first.
story: Mike Kurtz founded Mike's Hot Honey in Brooklyn in 2010 and went to work at Paulie Gee's pizzeria in Greenpoint the same year; the pizzeria put his honey on a soppressata pie called the Hellboy, which stayed a best-seller. He started a distribution operation in 2011 and got into Whole Foods, the first grocery chain to carry it, in 2014.

The category followed the brand rather than the other way round. Interest in hot honey rose as a trend in the early 2020s alongside the brand, tracked by a steady climb in Google search interest from early 2022; Business Insider called it a "new food obsession" in 2024, recipes spread on TikTok, and food companies including V8 and Tillamook put out hot-honey variants. By 2024 Mike's was carried in over 3,000 restaurants and 30,000 retail outlets in the United States.
how: Put on last. Honey burns and sugar goes bitter, so it goes on after the fryer, never before — drizzled over a dry-rubbed or lightly sauced wing so the crust stays audible, or cut into butter and hot sauce to make a sweet-hot toss.
- kin → hot-honey (sauce): The sauce the word names, and what is in a bottle of it.
- kin → nashville-hot (style): The other place a sweet-and-burning finish sits on fried chicken, built from lard and cayenne instead.
- kin → honey-bbq-sauce (sauce): The sweet wing sauce it arrived to compete with.
- kin → sweet-chili-sauce (sauce): Sweet-and-hot by a different route, from a different kitchen.
- kin → buffalo-chicken-pizza (dish): Pizza is where the word reached most people before it reached wings.
- kin → the-toss (fry): The step it deliberately comes after.
sources: s:wp-hot-honey — Hot honey; s:web-mikes-hot-honey — Mike's Hot Honey
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## mild sauce (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/word/mild-sauce-word/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/term/mild-sauce-word.json
id: mild-sauce-word
aliases: mild
said: 'Mild' alone, at the window: it names the sauce, not the heat you want.
root: mild + sauce; a heat word that stopped being a heat word and became the name of a specific thing · *Inference —* the name misleads everyone from outside Chicago exactly once. Elsewhere 'mild' answers 'how hot?'; on the South and West Sides it answers 'what sauce?', and a counter that also sells hot sauce will sell you mild sauce with hot sauce on it.
facets: letter=M · part_of_speech=noun
region: Chicago
what: Chicago's word for a red-brown condiment poured over fried chicken and fries at South and West Side chicken shacks and barbecue counters, and particularly associated with Black communities in Chicago. The sauce sits near barbecue sauce and near mumbo sauce; recipes vary substantially, and many formulations combine ketchup, barbecue sauce and hot sauce.
story: The word was made popular by the restaurants, not by a bottler: Harold's Chicken Shack, Uncle Remus Saucy Fried Chicken and Lem's Bar-B-Q are the names the record attaches to it. *Inference —* that is why there is no canonical recipe to argue about and no single owner to sue: the sauce was a house formula at dozens of counters before it was anybody's product, and each house still answers for its own.

Where it overlaps with mumbo, the two words carry a live argument about which city's condiment came first. Mumbo has a trademark and a dated registration behind it; mild sauce has restaurants. *Inference —* those are different kinds of evidence, and they do not settle each other.
how: Ordered as a quantity, not a choice: 'extra mild' means more sauce on the box, not less heat in it.
- kin → mild-sauce (sauce): The sauce the word names, with what goes in it.
- kin → chicago-mild-sauce (style): The wing style built on it.
- kin → harolds-chicken-shack (place): One of the counters that made the word travel.
- kin → uncle-remus-saucy-fried-chicken (place): Another, on the West Side, with its own formula.
- kin → mumbo (term): Washington's word for the cousin condiment, and the one with the trademark.
sources: s:wp-mild-sauce — Mild sauce; s:wp-mumbo-sauce — Mumbo sauce; s:wp-harold-s-chicken-shack — Harold's Chicken Shack
provenance default: cited · confidence: medium · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## mumbo (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/word/mumbo/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/term/mumbo.json
id: mumbo
aliases: mambo · mumbo sauce · mambo sauce
said: Spelled mumbo in Chicago and on the trademark, mambo on plenty of D.C. carryout menus. Same sound.
root: no agreed etymon. As a commercial name the chain runs Argia B. Collins Sr.'s Chicago barbecue sauce → the registered mark MUMBO → the D.C. carryout word; the D.C. spelling mambo may be reshaping by the dance name · first seen: 1950 as a trademark: Collins and his business used the Mumbo mark from at least as early as 1950, and his successor-in-interest Select Brands, LLC registered it with the USPTO on 25 May 1999, Registration No. 2,247,855 · *Folk —* the mambo spelling invites a story about the dance, and the dance-named D.C. go-go group Mambo Sauce took its name from the condiment rather than the other way round. No source this project found derives the word from the dance, and none derives it from anywhere else either.
facets: letter=M · part_of_speech=noun
region: Washington, D.C., Chicago
what: A word for a sweet-sour-hot red condiment, sold behind plexiglass in Washington carryouts and poured on fried wings, french fries, jumbo shrimp and fried rice. Barbecue-adjacent, sweeter than barbecue sauce, and by most accounts sourer or hotter as well; the recipe varies by counter.
story: The word is in dispute, and the dispute is on the record. Argia B. Collins Sr. used Mumbo for a barbecue sauce at his Chicago restaurant from at least 1950; Select Brands, his successor-in-interest, holds the registration and has challenged D.C. uses of the name as infringing.

Washington tells it the other way. Capital City Mumbo Sauce dates the sauce to a restaurant called Wings-n-Things in the late 1960s. Complicating both, John Young was serving Mumbo sauce on chicken wings at John Young's Wings 'n Things in Buffalo from the early 1960s, and Young himself credited a Washington restaurant for the sauce. Because Collins's mark runs back to the 1950s, it has been argued that the D.C. sauce is the Chicago sauce transplanted. After two years of proceedings the Trademark Trial and Appeal Board found that a D.C.-based company could not take the name from its Chicago founder.

The argument is not only legal. In 2018 D.C. Mayor Muriel Bowser called Mumbo Sauce "annoying" in a Facebook post and questioned whether it was "quintessential" D.C.; her spokesperson said the remarks were meant to liven Thanksgiving discussions. On 9 October 2023 McDonald's released a version as a limited-time dipping sauce, with a short documentary about the sauce's history alongside it.
how: Asked for by the container: 'mumbo on the side', or poured over the box so the fries under the wings take it too.
- kin → mumbo-sauce (sauce): The sauce the word names, with what goes in it.
- kin → dc-mumbo (style): The wing style built on it.
- kin → argia-b-collins (person): Used the name in Chicago from at least 1950; the registration runs through his successor.
- kin → john-young (person): Put Mumbo sauce on wings in Buffalo in the early 1960s and credited a Washington restaurant for it.
- kin → capital-city-mambo-sauce (place): Carries the D.C. account of where the sauce began.
- kin → mild-sauce-word (term): Chicago's word for a cousin condiment, and often compared to this one.
- kin → mumbo-fries (dish): The other thing the word gets poured on, usually in the same box.
sources: s:wp-mumbo-sauce — Mumbo sauce; s:wp-mild-sauce — Mild sauce; s:wp-buffalo-wing — Buffalo wing
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## naked (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/word/naked/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/term/naked.json
id: naked
aliases: naked wings · unbreaded
said: 'Naked or breaded?' — a question you hear where breading is the default, and almost never in Buffalo.
root: Old English nacod 'bare, unclothed' → Middle English naked; the menu sense is a metaphor, breading read as clothing · *Inference —* the word only exists because somewhere else is the default. A Buffalo bar has no use for it: its wings are unbreaded, so bare is the unmarked case and needs no name. Hooters, whose house style is hand-breaded, does need one, and prints it.
facets: letter=N · part_of_speech=adjective
region: The United States
what: Unbreaded. A wing fried in nothing but its own skin, no flour, no batter, no dredge. Hooters, which breads by hand as its original style, lists the alternative as Naked Wings and describes them: "Traditional style. No breading, but just as good. Order them with your favorite Hooters wing sauce or rub."
how: Say it before the sauce: naked, hot, ranch. Naked skin crisps and then goes soft under sauce fast, so naked wings are tossed later and carried out quicker than breaded ones — which is the argument for eating them at the bar rather than in a box.
- kin → naked-fry (fry): The method the word names — dry skin into hot oil, nothing between.
- kin → breaded-fry (fry): The thing it is defined against.
- kin → hooters (place): Prints the word on its menu because its own default is breaded.
- kin → rochester-breaded (style): Seventy miles from Buffalo and breading, which is what gives this word something to point at.
- kin → buffalo (style): Unbreaded by default, so the word is not needed there.
- kin → extra-crispy (term): The other instruction a counter takes about texture.
sources: s:web-hooters-wings-menu — Wings; s:wp-buffalo-wing — Buffalo wing; s:wp-hooters — Hooters
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## party wing (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/word/party-wing/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/term/party-wing.json
id: party-wing
aliases: party wings · wingettes and drumettes · split wings
said: Said by a package, not by a person. Nobody orders party wings in a bar.
root: party + wing; retail compound, on the pattern of party pack and party size, where party means quantity-for-sharing rather than any occasion · No dated first use found for this project. Newspaper and trade archives were not searched to exhaustion, and the phrase is a grocery coinage, so it may well predate anything indexed. Sanderson Farms prints it as 'Chicken Party Wings Flats & Drummettes' — the label carries both the marketing word and the two trade words at once.
facets: letter=P · part_of_speech=noun
region: The United States
what: A supermarket's name for wings already broken down: tips off, joint cut, drumettes and flats loose in one bag or tray. The work a bar's prep cook does, done at the plant. The word says nothing about seasoning and nothing about size — it says only that you will not be cutting anything.
how: Thaw, pat dry, cook. The pieces come mixed in whatever ratio the case gave, roughly one drumette per flat, which is why a home cook cannot order all flats and a chain sometimes can.
today: Sold fresh and frozen, plain and pre-seasoned, and the count drives January. Super Bowl week is the year's peak: the National Chicken Council put the 2026 game at 1.48 billion wings.
- kin → drumette (term): Half of what is in the bag.
- kin → flat (term): The other half, in about equal number.
- kin → wing-tip (term): Removed at the plant, which is the whole point of the product.
- kin → wing-cut (fry): The same two cuts, made by a machine before the bag was sealed.
- kin → super-bowl-sunday (event): The day these packs are bought for, in numbers a council counts.
- kin → air-fryer (fry): Where a lot of them now end up, bought split because the basket wants them split.
sources: s:web-openfoodfacts-party-wings — Chicken Party Wings Flats & Drummettes — Sanderson Farms; s:web-ncc-superbowl-lx — Americans to Eat 1.48 Billion Chicken Wings for Super Bowl LX; s:wp-buffalo-wing — Buffalo wing

## weck (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/word/weck/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/term/weck.json
id: weck
aliases: kummelweck · kümmelweck · kimmelweck
said: Rhymes with deck. 'Beef on weck', never 'beef on a weck'.
root: German Weck 'bread roll' (the word of the southwestern dialects — Palatinate, Saarland, Baden, Swabia; northern Germans say Brötchen) ← Old High German wecki, weggi 'wedge; wedge-shaped baked good' ← Proto-West Germanic *wagi ← Proto-Germanic *wagjaz 'wedge'. The full compound is kummelweck: German Kümmel 'caraway' (← Middle High German kümel, kumel ← Old High German kumil ← Proto-West Germanic *kumil 'caraway, cumin seed') + Weck. So the name means, exactly, caraway roll — and the bread is a wedge before it is a roll. · *Tradition holds —* a German baker named William Wahr, thought to have come from the Black Forest, made the kummelweck in Buffalo, possibly working from the Swabian Schwäbische Seele, a thin salt-and-caraway loaf left as a ceremonial offering for the dead; a Western New York butcher puts the sandwich's creation in the mid-19th century. The record calls the sandwich's origin not well established, and this project leaves it there.
facets: letter=W · part_of_speech=noun
region: Western New York
what: Half of a sandwich name that lost its other half. Weck is the kummelweck roll: kosher salt and caraway seeds baked onto the top, softer and fluffier than the German Kümmelbrötchen it descends from. Buffalo-area bakeries are the only commercial source for it. Beef on weck — rare roast beef, hand-carved thin, the top of the roll dipped in jus, horseradish spread to taste — is one of the three foods Buffalo is known for, with wings and sponge candy.
story: The roll is a German loan that stopped travelling. Weck is a dialect word from southwestern Germany, carried to a Great Lakes port by German bakers and then fixed to one sandwich in one region, where it stayed. *Inference —* that is why it reads as a Buffalo word rather than a German one: outside western New York nobody has a use for it, so nobody borrowed it further.

It reached the wing world sideways. Buffalo Wild Wings was started by former western New Yorkers and opened as "Buffalo Wild Wings and Weck", abbreviated BW3 — the third W was the weck. The company dropped the W in 1998, and some people still say BW3 anyway. The chain used to serve an updated version of the sandwich called the Thirty-Fifth Weck Sandwich.
how: Ordered beside the wings, not instead of them: a Buffalo table that has ordered wings for the room orders a beef on weck for whoever did not want sauce on their hands. A pub owner is said to have used the salty roll to sell more drinks, which is the same trade a wing night makes.
- kin → beef-on-weck (dish): The sandwich this word is the second half of.
- kin → buffalo-wild-wings (place): Opened as Buffalo Wild Wings and Weck, which is what the third W in BW3 stood for.
- kin → buffalo (style): The city's other famous plate, and the one wings share a table with.
- kin → wing (term): What gets ordered with it, by the room rather than the person.
- kin → the-pitcher (dish): The salt on the roll was said to be selling this, the way a wing special does.
sources: s:wp-beef-on-weck — Beef on weck; s:web-wiktionary-weck — Weck; s:web-wiktionary-kummel — Kümmel; s:wp-buffalo-wild-wings — Buffalo Wild Wings
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## wet and dry (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/word/wet-and-dry/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/term/wet-and-dry.json
id: wet-and-dry
aliases: lemon pepper wet · dry rub · wet
said: 'Lemon pepper. Wet.' Two words after the flavour, and the order changes.
root: wet + dry, plain antonyms recruited as a pair of menu terms: wet = finished in a liquid sauce, dry = finished in a powder · The pair reached a national audience through Atlanta. 'Lemon pepper wet' was invented at the American Deli in Atlanta; the second episode of the television series Atlanta put it in a character's hands from J.R. Crickets, which had no such item, and J.R. Crickets added it to the menu in 2017 in the show's honour. *Inference —* the phrase was counter shorthand long before the show; the show is only the first dated place this project can point at.
facets: letter=W · part_of_speech=phrase
region: Atlanta, The United States
what: A two-way choice about the finish, asked after you have picked a flavour. Dry means the cooked wing gets tossed in seasoning — powder on crust. Wet means it gets tossed in something liquid, so butter or sauce carries the same seasoning. Same flavour name, two different foods.
how: Order shape is flavour first, then the word: 'lemon pepper wet', 'hot lemon pepper dry'. Some Atlanta counters build wet by tossing in butter or buffalo sauce and then hitting the wings with dry seasoning anyway, which is a third thing with a two-word name. Dry travels better in a box; wet goes soft.
- kin → atlanta-lemon-pepper (style): The style this pair of words belongs to.
- kin → lemon-pepper-seasoning (sauce): The powder that 'dry' means.
- kin → lemon-pepper-wet (sauce): What 'wet' names when the flavour is lemon pepper.
- kin → american-deli (place): Where lemon pepper wet was invented, per the record.
- kin → jr-cricketts (place): Put the phrase on its menu in 2017 after a television episode sent people asking for it.
- kin → memphis-dry-rub (style): Dry as a whole style rather than an option.
- kin → the-toss (fry): The step both words describe: what goes in the bowl.
sources: s:wp-lemon-pepper-wings — Lemon pepper wings; s:wp-buffalo-wing — Buffalo wing
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## wing (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/word/wing/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/term/wing.json
id: wing
aliases: chicken wing · wings
said: An order is counted, not weighed: six, ten, twenty, fifty. 'A dozen' means twelve pieces, not twelve wings.
root: Old Norse vængr → Middle English weng, winge → English wing; the food sense is a straight transfer from the bird's limb · On a menu the word slid from the whole limb to the pieces it gets cut into, so one wing off the bird sells as two or three wings. *Inference —* the counting unit followed the knife, not the bird.
facets: letter=W · part_of_speech=noun
region: The United States
what: A chicken's wing, and the pieces it becomes. Off the bird it runs drumette, flat and tip; a kitchen cuts it at both joints and usually throws the tip into stock, so what a menu calls a wing is one of two pieces. Order twenty and twenty pieces arrive, roughly ten birds' worth of one wing each.
how: Say the number, then the sauce, then bone-in or boneless, then the dip. A counter that asks 'flats or drums?' is offering something most places will not.
- kin → drumette (term): The upper piece, the one that looks like a small drumstick.
- kin → flat (term): The middle piece, two bones and the most skin.
- kin → wing-tip (term): The pointed end, usually cut off and boiled for stock.
- kin → wing-cut (fry): Where the knife goes, and why a wing sells as two.
- kin → party-wing (term): What a grocery calls the drumette and the flat when it sells them already split.
- kin → boneless (term): Sold under this word, cut from the breast, and argued about in court.
sources: s:wp-buffalo-wing — Buffalo wing; s:wp-chicken-wing — Chicken wing
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## wing night (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/word/wing-night/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/term/wing-night.json
id: wing-night
aliases: Wing Wednesday · wing special · 25-cent wings
said: Named after the night, not the wing: Wing Wednesday, Thirsty Thursday with wings attached.
root: wing + night, on the pattern of ladies' night, trivia night, open-mic night — a weekday plus the thing that fills it · Alliteration decides the branding: Wing Wednesday is the name that repeats, because the W's match. *Inference —* the alliteration explains the name, not the practice; the practice sits on whichever night the bar is otherwise empty.
facets: letter=W · part_of_speech=noun
region: The United States
what: A weekly price special on wings, usually sold by the piece and usually paired with a drink minimum. The deal is the draw; the pitcher is the margin.
how: Which night? No single one owns it. Buffalo Wing Guide, which keeps a running list of western New York specials, files them under Monday through Sunday plus Every Day — every weekday carries some. A bar-marketing write-up describes the pull the other way round, saying wing night is what "makes a bar busy on Monday or Tuesday night". So the answer is that wing night lands where the week is slow, and the name it gets depends on which letter it can rhyme with.
today: Buffalo Wing Guide's 2026 list warns that "all wing specials and pricing are subject to change. Please call bar or restaurant to verify accuracy" — which is the state of every posted wing price after three years of wing costs moving.
- kin → the-pitcher (dish): What the special is really selling; the wings are priced to move it.
- kin → wing-basket (dish): The portion a wing night is counted in.
- kin → the-price-of-a-wing (story): Why a per-piece special is a harder promise some years than others.
- kin → buffalo-wild-wings (place): Ran the weekly special at national scale and made the day part of the brand.
- kin → super-bowl-sunday (event): The one wing night nobody has to advertise.
sources: s:web-buffalo-wing-guide-specials — Buffalo/WNY Daily Chicken Wing Specials & Deals; s:web-gourmet-marketing-wing-night — What is Your Bar's Wing Night? Using Food for Bar Marketing; s:wp-buffalo-wild-wings — Buffalo Wild Wings

## wing tip (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/word/wing-tip/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/term/wing-tip.json
id: wing-tip
aliases: tip · wingtip · third segment
root: wing + tip, a plain compound; the piece also answers to flapper and to pointer, and all three names describe the same shape from a different angle · Wikipedia's Buffalo wing article names the three segments "drumette, flat, and flapper or pointer"; its poultry article gives "the wing tip (also called the 'flapper')". *Inference —* tip is what a butcher calls it, flapper what a cook calls it, pointer what a diner calls it when handed one.
facets: letter=W · part_of_speech=noun
region: The United States
what: Third segment, the pointed end. Skin, cartilage, two slivers of bone, almost no meat. Usually cut off before the wing reaches a fryer and boiled into stock instead, though some restaurants serve it still joined to the flat.
how: Where it survives on the plate, it is eaten whole — crust, cartilage and all — or left in the bone bowl. Where it does not, it goes into a stockpot: collagen from the joints is what makes chicken stock set, so the least saleable piece of the wing is the one worth most to a kitchen that makes its own.
- kin → flapper (term): The same piece under the name a kitchen uses for it.
- kin → wing (term): The third of its three segments, and the one a menu usually leaves out of the count.
- kin → flat (term): What it is attached to, and what it gets cut away from.
- kin → wing-cut (fry): The cut that removes it, the first of the two.
- kin → party-wing (term): A pack defined partly by this piece's absence.
sources: s:wp-buffalo-wing — Buffalo wing; s:wp-chicken-as-food — Chicken as food; s:wp-poultry — Poultry
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## Buffalo murals (art)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/art/buffalo-murals/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/art/buffalo-murals.json
id: buffalo-murals
aliases: Buffalo wall art · Buffalo public art
facets: kind=mural · state=NY
region: Western New York
what: Buffalo paints its own story on its walls, and the wing is part of what gets painted. The city's public art runs from commissioned murals on Main Street and Hertel Avenue to neighbourhood walls raised by crowdfunding, and at least one of them exists to settle an argument: in November 2021 a mural went up at Jefferson and Carlton, on the corner where John Young's Wings 'n Things stood, recreating the artwork that had hung inside his shop. The murals are copyrighted by the people who painted them, and one Buffalo muralist has invoiced businesses for using images of his wall, which is why this page names walls and does not reproduce them.
- kin → the-origin-fight (story): One of these walls is a move in it: Young's claim, marked on the corner where his shop stood.
- kin → john-young (person): The mural at Jefferson and Carlton recreates the artwork from inside his Wings 'n Things.
- kin → buffalo (style): The style the city paints on its own walls alongside the bison and the grain elevators.
- kin → city-of-buffalo (org): Proclaimed a Chicken Wing Day in 1977; the walls are where the same civic claim now gets made.
- kin → buffalo-wing-trail (org): Visit Buffalo lists the murals the way it lists the wing shops, as a promoted route.
- kin → free-to-use (story): Why this site points at walls and does not print them: the paint is somebody's copyright.
- kin → wing-festival-posters (art): The same imagery with a date on it, printed instead of painted.
- kin → chicken-shack-signs (art): The smaller, working version of the same wall.

## Chicken shack signs (art)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/art/chicken-shack-signs/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/art/chicken-shack-signs.json
id: chicken-shack-signs
aliases: fried chicken signs · wing counter signage
facets: kind=sign
region: The United States, Chicago, Washington, D.C., The American South, Nashville
what: The sign over a wing or fried-chicken counter is a working document. It has to be readable from a car at thirty miles an hour, name the shop, say CHICKEN, and usually price something. It comes in two families that overlap: brush-lettered paint, on plywood, on stucco, on the window glass itself; and the internally lit plastic box with changeable letters underneath. The cartoon bird is optional and very common. Almost none of it is signed, almost all of it is made locally, and it is replaced rather than restored, which is why the record of it is photographic.
- kin → harolds-chicken-shack (place): A chain whose sign is its own argument, repeated across the South Side of Chicago.
- kin → princes-hot-chicken-shack (place): The Nashville counter whose signage carries the heat scale as the menu's main axis.
- kin → yums-carry-out (place): A Washington carryout of the kind whose menu board, not its facade, is the real sign.
- kin → uncle-remus-saucy-fried-chicken (place): Chicago signage where the sauce gets the biggest letters on the panel.
- kin → wing-cafe (place): An Atlanta counter of the sort this genre is written for.
- kin → neon-chicken (art): The lit version of the same bird, in glass tube instead of paint.
- kin → rooster-weathervanes (art): The oldest form of the same idea: a bird put up as a mark for the place beneath it.
- kin → hot-sauce-labels (art): The same trade of promising heat in a glance, at bottle scale instead of building scale.
- kin → buffalo-murals (art): What happens when the sign gets big enough to become the wall.

## Hot sauce labels (art)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/art/hot-sauce-labels/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/buffalo-wings/api/art/hot-sauce-labels.json
id: hot-sauce-labels
aliases: hot sauce bottle art · pepper sauce labels
facets: kind=print
region: The United States
what: A hot sauce label sells one thing before it sells any other: how much it will hurt. The genre has a settled vocabulary — devils, flames, skulls, warning text set like a hazard placard, a name that is a dare, and often a number. Beneath the artwork the same panel carries what federal law requires, including an ingredient list in descending order by weight, which is why this site can read a bottle's ingredient rank off a photograph of its back. The front is a promise. The back is a fact.
- kin → franks-redhot (sauce): The cayenne sauce the Buffalo bowl is built on; its 1965 label survives as a freely licensed image.
- kin → crystal-hot-sauce (sauce): The other bottle that turns up in a Buffalo bowl, with a label that has barely moved.
- kin → buffalo-sauce (sauce): What most of these bottles end up inside, once butter is melted into them.
- kin → mango-habanero (sauce): A flavour that lives mostly as a label and a menu line rather than as a bottle.
- kin → atomic (term): The heat word that gets printed largest, and that this site records verbatim as the maker's claim.
- kin → chicken-shack-signs (art): The same promise at building scale: say the heat before you say the name.
- kin → neon-chicken (art): Shares the flame vocabulary, lit instead of printed.
- kin → free-to-use (story): Why the back panel matters here: label data is public, label artwork is not.
